World.title: French centrists struggle to find unity candidate as extremes surge in polls
World.content:
Without a strong candidate from the center, their fear is that the election will slide inexorably into a clash between two anti-NATO euroskeptics who frighten financial markets: Le Pen on the far right and Jean-Luc Mélenchon on the far left.

The presidential election goes to a runoff if no one secures more than 50 percent of the vote. Le Pen appears all but certain to nab one of those spots given her polling numbers, but Mélenchon’s strong start to the campaign means he could well score ahead of Philippe and secure a spot in the second round.

Playing the long game

Despite the pressure to find a real challenger to Le Pen, the squabbling centrists hardly appear in a hurry to resolve their differences.

Attal, who trails Philippe in the polls, has in recent days tried to frame Philippe as out of touch. Asked about the remarks, Philippe responded that candidates sharing the center ground should direct their attacks against the extremes.

Attal’s campaign director Franck Riester told a small group of reporters Tuesday he doesn’t expect a resolution before February. Philippe said in an interview Tuesday he didn’t think a single candidate would emerge before next year.

Instead, Wednesday’s lunch — the latest in a series of regular parleys among the centrists — will be a moment to “air grievances,” according to Riester.

World.title: Merz’s SPD partners rebel after far-right rout
World.content:
That’s not the conclusion his center-left coalition partners have drawn: They argue the problem isn’t one of messaging but of substance.

“The path the federal government has taken with its reform plans has caused particular uncertainty,” Rasha Nasr, an SPD lawmaker in the Bundestag, told POLITICO’s Berlin Playbook Podcast. “It’s very important now that, unlike others in the coalition, we don’t just push this through. The people of Saxony-Anhalt have told us very clearly: ‘This far and no further,’” she added.

Merz has staked his chancellorship on tackling economic and welfare reforms that previous governments deemed too politically difficult, even branding himself the “reform chancellor.” His agenda includes raising the retirement age to shore up the pension system, cutting some health-insurance benefits to curb rising premiums and making it harder for workers to take sick leave in an effort to boost growth.

SPD general secretary Tim Klüssendorf, who has said there are reform measures that need to be addressed, at a press conference after an SPD leadership meeting in Berlin in March 2026. | John Macdougall/AFP via Getty Images

Until now, the SPD under the leadership of Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil has advanced the reform drive, portraying itself as willing to undertake the tough choices needed to restore Germany’s economy while fighting inside the coalition to resist conservative excesses.

But given Merz’s growing troubles — and rising questions about the durability of the coalition government — the party’s calculus appears to have changed. The shift also comes ahead of two additional state elections on Sept. 20 in which the SPD is hoping to score at least one much-needed win.

Klingbeil signaled a course change already on the night of the Saxony-Anhalt election. The result provides “a reason to reflect on policies here in Berlin and on the federal government’s reform agenda,” Klingbeil told public broadcaster ZDF as votes were still being counted. “And rest assured, that’s exactly what we’ll do.”

World.title: Far right’s rise in rapidly re-arming Germany gives Poland cause for concern
World.content:
“But we remember all too well where a rearmed Germany in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party can lead — and that is exactly what the AfD represents,” he added.

For Warsaw, the prospect of a far-right party gaining power in a heavily militarized Germany hits a deep historical nerve.

Parts of present-day Poland were occupied by Imperial Germany during World War I, and Nazi Germany invaded Poland in 1939, triggering World War II in Europe and subjecting the country to a brutal occupation.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk struck a similarly stark note after the Saxony-Anhalt vote, saying “only idiots or traitors” in Poland could celebrate the AfD’s triumph.

Merz pledged at the beginning of his term in 2025 to turn the Bundeswehr into “the strongest conventional army in Europe.” Germany also spent $114 billion on its military last year — almost as much as France and Poland combined — and Berlin is planning further increases.

As part of that wider rearmament drive, Germany is also planning for nearly €12 billion in long-range weapons capable of striking military targets hundreds or thousands of kilometers away, part of Berlin’s effort to deter Russia in the war against Ukraine.

World.title: The Draghi plan at 2: Competitiveness crusade runs into Europe’s old politics
World.content:
But political appetite for more eurobonds is low. Frugal nations are reluctant to keep raising EU debt, which fuels angry rhetoric from populist parties. A bold proposal from Spain for the Commission to borrow an additional €850 billion per year on behalf of EU countries landed on deaf ears among EU countries in the Council.

In its budget proposal, the Commission included several more realistic ideas to continue issuing joint debt over the coming seven years. While these proposals have faced strong opposition from frugal Northern countries, it remains unclear whether they will survive the endgame of the budget negotiations.

Draghi-ometer rating:

Automotive

The automotive sector is a shining example of the Commission implementing Draghi’s recommendations — but that doesn’t seem to have mattered when it comes to maintaining automotive jobs in Europe. At the start of this month, Volkswagen’s board unanimously approved a cost-cutting plan that will ax 100,000 jobs, or nearly 16 percent of its workforce, and shutter up to four factories on German soil. Suppliers aren’t doing much better.

Draghi also recommended giving automakers flexibility on emissions targets. The Commission has done away with a ban on combustion engines after 2035 and put forward a “technologically neutral” proposal for the emissions targets that automakers must reach. (It allows all powertrains past 2035, but requires carmakers to offset the extra emissions with investments in alternative fuels and green steel.) The industry and conservative-leaning parties say that’s not enough, and are negotiating a further weakening of the standards.

Recognizing the competitive threat from Chinese automakers, Draghi pushed for more investments to help the sector catch up on software and autonomous driving. Robotaxis are starting to pop up in European cities — but it’s American or Chinese tech that is powering them. A group of member states is calling on the Commission to move faster to push autonomous driving from pilot projects to full-scale deployment.

World.title: Majorité numérique : Macron tente le tout pour le tout pour imposer sa vision en Europe
World.content:
En coulisses, les équipes du Premier ministre, missionnées pour rédiger un nouveau projet de loi et le faire adopter avant le printemps, sont suspendues aux déclarations à venir de la présidente de la Commission. “En fonction de ce que dira Ursula Von der Leyen, le texte pourrait être réorienté pour s’aligner à la vision européenne”, glissent à POLITICO deux sources parlementaires.

“Cela paraît désormais difficile de revenir à un texte proposant spécifiquement une interdiction nationale. Pour en avoir discuté avec Matignon, ce qui est envisageable, par contre, c’est une pré-transposition du futur texte européen annoncé, à la fois respectueux du droit constitutionnel et conventionnel”, abonde la sénatrice centriste et ex-rapporteure de la loi Miller, Catherine Morin-Desailly (UC).

Impasse française

D’autant que la nouvelle rédaction du texte français se heurte déjà à une série de difficultés. Principal casse-tête — et pas des moindres : rendre l’interdiction conforme à la Constitution française et au droit européen.

Dans son avis, rendu le 14 août, le Conseil constitutionnel a reconnu la nécessité de limiter l’accès aux plateformes pour “l’intérêt supérieur de l’enfant”. Il a toutefois demandé au législateur français de mieux définir le périmètre de cette interdiction. En d’autres termes : il lui faut préciser quels types de fonctionnalités — et par conséquent quels réseaux sociaux — sont interdits aux mineurs.

Un pouvoir de régulation qui revient normalement à la Commission européenne, en vertu du règlement sur les services numériques (DSA). “Le gouvernement peut toujours proposer un texte conforme aux attentes du Conseil constitutionnel, quitte à négocier avec l’Union européenne pour avoir marché sur les plates-bandes du droit communautaire”, souligne, optimiste, le sénateur David Ros (PS), qui a participé à la commission mixte paritaire sur la loi Miller.

Plusieurs pistes de rédaction viennent d’ailleurs d’être envoyées pour avis au Conseil d’Etat, révèle à POLITICO un conseiller parlementaire du Premier ministre. Lui-même doute toutefois de “l’existence d’un trou de souris entre le Conseil constitutionnel et le droit européen”.

World.title: Delay tactic or genuine solution? Carbon capture under fire again as EU invests in ‘unproven’ technology
World.content:
CO2 emitted by a fertiliser factory in the Netherlands will be stored underneath the seabed in Norway, in what the owners are calling the “largest commercial carbon capture and storage (CCS) project in Europe”.

 

At an opening ceremony this week, the ammonia and fertiliser plant announced that it will capture 800,000 tonnes of CO2 a year then liquefy it to be sent by ship to Norway.

Having funded the project, the European Commission was keen to promote its investment – with the Commissioner for Climate, Net Zero and Clean Growth attending the inauguration alongside the Prime Ministers of both countries.

While the Commission says the Sluiskil plant, run by Norwegian chemical company Yara, is a “strategic investment”, opponents say it is “risking billions in taxpayers’ money to fund a dangerous distraction that delays climate action”.

As one of the most divisive topics in climate action, we look into the facts about carbon capture and how the EU came to be funding this experimental technology.

What is carbon capture and storage?

Carbon capture and storage (CCS) refers to technologies designed to prevent CO2 from entering the atmosphere in the first place and/or to remove it after it has been emitted.

As is done at the Sluiskil plant, most projects use a liquid to chemically remove the CO2 emitted from the production process, where it is then compressed into a liquid-like state and transported typically through a pipeline to a storage site. At that point, it’s either stored deep underground or is transformed into things like building materials or synthetic fuel. In the case of the latter, this technology is referred to as CCUS, where the ‘U’ stands for utilisation.

As of February 2026, there were 75 operational CCS projects around the world, according to climate change publication Carbon Brief. Almost all of them are at fossil-fuel extraction and processing sites, according to the IEA’s database. Together, these projects capture 62.5 million tonnes of CO2 (MtCO2) each year. This is equivalent to 0.2 per cent of total global emissions in 2025.

While Yara’s chief executive, Svein Tore Holsether, said in a statement, “The carbon capture facility in Sluiskil proves that large-scale industrial decarbonisation is possible today”, the cumulative emissions saved are a very, very tiny drop in the ocean.

US non-profit the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) has conducted in-depth research into CCS. Their Energy Finance Analyst, Andrew Reid, says: “Despite the political and financial support that has been pointed to CCS over the past three to four years, it remains technically uncertain, very high cost, and reliant upon huge subsidies to move from feasibility to construction and operation.”

CCS: To help the fossil fuel industry to extract and sell more oil and gas

To understand its uses, it’s important to understand where carbon technology originates from. According to Carbon Brief, it “was originally rolled out at US and Canadian oil wells in the early 1970s as a way to achieve “enhanced oil recovery”. This involves injecting captured CO2 into depleted wells – a process that stores the gas, but also helps to extract more oil.” This is by far the most significant use for carbon capture worldwide, with three-quarters of it used for this purpose.

This means that “the majority of CO2 that is both captured and used today helps the fossil-fuel industry to extract and sell more oil and gas,” according to Carbon Brief.

How did the EU end up funding carbon capture and storage?

One of the arguments against CCS, which campaigners have been making for years, is that it is a way for polluters to keep polluting, rather than emitting less of the gases which are heating up the planet at alarming rates.

“All capture and storage projects suffer from the same problem: they distract attention and resources from cutting emissions at source and give polluting industries like fertiliser production a pass to keep on polluting,” says Rachel Kennerley, Senior International Carbon Capture Campaigner at the Center for International Environmental Law (CIEL).

Belén Balanyá, researcher and campaigner at Corporate Europe Observatory (CEO), has been tracking the lobbying efforts of the fossil fuel industry for 25 years. She has recently focussed on lobbying by the CCS industry. The outcomes of annual COP climate talks are known to be influenced by lobbyists representing industry. Balanyá found that around 500 CCS lobbyists were at COP29 in 2024. A year earlier, at COP28, CCS proponents (largely tied to fossil fuel industries) scored a significant win with the endorsement of “abatement and removal technologies” in the agreement.

Referring to fossil fuel industries, Balanyá says, “You look at what’s on the agenda and it’s always escape hatches to stay in business,” she tells Euronews Green. “It’s where they move when they’ve been forced to – when there’s more knowledge and more acceptance about climate change and their role and that they have to decarbonise.”

CCS being endorsed in a COP agreement may have contributed to its legitimacy in political circles within the EU. The CCUS Forum (now the Industrial Carbon Management (ICM) Forum), set up by the European Commission in 2021, is an annual event with working groups that feed directly into EU policymaking. CEO found that every group has been co-chaired by the fossil fuel industry or associated organisations.

A newly released report from the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) details the risks of overshooting 1.5°C of warming and how we can limit them. It assessed what it called Carbon Dioxide Removal and found that many issues remain with the technology, such as whether it can scale sustainably (due to costs, land and energy use), whether it would actually keep CO2 out of the atmosphere permanently and who’s responsible for regulation and leaks.

CCS: Good or bad?

Wherever commentators stand on CCS, there is some agreement that for some industries, the technology can be useful. Yara’s project targets emissions from ammonia production which “provides a relatively concentrated CO2 stream, making this one of the more straightforward industrial applications of carbon capture rather than an example of the very hardest emissions to abate,” according to Domien Vangenechten, Programme Lead in Clean Economy at E3G.

“The lesson should therefore not be that Europe needs CCS everywhere, but that we should pragmatically deploy it where it can cut substantial emissions today.”

World.title: Getting those steps in does reduce the risk of early death. But it is also the pace that matters
World.content:
It is both: the number of steps and the walking pace that count against all-cause and cardiovascular disease mortality, a new study published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine found. This means different combinations of the number of daily steps and walking pace can be associated with a lower risk of early death.

 

“Our findings inform flexible step-based pathways to lower mortality risk for middle-aged and older adults, particularly those with barriers to increasing daily step counts or stepping intensity,” researchers said, highlighting that most of the studies did not look at the association of different combinations of daily step counts and stepping intensity with mortality risk.

The researchers analysed activity-tracker data from middle-aged participants in the UK Biobank, who wore a device for seven days between 2013 and 2015.

After looking at wearable device data from 64,743 participants aged 40 to 69 years who took from less than 5,000 to over 10,000 steps per day at different paces researchers found that taking between 7,500 to 10,000 steps per day showed the biggest reduction in early death irresponsible of the pace.

In the meantime, a brisker pace for at least 30 minutes every day – taking 90 steps per minute – was also associated with a lower risk of death from any cause, irrespective of how many steps were taken.

“Regardless of total daily step counts, maintaining higher walking cadence maybe a promising target for preventing premature mortality,” researchers said.

For those living a sedentary lifestyle with less than 5,000 steps per day, “increasing stepping pace may substantially lower all-cause and cardiovascular disease mortality risk,” researchers said. In the meantime, those who prefer to walk slower can benefit from taking more steps instead.

World.title: Why a 50% harvest collapse won't leave shelves short of Champagne
World.content:
France’s Champagne region is facing an extraordinary harvest collapse. Yet consumers should not expect the number of bottles reaching shops to halve — at least not yet.

 

The reason is that this year’s harvest does not determine how many bottles can be sold immediately. Champagne takes several years to make, and producers hold substantial stocks and reserve wines from earlier harvests to help maintain supply when a crop is poor.

And across France, wine production is expected to reflect a very poor harvest this year. According to preliminary estimates from Agreste, the French Agriculture Ministry’s statistics office, overall wine production is to fall to 3.39 billion litres in 2026.

That would be 6% less than in 2025 and 28% below the 4.72 billion litres produced in 2023.

If confirmed, it would also be France’s smallest wine crop since 1957, when output stood at 3.25 billion litres, according to the International Organisation of Vine and Wine.

The decline partly reflects a 2.5% reduction in the area of French vineyards in production. But drought and repeated heatwaves have had the greater effect by reducing the amount of wine produced from each hectare.

“Evidence strongly suggests that heat and drought, through lower yields per hectare, are the dominant explanation for this year’s exceptionally low harvest,” Jean-Marie Cardebat, Professor at Bordeaux University and affiliated to INSEEC Business School, told Euronews Business.

The regional figures support this. Some of the steepest falls are in areas where relatively few vineyards have been removed.

Bordeaux and Languedoc-Roussillon, where large areas of vines have been uprooted, are expected to produce 10% and 5% more wine respectively than in 2025, although both remain below their recent averages.

Why has Champagne been hit so badly?

Wine production from this year’s harvest in the Champagne region is forecast to fall by 48%, from 2.57 million hectolitres in 2025 to 1.34 million this year.

For wine carrying the Champagne protected designation, the fall is slightly steeper. Output is expected to drop by 49% to 1.24 million hectolitres, 47% below the five-year average.

However, these figures refer to wine made from grapes harvested this year. Not the number of bottles of Champagne to be sold.

After Champagne, the worst affected regions are Jura, where production is forecast to fall by 36%, and Bourgogne-Beaujolais, where it is expected to decline by 33%. Losses for Burgundy Pinot Noir exceed 50%, according to Agreste.

In Champagne, harvesting began in mid-August and the grapes reached exceptional ripeness. But frost in the Aisne, hail and drought since March severely reduced the crop. The average weight of grape bunches fell to its lowest level in 20 years.

Will fewer bottles of Champagne be sold?

The crop damage is severe, particularly for individual growers. But a 49% fall in wine produced from this year’s grapes does not mean the supply of finished Champagne will immediately fall by the same amount.

Before the full scale of the damage was clear, the industry had set the amount of the 2026 harvest that could be sold at 8,800 kilograms of grapes per hectare. That was only around 2% below the 9,000 kg/ha limit set in 2025 and reflected weaker demand and the need to manage stocks.

The actual harvest is now expected to average no more than around 7,000 kg/ha, according to the Syndicat Général des Vignerons de la Champagne. That would be the lowest level since the 1980s.

Growers who fail to reach the permitted level cannot make up the missing grapes. Champagne houses, however, can soften the impact by drawing on wines held in reserve.

“Champagne has lost roughly half of a normal harvest, but this will not translate into an immediate 50% fall in sales because producers can draw on extensive stocks and reserve wines,” Professor Cardebat said.

He called the production loss “extremely significant”, adding that the lost production was “equivalent to approximately 140 million 75-centilitre bottles”.

This represents about €2.7bn in potential commercial value, according to the professor, based on the average turnover generated per bottle shipped in 2025.

However, he stressed that this was not an estimate of immediate revenue losses because producers can draw on substantial stocks and reserve wines.

Professor Cardebat described the situation as “a major production and productivity shock”, adding that the longer-term risk would arise if very small harvests became recurrent.

“Then stocks would decline, costs would rise, and Champagne could eventually become less able to supply all its markets,” Professor Cardebat told Euronews Business.

A smaller harvest is not entirely bad news - yet

Overall, the smaller harvest is not expected to have an immediate significant impact on wine producers’ revenue.

According to Professor Cardebat, the greater economic concern is the accumulation of poor harvests. “This will be the third consecutive very small French harvest,” he said, adding that many producers were already financially fragile because demand had weakened while the costs of energy, labour, machinery and financing had risen.

Lower yields also mean that producers must spread many of their costs across fewer bottles, pushing up the cost of each one and squeezing profits. Even if stocks delay the impact on revenue, another poor harvest could further weaken cash flow and producers’ ability to invest.

Producers also risk losing shelf space if they cannot supply retailers consistently. If Champagne shortages persisted, competitors such as Prosecco and Crémant could gain ground among shops and consumers.

However, France has also been struggling with excess supplies of some wines, particularly red wine, as consumption declines. A temporarily smaller harvest can help reduce stocks and bring supply closer to demand without permanently removing more vineyards.

According to Professor Cardebat, this creates a paradox: "Economically, lower productivity is bad for producers, but lower aggregate supply can help rebalance a market suffering from excess production".

He also added that the regions suffering the largest shock from bad weather conditions this year are not those facing the greatest structural financial risk. Champagne benefits from a powerful global brand, relatively high margins and its reserve system.

According to Professor Cardebat, the bigger structural risks were in Bordeaux, the South-West and parts of Languedoc-Roussillon, where producers have faced weak demand, low prices and vineyard removals. Those relying heavily on red wine are generally more exposed than producers of white or sparkling wine.

The Champagne harvest is therefore the most dramatic part of France’s 2026 wine story, but not necessarily its greatest financial crisis. Its reserves should keep bottles moving for now. The test will come if harvests of this size stop being exceptional.

World.title: Privacy screens and sculpted headrests: What's new in premium economy?
World.content:
If you, like me, prefer to maximise your travel budget for on-ground experiences rather than flight fares, but are on the taller side and do like a bit of extra leg room (plus an excuse to splurge just a little bit), premium economy can be a happy medium between a standard economy fare and business or first class.

 

And the perks of premium economy travel doesn’t start and end in the sky. Think more generous baggage allowances (at least compared to economy), speedier check-in and not having to wait as long to board.

Now it seems airlines are betting that more passengers are willing to pay slightly more for this middle ground, with a new wave of offerings set to make the premium economy cabin more private, spacious and, perhaps, more luxurious.

From privacy screens and sculpted headrests to sleep pods and cozy slippers, here’s what’s on the horizon for premium economy class passengers.

Emirates’ privacy screens

This month, Emirates unveiled what it says is the “world’s first electric premium economy seat with full-height privacy screen”.

The Dubai-based airline's latest offering will be rolled out on its Airbus A350 aircraft, with a 2-3-2 configuration across 28 seats.

Passengers will be able to raise and lower the divider using the seat controls. They can also adjust their seating position with the control unit.

And for those who like to keep their phone charged in the sky, Emirates is also introducing wireless charging facilities to its premium economy cabins.

Emirates’ premium economy seats will have an adjustable privacy screen The Emirates Group

American adds more premium economy seats

Also in September, American Airlines launched its first retrofitted Boeing 777-300ER into commercial service, featuring 44 premium economy seats and being deployed on some of the carrier’s long-haul routes.

The redesigned seats come with sculpted headrests, adjusted calf and foot rests, wireless charging and both USB-C and AC power.

American, which has recently announced a number of new European flights for next summer, also rolled out 30 extra leg room seats as part of its Main Cabin Extra offering. Here, passengers can watch hundreds of titles as part of its inflight entertainment and enjoy free high-speed wifi if they are an AAdvantage member.

Lufthansa’s culinary upgrades and cozy slippers

As part of its “Future Onboard Experiences” initiative, stylised as FOX, Lufthansa introduced revamped in-flight offerings in May, coinciding with the 100th anniversary since it was founded.

Lufthansa’s upgrade to the premium economy cabin included revamped dining options, such as a business class-level appetizer offering and three hot main meals to choose from, with a side of toasty bread. The meal is rounded off with pastries or a slice of cake.

For extra comfort, the premium economy cabin also provides passengers with “cozy” slippers.

TAP Air Portugal introduces premium economy cabin

In June, TAP Air Portugal launched its premium economy offering on select fleets.

Branded “Economy Prime”, the cabin class is only available on the carrier’s long-haul flights. There are 12 seats in total, with four seats per row, however, passengers will always have the seat next to them left empty.

When it comes to in-flight dining, there’s a choice of two hot dishes, followed by a snack served before reaching the destination.

Economy Prime travellers are also given an amenities kit and can enjoy a selection of films and series on the carrier’s 13-inch HD screens.

On ground, passengers benefit from premium check-in, fast track, premium boarding and priority baggage, as well as an allowance of one 10kg cabin bag and two 23kg checked bags.

Divided into two fare options, Prime and Top Prime, the latter adds flexibility, giving passengers the option to change or refund their ticket, at no added cost.

Wizz Air's unique spin on premium economy

Hungarian low-cost carrier Wizz Air launched “Wizz Class” earlier this year. The premium add-on gives passengers a seat in the first row, with a choice of window or aisle, while the middle seat is kept empty for extra space.

Other perks include extra leg room seats, priority boarding, two items of cabin baggage, plus a snack and soft drink onboard.

The service is available for purchase on selected flights to and from Budapest, Bucharest Otopeni, London Luton, London Gatwick, Rome Fiumicino, and Warsaw.

Air New Zealand's new Skynest sleep pods will launch on select flights from December Air New Zealand

Air New Zealand’s world-first sleep pods

Air New Zealand is set to give passengers a chance to lie down mid-air with its Skynest sleep pods, which it says would be a world first.

Skynest will make its debut on the carrier’s ultra long-haul flights between New York and Auckland starting in late December, where up to six premium (and standard) economy travellers at a time can swap their seat for a bed.

Passengers can book a four-hour session to “recharge in comfort” in their own private pod, which comes with a privacy curtain, ambient lighting, USB charging outlets and personal stowage.

The sessions are priced from NZ$495 (€250.45), which includes an appropriately named “Nestcessities” kit containing earplugs and an eye mask, because if you’re willing to pay extra to sleep at 35,000 feet above sea level, you may as well make yourself as comfortable as possible.

World.title: UK airports face more disruption after air traffic control glitch with 177 flights axed
World.content:
UK travellers face more misery on Wednesday with more than 150 flights scrapped across the country, as Britain's air traffic control service scrambled to recover from a technical glitch that sparked chaos.

 

Aircraft tracking website FlightRadar24 said 177 flights scheduled for Wednesday had already been axed, following 1,300 cancellations to and from UK airports on Tuesday.

Nearly all the flights cancelled on Wednesday were at Britain's busiest airport Heathrow in London, FlightRadar24 wrote on X.

The National Air Traffic Services (NATS) said late on Tuesday it was still working to resolve disruption following a "system issue."

"Work is continuing to assist airlines and airports recover from today's disruption," NATS posted on X.

"This has been a very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover."

Heathrow said late on Tuesday that departures had resumed, after the "technical issue" forced the airport to suspend arrivals the same day.

But it warned that "disruption is expected to continue," asking passengers in an X post to check with their airline before travelling to the airport.

NATS said earlier it had "resolved" the glitch that caused the disruption and was "working as hard as possible to clear the backlog of flights."

"We know this is hugely frustrating and apologise unreservedly," the organisation wrote on X.

Tuesday's chaos follow a technical glitch in July last year that saw scores of flights to and from the UK cancelled, prompting anger from airline chiefs.

Britain saw its worst air systems failure in years in 2023, with more than 700,000 passengers affected after hundreds of flights were delayed or cancelled.

'Absolute nightmare'

Heathrow in west London and Gatwick to the south of the UK capital confirmed they were affected.

"It's just an absolute nightmare down there," healthcare worker Josie Donoghue said of Gatwick after leaving the airport, having had to disembark her flight to Ireland after three hours stuck on the runway.

"Getting through that airport was like trying to get out of Alcatraz," she told the UK's domestic Press Association news agency.

Liverpool, Birmingham and Edinburgh airports were also affected, while Dublin Airport in Ireland said it had cancelled dozens of flights.

British Airways said it was forced to cancel or divert more than 100 flights, impacting tens of thousands of its customers.

Heathrow Airport in London seen from the air, 6 October, 2025 AP Photo

Irish budget carrier Ryanair said more than 65,000 of its passengers had been disrupted and it had cancelled more than 50 flights.

Arsenal, due to play Napoli in the Champions League in the southern Italian city on Wednesday, were forced to cancel a news conference ahead of the match after the team's flight was delayed.

British Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said on X she was "seeking assurances that lessons will be learned and systems that support aviation are up to the job."

But Ryanair COO Neal McMahon repeated his calls for NATS chief executive Martin Rolfe to be fired, accusing him of having again "failed UK travellers."

"Enough is enough, it's time for the UK government to intervene...and put somebody in charge who can do the job."

World.title: Croatia on wheels: the great Adriatic motorhome route
World.content:
Travelling by motorhome lets you move at the pace of the landscape and stop in places that would probably never make it onto a conventional itinerary. We set off from Rovinj, in the north of the Istrian peninsula, heading for Dubrovnik at the southernmost tip of the country. Along the way you pass a succession of historic towns, national parks, fishing villages, fortresses and islands, with the Adriatic as a constant backdrop.

 

But travelling Croatia on four wheels is not always straightforward. The coastal road is, in places, narrow and winding. And you cannot park the motorhome just anywhere: you have to rely on campsites and authorised areas, which are sometimes a long way from the historic centres and, on occasions, charge eye-watering prices.

In high season, especially in July and August, the problem only gets worse. That is why spring, early summer or autumn can be a better time to set off on this route.

Istria, Croatia's most Italian side

The journey begins in Rovinj, one of Istria's must-visit towns. Its historic centre of narrow, cobbled streets stands on what was once an island and is dominated by the church of St Euphemia. Colourful facades, the harbour and the small islands scattered just off the coast make the town one of the most recognisable sights on the Croatian Adriatic.

Further south lies Pula, at the southern tip of Istria. The city combines crystal-clear waters with one of Croatia's greatest Roman legacies. Pula Arena, built in the first century AD, is one of the six largest surviving Roman amphitheatres in the world. Today its stands host concerts, festivals and shows, weaving antiquity into contemporary cultural life.

A tour of Pula also takes in the Arch of the Sergii on the main street, the Gate of Hercules and the Kaštel fortress. This 17th-century Venetian castle stands on a hilltop and offers sweeping views over the harbour and the city's rooftops.

Istria stands apart from the rest of the Croatian coast. The heart-shaped peninsula is divided between Croatia, Slovenia and Italy and retains a strong Italian influence. Its green hills, vineyards, olive groves, forests and medieval hill towns have earned it the nickname 'the Tuscany of the Adriatic'. Inland, hilltop towns such as Motovun command the views. However, the lack of suitable facilities for motorhomes forced us to leave it off our itinerary.

From the elegance of Opatija to the lakes of Plitvice

After covering much of Istria, our next stop was Opatija, very different from the rest of the coast. Here grand villas, historic hotels and gardens dominate, all steeped in Austro-Hungarian elegance. For decades it was one of the favourite retreats of the Austro-Hungarian aristocracy, drawn by its spas and mild climate.

The Lungomare, a seafront promenade of around ten kilometres, runs along the coast past villas, small coves and crystal-clear waters. The best way to enjoy it is to stroll slowly and stop in the various little nooks for a swim. It is also worth continuing as far as Volosko, a charming old fishing village.

The fishing harbour of Volosko David del Valle

From Opatija you can continue south along the coastal road beneath the Velebit mountains, in one of the most spectacular stretches of the journey. In our case we chose the motorway to reach Nin, near Zadar. There the scenery changes once again.

The compact historic centre of Nin sits on a tiny island surrounded by lagoons. The town preserves some of the oldest traces of Croatian history and its 9th-century Church of the Holy Cross is one of its main landmarks. It is traditionally known as the smallest cathedral in the world. Nin is also known for its sandy beaches, therapeutic mud and salt pans.

In Zadar, motorhomes have a harder time finding somewhere to park, but the visit is well worth the effort. Amid Roman and medieval remains, the seafront concentrates two of its main attractions: the Sea Organ, which turns the movement of the waves into sound through pipes installed beneath the stone steps, and the Greeting to the Sun, a circle of solar panels that lights up at dusk.

Sunset is Zadar's calling card. The phrase attributed to Alfred Hitchcock, who described it as the most beautiful in the world, has become part of the city's tourist lore. From here we left the blue of the Adriatic behind for a day to plunge into the greenery of Plitvice Lakes National Park. Its 16 lakes, arranged in tiers at different levels and linked by rivers and waterfalls, form one of Croatia's most breathtaking natural landscapes. A UNESCO World Heritage Site, the park is the perfect counterpoint to the coast.

A view of Plitvice National Park, far from the coastal strip David del Valle

You explore it along footpaths and wooden boardwalks, with electric boats and internal vehicles used on some routes. The great waterfall, Veliki Slap, rises to about 78 metres and is the highest in Croatia. Although the turquoise water and the heat may tempt you in, swimming in the lakes is forbidden.

Šibenik, Trogir and the heart of Dalmatia

Back on the coast we reach Šibenik, a city of white stone, alleyways, staircases and small squares. St James's Cathedral, a World Heritage Site, was built entirely of stone and features an unusual frieze of 71 sculpted human heads, each one different. About 50 kilometres further on lies Trogir, a small island town that feels like Dalmatia in miniature.

The best thing to do is to lose yourself in its narrow stone streets before continuing to Split, the urban heart of the region. Split grew up around the vast palace of the Emperor Diocletian, built more than 1,700 years ago. Today its ancient walls, passageways and chambers form a living city centre where homes, shops, restaurants and cafe terraces all rub shoulders.

Its harbour is also one of the main gateways to the Adriatic islands, with ferries and catamarans to Brač, Hvar, Šolta and Vis. In high season passenger traffic is frantic and ticket prices can be steep. Croatia has more than 1,200 islands, although only around 60 are inhabited. On our trip we visited Korčula, Lopud and Lokrum, the latter just off Dubrovnik's old town and known for its small saltwater lake, the Dead Sea.

The Makarska Riviera and the Pelješac peninsula

Leaving Split, the road once again hugs the Adriatic and one of the most scenic sections of the journey begins: the Makarska Riviera. On one side lies the sea; on the other, the sheer Biokovo mountains. The distance between mountain and coast is minimal, and the bends offer some of the finest viewpoints on the road to Dubrovnik. Before reaching the walled city, we turn off towards the Pelješac peninsula.

Ston is one of its big surprises: a small town protected by a wall that climbs up the hillside, considered one of the most impressive defensive systems in Europe. Mali Ston Bay is famous for its oysters. Eating them freshly opened, raw and with a squeeze of lemon is one of the region's must-try food experiences.

After a stop at Prapratno beach, we continued to Orebić to board a boat to the island of Korčula. Its old town is laid out like a fishbone, a design intended to encourage air circulation and protect the streets from the winds. Korčula claims to be the birthplace of Marco Polo and his figure appears all over the town. Walls, towers and stone buildings recall centuries of Venetian rule.

Before leaving Pelješac, Žuljana offers a quieter reward: crystal-clear waters, mountains and coves with a distinctly Mediterranean feel. One useful tip for enjoying the sea: Croatian beaches are, with few exceptions, pebbly rather than sandy. It is worth bringing mats or airbeds, as locals do, and not forgetting water shoes.

Dubrovnik, the grand finale

The road to Dubrovnik marks the transition from a laid-back Croatia to its main tourist hotspot. After one last bend, the walled city comes into view, one of the most iconic sights on the Adriatic.

Impressive Dubrovnik, transformed after the Balkan wars into one of Europe's most overcrowded destinations David del Valle

In high season thousands of visitors throng Stradun, the main thoroughfare, stopping at every corner to take photos. The city walls, cathedral and narrow lanes of the old town can be seen in a day, although spending three days lets you explore at a gentler pace and add a boat trip to one of the islands. A good option is to explore Dubrovnik at sunset, when many day-trippers have already left.

From Rovinj to Dubrovnik, Croatia changes face time and again. Istria brings its Italian heritage; Dalmatia, its stone-built cities and islands; Plitvice, its forests and waterfalls; and Dubrovnik, the great historical stage facing the sea. That variety, packed into a relatively compact coastline, explains why Croatia now competes with Europe's heavyweight tourist destinations and still offers far more than just sun and sea.

World.title: A European Central Bank rate hike is all but certain, the reasoning less so
World.content:
Frankfurt will almost certainly move on Thursday.

 

Market odds put a quarter-point hike at close to certainty, which would lift the European Central Bank's deposit rate from 2.25% to 2.5%.

What makes this a difficult call is not whether the ECB acts, but why, and whether the reasoning survives contact with the data.

The path here has been compressed as the ECB raised rates on 11 June for the first time in three years, lifting the deposit rate from 2% to 2.25% in response to the energy shock from the Iran war, and then held rates in July while Christine Lagarde pointed hawkishly towards September.

August's inflation figures removed any remaining doubt with eurozone inflation hitting 3.3%, up from 2.9% in July and the highest since September 2023, as energy inflation surged to 14.3% from 10.3%.

The inflation is not spreading

Look beneath the headline inflation and the picture inverts.

Core inflation, which strips out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, actually fell to 2.4% from 2.5%. Services inflation, the component most closely tied to wages and domestic demand, dropped to 3% from 3.3%.

In other words, there is still little evidence that expensive energy is feeding through into everything else. That is what economists mean by "second-round effects", and their absence is the strongest argument against tightening.

The ECB's own research also supports the distinction.

In a paper published on Tuesday, ECB economists found that adverse energy supply factors, driven by geopolitical tensions, accounted for around 90% of the rise in energy inflation between January and May.

"This time the energy supply shock dominates, while demand and public policy stimulus have minor roles," the economists wrote, adding that "these differences are key to explaining why monetary policy responses differ."

The 2021-22 surge, by contrast, came from "a combination of large and unprecedented supply and demand-side factors," which is why the ECB then "raised interest rates forcefully and persistently" rather than gradually.

The national spread across the EU further underlines how uneven this is.

August inflation ran at 4.5% in Spain, 2.9% in Germany and 2.7% in France, three economies facing the same energy shock with very different results, all governed by one interest rate.

Economic growth is the other complication.

The eurozone has proved more resilient than expected, which ING attributes partly to luck, partly to Asian competitors suffering more from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and partly to fiscal stimulus. However, resilience does not mean the growth could not, or should not, accelerate.

ING characterises Thursday's expected move as "another insurance rate hike", or "a dovish rate hike," noting that even at 2.5% the deposit rate sits within the range the ECB itself considers neutral.

Going further would mean deciding restrictive policy is required, which would be a different judgement entirely.

Everyone is looking to hike at the same time

The ECB is not acting alone, and that matters for the euro.

The Federal Reserve meets on 15 and 16 September, with Chair Kevin Warsh having used his first Jackson Hole address to argue that financial conditions are not restrictive and underlying inflation has not improved.

Investors had put the odds of a US hike at roughly one in three before those remarks, but now price a 60% chance the Fed hikes the target range from 3.5%-3.75% to 3.75%-4%.

The Bank of Japan follows on 17 and 18 September, with markets pricing an 80% to 90% chance of a move to 1.25%.

On the other hand, the Bank of England is expected to hold rates at 3.75% on 17 September as it currently maintains a much higher interest rate than the rest.

FILE. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh talks to Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey and Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem at the Jackson Hole Symposium, 28 Aug. 2026 AP Photo/Amber Baesler

If the Fed were to hike while the ECB held, the dollar would strengthen against the euro and that would cut both ways for Frankfurt.

A weaker euro makes European exports more competitive, but it also makes imports dearer, and since oil and gas are priced in dollars, it would push up precisely the energy costs driving the inflation problem in the first place.

Overall, we can assume a September rate hike is a done deal for the ECB but we can also project that it won't solve the central bank's current dilemma of raising borrowing costs against an inflation it cannot reach, while withdrawing support an economy could still use.

World.title: US destroys five Iranian tankers as Tehran launches retaliatory strikes on Jordan
World.content:
The US forces have destroyed five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday in response to the latest attacks on its warships, US Central Command said. Following the American strikes, Iran launched missiles at US targets in Jordan, according to Iranian state-run media.

 

US said the military struck the tankers on Tuesday after the Revolutionary Guards targeted a Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days. Stating that the US warship "successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and that no American personnel were harmed.”

The statement added that the crews of the five destroyed vessels, Kivik, Charminar, Horizon 1, the Riesco and Derya, were told to abandon ship before the attacks.

Meanwhile, Jordan’s military said its air defence systems intercepted 18 ballistic missiles launched toward its territory, and two others fell in places where no one lives. It said it has no reports of casualties. As a staunch US ally that hosts American forces, Jordan's military bases have become a target of repeated Iranian strikes.

The latest exchange of strikes has brought the sides back toward open hostilities in a war that has been ongoing for more than six months.

After claiming to strike a US Navy sea drone on Sunday, Iran captured an unmanned US underwater vessel at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz at dawn, Iranian state television reported, and broadcast images of the purported captured drone.

Trump administration on Tuesday added new sanctions on elements of Iran’s aviation industry, targeting more than two dozen commercial and private airlines as well as foreign cargo service providers, in its new push to isolate Tehran from its remaining trading partners.

Both sides are seeking to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz, where about one-fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war began.

World.title: Turkey seeks Black Sea shipping deal as attacks threaten grain trade
World.content:
Turkey is racing to restore safe passage for cargo ships in the Black Sea as attacks on shipping disrupt grain exports and push up prices. Russia and Ukraine are major global wheat exporters, but Black Sea trade has been severely disrupted as both sides step up attacks on shipping and port infrastructure.

Advertising

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan announced this week that Turkey was working on a plan to ensure safe passage in the Black Sea for commercial shipping and said he was in touch with both Ukraine and Russia.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan confirmed that he raised the issue with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, on the sidelines of a gathering of regional leaders in Kyrgyzstan.

The Turkish move comes as Ukraine and Russia have ramped up their attacks on shipping and ports in and around the Black Sea. In 2022, Turkey and the United Nations brokered a deal between Ukraine and Russia to ensure safe passage for Ukrainian grain exports through the Black Sea.

The agreement lasted a year.

While Turkey has maintained good ties with both sides, reaching another agreement will be much harder, warned international relations professor Huseyin Bagci of Ankara’s Middle East Technical University.

“The tension is increasing more than ever before,” Bagci said. “It's not enough to have good relations, because the two sides – the Ukrainians and Russians – should sit down and talk about a common solution to this problem. Turkey cannot solve this problem alone.”

What the SDF’s dissolution means for Syria’s Kurds and neighbouring Turkey

Growing attacks

In August Ukraine offered a ceasefire on commercial shipping, but the offer was rejected by Moscow, which said it wanted a broader deal. Ukrainian drones continue to strike Russian shipping, while Russia has continued missile attacks on Ukrainian ports and ships.

This surge in attacks comes as both nations rush to export their grain harvests.

Grain prices have risen sharply, by as much as 30 percent, international grain broker Can Atbasoglu said, even as both sides scramble to find new routes for their exports.

“Russia will do their best to export as much as they can, both from Russian Baltic ports and EU Baltic ports like Latvia and Lithuania; they're also exporting,” Atbasoglu said.

“Ukraine will also export as much as they can from Romania as well and through the Danube ports. But the export pace will be definitely lower. So it will definitely stay bullish for the markets. Prices are definitely going to stay like this or can have a further increase.”

Fears of wheat price surge amid Ukraine-Russia clashes in the Black Sea

Ships staying put

At one of Istanbul's many shipyards, the docks are crowded with ships that once braved the Black Sea. One vessel bears the scars of a drone attack and is under repair. Others undergo routine maintenance as shipowners hesitate to risk new journeys into dangerous waters.

The superintendent of one ship, speaking anonymously, says repairs are nearly finished, but uncertainty clouds the future.

“We wanted to take the ship out to the Black Sea before entering the shipyard, but because of that risk, we didn’t enter the Black Sea and didn’t take on any cargo. We’ve been in the shipyard for 50 days for repairs, but we don’t know what will happen once the repairs are finished,” the superintendent said.

Turkish shipowners warn that many are on the brink of bankruptcy, as idle ships rack up costs of up to 50,000 euros a month in mooring and crew expenses.

Ziya Ustel, CEO of Turkish shipping company VI-ZA STAR, says high freight rates are being offered for Black Sea routes, but the risks are too great.

“They are offering high freight rates, etc,” Ustel said.

Without a diplomatic solution, few shipowners will be prepared to risk their vessels, Ustel warned.

“The main thing is to find out a real solution,” Ustel added. “Otherwise, no one will try anything anymore.”

Turkish diplomacy

Ankara is expected to step up its efforts to find a solution.

Grain brokers say hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough may be one reason prices have so far remained below the record highs seen at the start of the war.

But if Turkish efforts fail and attacks on Black Sea shipping continue, higher grain prices could have a considerable impact, especially on the world’s poorest nations, many of which depend on Russian and Ukrainian grain.

World.title: Trump escalates trade war with Canada with import bans, 50% tariffs
World.content:
US President Trump has announced new import bans and 50% tariffs on some Canadian goods as tensions between the two countries intensify. This comes a day after Ottawa's retaliatory tariffs on US products took effect.

Canadian dairy products, motorcycles and alcoholic beverages face import bans in the United States, while other goods from across the border will be hit with 50% tariffs, the White House said Tuesday, as President Donald Trump escalates a trade war with Ottawa.

The import ban is scheduled to take effect on September 29.

Trump also ordered a 50% tariff on additional Canadian goods, including mattresses, motorboats and golf carts, starting September 15.

The latest moves came after Canada imposed retaliatory tariffs of up to 50% on about $20 billion (€17.2 billion) of US goods on Monday, following Washington's decision last month to levy 50% tariffs on selected Canadian imports.

Why is Trump imposing an import ban?

The White House said the alcohol ban was partly in response to provincial boycotts of US alcohol. Canadian provinces have removed many US wines and spirits from store shelves amid a widespread boycott of American goods, a move Trump called "discriminatory."

"President Trump is doing this to make sure, again, that we keep a level playing field, deter retaliation, and of course protect American production," a senior administration official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.

Trump also directed the US General Services Administration to exclude Canadian products from its long-term government procurement contracts unless Ottawa restores what he called "full and fair reciprocity" for American farmers and companies.

On Monday, Trump threatened to block Canadian aircraft maker Bombardier from selling planes in the US unless it manufactures them in the United States.

What did Canadian Prime Minister Carney say?

Nearly 68% of Canadian exports headed to the US this year, with about 80% of those shipments entering duty-free under the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) exemptions, data showed.

However, the latest escalation also cast a shadow on the future of the three-nation trade pact.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said his country would accelerate efforts to reduce its dependence on the US.

"It's about ensuring that no country can hold us hostage. And that we can live how we want to live," Carney said on Tuesday.

Aside from tariffs, Canadians were also irked by Trump's repeated reference to their country as the 51st US state and an order renaming of Lake Ontario to Lake America.

Trump pushes Canada toward EU

Trump wielding tariffs as a tool to force smaller partners to agree to lower tariffs in return for market access, investment pledges or alignment with US policy has other governments watching to see how Canada's standing up to Trump plays out.

Recent developments have pushed Ottawa to explore a deeper relationship with the European Union.

Next week, Carney is due in Strasbourg, France, and scheduled address the European Parliament.

World.title: Israel's Netanyahu denies UAE warned him of October 7 attack
World.content:
Israeli media reported that the UAE contacted Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu before the October 7, 2023 attacks, warning him that Hamas was planning a major operation. The prime minister has rejected the reports.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office on Tuesday denied a report by left-leaning Israeli newspaper Haaretz that he received a warning from the United Arab Emirates prior to the October 7, 2023 terror attacks by Hamas.

"No warning was given to the Prime Minister from the United Arab Emirates before October 7," Netanyahu's office said in a statement.

What did the reports divulge?

Haaretz, in a report based on a book excerpt by two of the newspaper's journalists, said that UAE President Mohammad bin Zayed spoke with Netanyahu 10 days prior to the attack. In that conversation, bin Zayed said Hamas and its then-leader Yahya Sinwar were planning a major operation targeting Israel.

The UAE's Foreign Ministry, meanwhile, did not explicitly confirm the report but said, "When necessary, all relevant intelligence has been and continue to be communicated between the relevant entities." The UAE normalized relations with Israel in 2021 as part of the Abraham Accords.

According to Haaretz, bin Zayed told Netanyahu that the Hamas operation could disrupt the Middle East region and undermine the Abraham Accords. Prior to October 7, there were signs that Saudi Arabia and Israel could soon formalize ties.

In the call with bin Zayed, Netanyahu reacted with "relative calm" to the UAE's president warning that Hamas could launch an operation. Netanyahu said Israel was prepared for any scenario and that an attack was more likely to come from the West Bank.

The Haaretz report was also confirmed by The Times of Israel (TOI) on Tuesday, with TOI citing an Emirati source that bin Zayed had warned Netanyahu of the Hamas attack.

The Haaretz article comes after centrist Israeli newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth reported last year that Egyptian intelligence officials had warned Israel that "something big is going to happen" shortly before the October 7 massacre.

The Hamas terror attack on October 7 killed some 1,200 people in Israel, with the group also taking another 251 hostages into Gaza. It was the single deadliest day for Jewish people since the Holocaust.

Survivors mourn victims of October 7 music festival killings To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Netanyahu chided by political rivals over report ahead of elections

The latest reports that Netanyahu had advance notice of a major Hamas operation came ahead of Israeli elections next month.

Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, whose centrist Yashar party is frequently leading Netanyahu's center-right Likud in the polls, said "More and more signs point to the fact that Netanyahu blindly led Israel into the disaster of October 7."

Eisenkot, Netanyahu's top rival in the upcoming elections, was formerly the chief of staff of the Israeli military [FILE: August 14, 2022] Image: Tsafrir Abayov/AP Photo/picture alliance

Eisenkot has pushed for an official state commission of inquiry into the October 7 attacks, an idea which Netanyahu has rejected.

Naftali Bennett, another Netanyahu opponent running in the election who earlier served as prime minister, said, "Netanyahu bears personal and direct responsibility for the failure that led to the deaths of thousands of Israelis on his watch."

Yair Golan, the chief of the center-left Democrats party, posted a message on X to Netanyahu: "You knew, you ignored, you failed, you are to blame."

October 7 had wide-ranging consequences

The October 7, 2023, attacks had massive consequences not only for Israeli society but also for Palestinians in Gaza, where Hamas was in charge.

How much of Gaza has been destroyed since October 7, 2023? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Following the Hamas attacks, the Israeli military began a war targeting Hamas in Gaza. That offensive left more than 73,650 Palestinians in Gaza dead, according to Gaza's Hamas-run Health Ministry, with a UN Commission of Inquiry last year finding that Israel committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

World.title: US strikes oil tankers off coast of Iran
World.content:
The US attacked four oil-carrying vessels in the Gulf of Oman and one in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it would strike ships off Bahrain and Kuwait in retaliation.

The US military struck five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday.

The US Central Command (CENTCOM) said it struck the ships "after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targeted a US Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days."

"The US warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and continued to patrol regional waters. No American personnel were harmed," it added.

CENTCOM said it directed the crews to abandon ship shortly before the strikes. The were no immediate reports regarding casualties.

Iranian media reported explosions were heard near the southern port of Jask and on Kharg Island — both key ports for the country's oil exports.

What do we know about the ships that were attacked?

US forces attacked four Iranian oil carriers in the Gulf of Oman: the M/T Kaviz, the M/T Charminar, the M/T Horizon 1 and the M/T Riesco.

US forces also attacked the M/T Derya near Kharg Island in the Strait of Hormuz.

CENTCOM linked these five vessels to the IRGC.

"Iran has used the tankers as part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies," CENTCOM said in a statement.

"Iran has no means by which to defend these vessels."

Iran announces retaliation

Iranian state media reported that Iran launched missiles toward US targets in Jordan.

Jordan's army said Wednesday it shot down 18 missiles from Iran. Jordan is a US ally and hosts an American military facility.

"Jordan's air defense systems engaged 20 ballistic missiles launched toward Jordanian territory, successfully intercepting and destroying 18 of them, while two missiles fell in unpopulated areas," the army statement said, adding that Iran fired the missiles.

The IRGC said it also targetedtwo US ships, eight oil tankers and 10 other "non-compliant vessels" that it said were "attempting to pass through the prohibited and unsafe zone."

Earlier on Wednesday morning, the IRCG warned it would target oil tankers off the coast of Bahrain and Kuwait in particular.

"We warn all oil tankers in the Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports... whether they are anchored or docked — we warn them to leave their vessels because they will be targeted," the IRCG said in a statement.

World.title: German economy frets about Saxony-Anhalt election results
World.content:
The AfD won the election in the eastern German state by a wide margin. While politicians and election analysts are still debating the reasons for the far-right party's popularity, economists are sounding the alarm.

The results came in as predicted: The AfD, which is considered far-right extremist in parts, won the election in Saxony-Anhalt and could now put forward the state’s minister-president and take over the state government.

What hardly anyone expected, however, was this: The governing CDU is now barely half as strong as it was, while the other parties have been left far behind. Calling it a landslide victory for the AfD is no exaggeration. And many commentators go so far as to call it a turning point in Germany’s postwar history.

Keep calm and carry on?

"A state government led by the AfD would certainly be seen by many as a turning point and would further fuel the debate over how best to deal with the party," Commerzbank economist Ralph Solveen told Reuters.

At the same time, he advises waiting to see what happens, saying that things are rarely as bad as they seem.

"Many of these decisions are unlikely to affect the economy until the medium to long term," he said. "Decisions on most taxes, the structure of the labor market and social security systems are made at the federal level. That is why the AfD, in many of its pledges, only promises to advocate for something in the Bundesrat, which is unlikely to succeed given the foreseeable isolation of an AfD-led government."

What next after far-right AfD win in regional election? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Local political pragmatism?

Many business community concerns had already been raised before the election. It also became clear that there are differing views within the AfD, which could lead to unpredictable policies.

For example, DW reported two months ago that Hannes Loth, a member of the AfD and the mayor in Raguhn-Jessnitz, Saxony-Anhalt, sought to have six new wind turbines installed. This pledge puts him at odds with the official stance of his own party.

Whether this is a sign of internal party pluralism or simply local political pragmatism will become clear during the coming legislative term, especially if the AfD ends up in the state government. It is not, however, serving to reassure business leaders.

Consequences of xenophobia

One issue the AfD campaigned on was a promise to limit the number of foreigners. But will the party actually be able to implement its goal? On this point, Michael Berlemann, director of the Hamburg Institute of International Economics (HWWI), remains skeptical.

"A large part of the measures it has promised cannot be implemented at the state level because the federal government is responsible for them," he said. "Another part would be illegal and would be overturned by the courts after some delay: The AfD cannot restrict the immigration of foreign skilled workers in Saxony-Anhalt."

ING chief economist Carsten Brzeski pointed to the national shortage of skilled workers: "Forced deportations in Saxony-Anhalt would probably be limited. However, the symbolic effect cannot be underestimated. As with Trump, such headlines would act as a deterrent for foreign skilled workers."

Wido Geis-Thöne, an economist at the German Economic Institute in Cologne, sees it the same way.

He told DW that the AfD would "do everything in its power to pursue its migration policy goals." However, it could only "do things that actually fall under the responsibility of the state rather than the federal government."

Economic fallout for Saxony-Anhalt

Geis-Thöne said the state itself would be the main victim of such a policy: "With an anti-immigration state government, Saxony-Anhalt will become significantly less attractive a destination for foreign skilled workers, regardless of whether anything actually changes for them from a legal perspective."

For HWWI Director Berlemann, the indirect impacts of the AfD's plans are particularly problematic. The measures announced would mean "that many skilled workers who are particularly needed in health care and nursing, hospitality and tourism, the food industry and agriculture and in construction and logistics will avoid the state in the future."

This would exacerbate the shortage of skilled workers and widen the state's economic gap.

Openness and diversity are key

Saxony-Anhalt must remain a state where people from around the world want to live and work and where companies want to invest and new technologies can emerge, Bitkom President Ralf Wintergerst warned.

He told the Catholic News Agency KNA: "The digital economy thrives on openness, diversity and international cooperation. Companies invest where they find good conditions and where skilled workers from Germany and abroad are welcomed."

Regarding foreign investment, ING Chief Economist Carsten Brzeski told Reuters: "Sure, there could be a symbolic effect on foreign investors. But let's not forget: Saxony-Anhalt is not the entire German economy."

What the AfD's Saxony-Anhalt win means for Germany To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How should Berlin react

DIW President Marcel Fratzscher painted a bleak picture of the economic future after the Saxony-Anhalt election.

"Regardless of the makeup of the next state government, a controversial or weak government and the polarization during the election campaign are likely to accelerate the departure of people and companies from Saxony-Anhalt, thereby significantly worsening conditions in the state," he said.

He told Reuters that the election result was "above all a vote of no confidence in the federal government." The consequence, he added, must be "that the federal government changes course and implements far-reaching structural reforms involving subsidies, bureaucracy, taxes, the social security system and Europe."

Tanja Gönner, managing director of the Federation of German Industries (BDI), took a similar perspective. Following the state election, she called on the federal government to be single-minded in pursuing a reform agenda.

"The response to this state election result must not be political paralysis at the federal level," she said.

The federal government must now consistently implement and expand reforms to boost investment, innovation and growth, she told RedaktionsNetzwerk Deutschland, adding that "the positions of radical parties are not suitable for this."

The political center must now show that it is capable of taking action, BDI's managing director said, adding that what is needed is a policy focused on competitiveness and growth at both the state and federal levels. A single state election result must not distract from that goal, she concluded.



This article was originally published in German.

World.title: EU, UK express dismay over Mladic funeral in Serbia
World.content:
The EU is deliberating an official response to the glorification of war criminal Ratko Mladic in Belgrade. The UK, meanwhile, summoned Serbia's charge d'affaires over the display.

Both the EU and UK on Tuesday expressed dismay over the funeral in Belgrade, Serbia of late war criminal Ratko Mladic a day prior.

Thousands of people, including at least six Serbian ministers, attended the event on Monday which was seen as glorifying Mladic. He received military honors at the funeral, with the head of Serbia's Orthodox Church presiding over the ceremony.

The Bosnian Serb commander died last month at The Hague, where he had been imprisoned for life. Mladic was convicted in 2017 of genocide, having orchestrated the July 1995 Srebrenica massacre, where 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed.

Mladic, called the "Butcher of Bosnia" by some international press, is a revered as a war hero by many Serbian nationalists in both Serbia and Bosnia.

EU leader call Mladic state funeral 'deeply regrettable'

EU leaders condemned the funeral, with the bloc weighing an official response to the event.

"The elements of official support and the presence of some senior Serbian officials at the funeral are deeply regrettable," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa said in statements posted on X.

"They demonstrate a failure to confront a dark chapter in Europe's recent history and contradict the values underpinning Serbia's path towards the European Union," they added.

A European Commission spokeperson, in comments to German news agency DPA, said next steps were being evaluated.

EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas added: "Serbia's path into the European Union requires an unequivocal commitment in fundamental European values and historical truth."

Serbia first applied for EU membership in 2009. Serbia's EU candidacy was confirmed by the European Council in 2012.

Serbia: Thousands attend 'Butcher of Bosnia' funeral To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

UK summons Serbian envoy

The UK, meanwhile, summoned Serbia's charge d'affaires in response to the funeral.

"As a military commander, Mladic presided over crimes that are among the worst committed in Europe since the Second World War," the British Foreign Office said in a statement.

"The thoughts of the UK Government are with Mladic's victims and their families. They deserve respect, compassion and accountability, not efforts to rewrite proven history," the statement added.

The UK said that the "glorification of a convicted war criminal directly undermines trust, fuels division, and is incompatible with the process of reconciliation within Bosnia and Herzegovina and the region."

Bosnia expels Serbian diplomats, says Belgrade crossed 'red line'

In its reaction to the funeral, neighboring Bosnia expelled two Serbian diplomats, saying Serbia crossed a "red line" in its display of reverence for Mladic.

"They crossed every red line with what they did yesterday, the day before, and in the days leading up to the reception," Bosnian Foreign Minister Elmedin Konakovic told a Sarajevo press event.

Konakovic had also said he would withdraw most staff from the Bosnian Embassy in Belgrade in an effort to reduce ties to "the lowest possible level"

Serbian President Aleksander Vucic was not present at Mladic's funeral, although his son Danilo, did attend the event. Vucic rejected allegations that Mladic was being glorified at the funeral and said the event was put together by Mladic's family rather than the state.

The controversial funeral comes ahead of snap elections next month. Serbia has faced a political crisis in the past two years triggered by the collapse of a concrete canopy at a railway station in Novi Sad.
