World.title: BARMM election faces low-turnout risk amid violence, voter uncertainty
World.content:
MAJESTIC. The Grand Mosque stands in Cotabato City, the regional center of the Bangsamoro region, serving as a cornerstone of Islamic life in Mindanao and a symbol of the region’s aspirations for peace and stability under autonomous governance.

Some of the forces the peace process was meant to overcome remain powerful enough to influence whether people turn out to vote in the BARMM on September 14

CAGAYAN DE ORO, Philippines – The first parliamentary election in the seven-year-old Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) is approaching with this possibility: Voters may be too frightened, distrustful, or uncertain about the new political system to turn out in the numbers election officials are counting on.

Climate Conflict Action Asia (CCAA), a group that monitors conflict in the predominantly Muslim region, warned that violence and low public confidence in the electoral process could depress turnout and undermine the credibility of the September 14 election.

The warning carries particular weight because the Commission on Elections (Comelec) is targeting a turnout of at least 70% to 75% among the BARMM’s 2.39 million voters.

Next week’s parliamentary election is meant as a start of a new chapter for the region that emerged from decades of armed conflict through a 2014 peace agreement between the government and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), which resulted in BARMM’s creation in 2019.

But CCAA’s monitoring in the weeks before the vote suggests that some of the forces the peace process was meant to overcome — guns, clan rivalries, political polarization, extremist violence and distrust of government — remain powerful enough to influence whether people go to the polls.

Is the gun ban working?

The numbers offer one of the clearest warnings.

CCAA’s Critical Events Monitoring System recorded 58 gun-related incidents from July 16 to August 31, after the election gun ban in the region took effect. That compared with 44 incidents from June 1 to July 15, before the ban.

Deaths from gun-related violence also increased, from 34 before the ban to 39 afterward.

CCAA recorded 14 more gun-related incidents, an increase of about 32%, and five more deaths, or about 15%, after the ban took effect.

The figures do not mean that the gun ban factored in any way to the increase. But they show that, during the period monitored by CCAA, restrictions on firearms had not produced the reduction in violence voters might expect from an election security measure.

Instead, violence continued in communities where politics, clan loyalties and access to firearms overlap.

CCAA is not the first to point out that the persistence of violence shows a problem that goes beyond election security. An earlier assessment by the Brussels-based International Crisis Group found that more than a decade after the peace agreement, clan feuds, political rivalries and criminal networks continued to thrive where state institutions remained weak.

‘Peace is our shared responsibility’

On Tuesday, September 8, the Lanao del Sur-based Moro Consensus Group (MCG) called on candidates, security forces, and voters in the region to help ensure a peaceful and credible first parliamentary election in the BARMM.

In a statement, MCG chairman Drieza Lininding called on the region’s political parties and candidates to avoid violence, vote-buying, harassment and intimidation, and to respect voters’ right to make their choices freely.

The civil society group also called on the military, police and other security agencies to remain neutral, protect polling centers and election workers, and enforce election laws without political bias.

MCG said Bangsamoro voters, including Muslim Filipinos, indigenous peoples, Christians, women, and young people, should be able to take part in the election without fear or coercion.

It urged BARMM leaders and politicians to respect the outcome and accept the choice of voters.

“Peace is our shared responsibility,” the group said, urging Bangsamoro voters to take part in the election “with courage, discernment, and peace.”

Tensions high

CCAA said tensions worsened after Bangsamoro interim Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua was ambushed on August 15, an attack it said deepened divisions within the MILF and intensified political polarization.

In Shariff Saydona Mustapha in Maguindanao del Sur, a recurring rido (clan feud) displaced about 30 families in late August.

In Basilan, arrest warrants were issued against the mayor and seven others over an ambush involving supporters of a former mayor during the 2025 midterm elections. The warrants were issued about a month before the parliamentary election, CCAA said, after the incumbent mayor aligned herself with a political camp opposed to the governor.

The government has imposed a gun ban and deployed large numbers of military personnel to secure the election.

But CCAA said armed groups, political parties and local power structures remained closely linked in parts of the region.

It also raised questions about the weapons and armed capability of the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP), the MILF’s political party.

CCAA said there had been no concrete steps toward decommissioning the weapons and armed forces linked to the MILF.

The government and the MILF signed guidelines on August 31 governing ceasefire-related functions during the election. Two days later, the military stopped an MILF convoy in Kolambugan, Lanao del Norte, because most of its members were armed.

Lanao del Norte, a province led by the Dimaporos – a Muslim Filipino family – did not join BARMM and is part of the predominantly Catholic region of Northern Mindanao.

As a result, the military called on the MILF to coordinate movements through mechanisms established under the Bangsamoro peace process.

Voter concerns

Security is only part of the problem. CCAA’s monitoring also found uncertainty among voters about how to participate in the new parliamentary system.

In interviews with residents, CCAA said it found people who were still unsure how to vote and others who said they had received little voter education. Some said political parties had turned voter education into another form of campaigning, telling people whom to support rather than explaining how the new parliamentary system was supposed to work.

For generations, elections in Muslim-majority areas of Mindanao had been more personal and familiar. Voters knew local candidates, their families and often the clans and political alliances behind them. Now, they are being asked to choose representatives to a regional legislature through regional political parties and parliamentary districts – a system that remains unfamiliar to many.

That lack of understanding carries another risk. CCAA said local electoral boards had come under pressure in previous elections from political groups seeking to influence or intimidate voters. A voter unfamiliar with the system and looking to an electoral official for guidance could therefore be especially vulnerable.

The question is what that uncertainty will mean on election day.

CCAA said weak participation could signal more than confusion over a new ballot, and it could show a deeper lack of faith in the BARMM government and the political groups competing to control it.

That skepticism has a tangible backdrop of poor health and education services and corruption allegations involving the BARMM education ministry.

Poverty has declined but economic hardship remains widespread, CCAA said. – Rappler.com

World.title: Southwest monsoon bringing moderate to heavy rain to over 20 areas
World.content:
Floods and landslides remain possible on Wednesday, September 9, due to rain from the southwest monsoon

MANILA, Philippines – Nearly two dozen provinces, almost all in Luzon, are seeing significant rainfall due to the southwest monsoon or habagat in the next 24 hours, the weather bureau’s 11 am advisory showed on Wednesday, September 9.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said the southwest monsoon is still affecting Luzon and the Visayas, with rain expected to be heaviest in the following areas:

Wednesday noon, September 9, to Thursday noon, September 10

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 millimeters): La Union, Pangasinan, Nueva Ecija, Mountain Province, Quirino, Aurora, Nueva Vizcaya, Ifugao, Benguet, Tarlac, Zambales, Bataan, Pampanga, Cavite, Batangas, Romblon, Occidental Mindoro, Oriental Mindoro, Palawan, Camarines Sur, Albay, Aklan, Antique

Thursday noon, September 10, to Friday noon, September 11

Heavy to intense rain (100-200 mm): Occidental Mindoro

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Pangasinan, La Union, Benguet, Nueva Vizcaya, Quirino, Aurora, Zambales, Bataan, Tarlac, Pampanga, Nueva Ecija, Bulacan, Metro Manila, Rizal, Cavite, Batangas, Laguna, Quezon, Oriental Mindoro, Marinduque, Romblon, Palawan, Camarines Norte, Camarines Sur, Albay, Catanduanes, Aklan, Antique

Friday noon, September 11, to Saturday noon, September 12

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Zambales, Bataan, Tarlac, Pampanga, Cavite, Batangas, Occidental Mindoro, Pangasinan, La Union

On Wednesday, other parts of Luzon and the Visayas not mentioned above could have isolated to scattered rain or thunderstorms from the southwest monsoon.

Floods and landslides remain possible.

So far, there are no new low pressure areas (LPAs) or potential tropical cyclones inside or outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR).

But PAGASA reiterated on Wednesday morning that it is not ruling out the possibility of LPA formation during the week.

The weather bureau expects two or three tropical cyclones to develop within or enter PAR in September. The next three local tropical cyclone names are Queenie, Rosal, and Samuel. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Pinoy Criminology] Like Martin Romualdez, can ordinary accused avail themselves of hospital arrest?
World.content:
I cannot help but comment on the arrest of former House speaker Martin Romualdez. He was arrested for plunder involving allegations of billions of pesos in kickbacks. When the warrant was served, however, he was already confined at Cardinal Santos Medical Center after allegedly experiencing a cardiovascular event, and his lawyers subsequently asked the Sandiganbayan to allow his continued hospital confinement.

There is nothing inherently wrong with that. If Romualdez truly has a medical condition, then he deserves to be medically attended to. He is not yet convicted guilty, and preventive detention should not be punishment, much less medical deprivation that could lead to death.

The problem is not that Romualdez is receiving medical attention. The problem is whether the same consideration is available to everyone else. Because, right now, how many old, sickly, and terminally ill accused are languishing in our jails, undergoing trial for offenses far less serious than plunder? (READ: [Pinoy Criminology] Protecting the old and sickly from prolonged pre-trial detention)



Some have been there not for one month but for years, with no end in sight. Some suffer from diabetes, hypertension, cancer, tuberculosis, heart disease, and other debilitating illnesses. They are also presumed innocent, except that poverty seems to make that presumption considerably less comfortable.

Where is their hospital detention? Where is their humanitarian consideration? Where is the urgent medical attention when the person asking for it has no money, no powerful lawyers, and no famous surname?

We have been pushing for medical and humanitarian release for individuals with serious medical conditions. They can be supervised, required to report regularly, prohibited from traveling, and monitored by authorities. They can also be returned to detention when they violate the conditions of their release.

Medical considerations, however, have appeared selectively available to the rich and powerful. We saw humanitarian considerations invoked in the case of Juan Ponce Enrile, when the Supreme Court considered his advanced age, health, and flight risk in granting bail (Enrile v. Sandiganbayan, G.R. No. 213847, August 18, 2015). We have likewise seen former presidents Joseph Estrada and Gloria Macapagal Arroyo receive special detention or medical arrangements.

The answer is not to deny these accommodations to powerful people simply because poor people suffer in jail. The answer is to make humanitarian consideration available to poor people under the same objective standards. Humanity should not become a privilege that depends upon one’s bank account, political position, or surname.

That is where risk assessment becomes important. A rational criminal justice system should not merely ask what crime an accused allegedly committed. It should also ask whether the person poses a flight risk, threatens witnesses, presents a danger to the community, or can be safely supervised outside jail.

Congress should therefore pass a law expanding alternatives to pretrial detention, including medical recognizance and humanitarian release based on medical need and criminogenic risk assessment. The Supreme Court should likewise promulgate clear rules governing medical release for pretrial detainees. Who can avail, what are the criteria, what are the procedures, how can they be applied equally, and how can abuse be avoided?

The placement of Romualdez under hospital confinement may be entirely appropriate. He may truly have a heart condition, and if he does, let him receive the treatment he needs while remaining accountable to the courts. But whatever criteria apply to Romualdez should also apply to thousands of poor Filipinos now languishing in overcrowded jails nationwide.

Not automatically, and certainly not indiscriminately, but rationally, transparently, and equally. If humanitarian justice is good enough for the powerful, it should be good enough for the poor. That is not special treatment; that is equal treatment. – Rappler.com

Raymund E. Narag, PhD, is an associate professor in criminology and criminal justice at the School of Justice and Public Safety, Southern Illinois University, Carbondale.

The author originally posted this to Facebook on September 8, 2026.

World.title: Romualdez joins list of officials who cite illness to delay custody
World.content:
The Leyte lawmaker adds to a growing list of political figures who invoked health concerns amid legal cases

Hours before his arrest on September 7, Leyte 1st District Representative and former House speaker Martin Romualdez was confined at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City.

This is not the first time that a high-profile official has cited medical conditions to justify hospitalization. While some, like Romualdez, reported illness before they were detained, others experienced them during detention.

In the last two decades, at least eight government officials who were charged with various offenses mentioned a variety of health issues affecting the eyes, ears, heart, spine, knees, and even the neck. Who are they?

Martin Romualdez

Romualdez is the latest high-profile individual to be arrested. He was charged with plunder for allegedly receiving approximately P7.44 billion in kickbacks related to flood control projects.

PROBE. Leyte 1st District Representative Martin Romualdez appears before the Independent Commission for Infrastructure on October 14, 2025.

The Ombudsman considered President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s cousin as one of the “central figures” in the massive corruption scheme.

He is currently confined after experiencing a “cardiovascular event, unstable blood pressure, and anxiety attacks,” according to Department of the Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla.

Manuel Bonoan

Former Department of Public Works and Highways secretary Manuel Bonoan was also arrested on June 1 after being charged with plunder and graft for his involvement in the flood control scandal. He was immediately brought to the Philippine National Police General Hospital (PNPGH) due to hypertension.

BONOAN. Former Public Works secretary arrives at the Sandiganbayan in Quezon City on June 2, 2026, for his arraignment for graft.

On June 5, he was put under hospital arrest by the Sandiganbayan 5th Division when his personal physician issued a medical certificate stating that Bonoan is suffering from:

Chronic Renal Disease (stage 4)

Hypertension

Diabetes

Gouty arthritis

Spondylolisthesis (spinal ailment)

Dyslipidemia (abnormal amount of lipids)

Prostate cancer

The Sandiganbayan dropped the charges against him on September 2 after the Ombudsman listed him as its latest state witness. A day later, he regained temporary freedom after being released.

Rodante Marcoleta

Senator Rodante Marcoleta was also arrested on July 6 for plunder over his undeclared P75 million campaign donations.

DETAINED. Senator Rodante Marcoleta, accompanied by PNP Criminal Investigation and Detection Group personnel, leaves the anti-graft court Sandiganbayan on July 15, 2026, and brought to the Quezon City Jail in Payatas.

On the same day of his arrest, he complained of chest pain. Marcoleta was confined at the PNPGH in Camp Crame and placed under medical observation due to hypertension and other health issues.

Days later, on July 15, the Sandiganbayan Third Division ordered Marcoleta to be transferred to the Quezon City Jail Male Dormitory. Doctors also said that the senator’s condition improved and does not need hospitalization.

Jinggoy Estrada

Senator Jinggoy Estrada was also arrested on June 1 for his third plunder case. He cited different medical conditions each time.

BJMP. Senator Jinggoy Estrada arrives at the Sandiganbayan graft court in Quezon City on June 2, 2026, for the arraignment in his graft case.

His latest arrest was due to the flood control scandal, a widespread corruption scheme involving substandard or non-existent government projects, kickbacks, and budget insertions. Jinggoy voluntarily surrendered after his press conference in the Senate on June 1.

On August 26, the senator was hospitalized at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center after an alleged knee injury from walking.

Before his arrest, Remulla said that Jinggoy was suffering from a knee ailment. The senator’s lawyer, however, said he is suffering from osteoarthritis, a condition in the joints.

Jinggoy already complained of knee problems while under detention in 2017, for which the court allowed him to undergo an X-ray and MRI tests.

In 2014, Jinggoy was arrested for plunder and 11 counts of graft due to his involvement in the pork barrel scam, which involved the misuse of public development funds through fake projects and kickbacks. At the time, he complained of recurring shoulder pain, later diagnosed as “frozen shoulder” also at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center.

A year later, he went for a check-up in the same hospital, this time after experiencing light-headedness and acid reflux.

In 2002, he filed another motion to undergo medical treatment because of rectal bleeding.

He was also charged in 2001 for conspiring with his father, then-president Joseph “Erap” Estrada, to gain wealth through the numbers game jueteng. In the same year, he experienced an infraction of the heart due to “psychological stress.”

He was confined twice in Makati because of the condition.

Joseph “Erap” Estrada

On April 25, 2001, the former president was arrested for plunder charges, alongside other co-perpetrators, after amassing substantial wealth through illegal gambling.

ERAP. Former president Joseph ‘Erap’ Estrada sits down in an interview with Rappler in 2013.

He was detained with his son Jinggoy in a presidential suite at St. Luke’s Medical Center a month after his arrest. There, he complained of fever and chills.

Later on, he was found to have chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

The Sandiganbayan allowed Estrada to be transferred to the Veterans Memorial Medical Center (VMMC), where he remained for nearly two-and-a-half years

He was later moved into a rest house in March 2004, where he stayed until his plunder conviction on September 12, 2007.

Imelda Marcos

The anti-graft court Sandiganbayan convicted former Ilocos Norte 2nd District Representative Imelda Marcos of seven counts of graft in 2018.

MOTHER. Former first lady Imelda Marcos at then-senator Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s rally in Mandaluyong.

When Marcos was seeking bail, she claimed in a pleading that she was suffering from “multiple organ infirmities” and was advised by her physician to avoid stress. According to her medical certificate, she was experiencing the following:

diabetes

hypertension

Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease

mini strokes

hearing loss

recurring Urinary Tract Infection

Chronic Recurrent Gastritis

colon polyps

recurring respiratory tract infection

Marcos was granted post-conviction bail in December 2018 by the Sandiganbayan due to her old age and health condition. She was 89 at the time.

Juan Ponce Enrile

The late senator Juan Ponce Enrile was also arrested for his involvement in the pork barrel scam.

ACQUITTED. Then-chief presidential legal counsel and former senator Juan Ponce Enrile arrives on October 4, 2024, at the Sandiganbayan for the promulgation of the P172-million plunder case filed against him, in connection with the pork barrel scam.

The 90-year-old Enrile was placed under hospital arrest on July 4, 2014, because of medical conditions. At the time, Enrile had to receive eye injections twice a week and was reported to be suffering from high blood pressure.

Government doctors also said that Enrile was suffering from a cardiovascular disease, atrial and ventricular arrhythmia, and postnasal drip.

Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo

In 2011, former president Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo was arrested for electoral fraud. She was not allowed to travel abroad to get medical treatment.

NECK BRACE. Former president Gloria Macapagal Arroyo wearing a neck brace while surrounded by security and medical personnel.

The former president, said to be experiencing neck pain, was rushed to St. Luke’s Medical Center, where she had an operation on her cervical spine and two surgeries for bone grafting. This led to the infamous neck brace and wheelchair public appearance.

After posting bail, Arroyo was again arrested in 2012 at the VMMC for plunder charges.

She was placed under hospital arrest for four years before the Supreme Court acquitted her in 2016.

Selective consideration

Southern Illinois University Professor Raymund Narag said medical care for accused individuals was “selectively available to the rich and powerful.”

He compared the unequal consideration to other sick, old, and terminally ill individuals with lesser offenses who remain detained.

“The problem is not that Romualdez is receiving medical attention. The problem is whether the same consideration is available to everyone else. Because right now, how many old, sickly, and terminally ill accused are languishing in our jails, undergoing trial for offenses far less serious than plunder?”

Narag called for the same criteria of medical consideration given to Romualdez to be applied to other detainees. – Rappler.com

World.title: Corona precedent: Can constitutional provision hamper bid to summon Sara Duterte?
World.content:
Months before then-chief justice Renato Corona voluntarily testified in his own trial in 2012, the impeachment court junked the prosecution's request to compel him to take the witness stand

The prosecution team in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte has expressed its desire to call her to the witness stand.

While prosecutor Lorna Kapunan said her team will make the request for subpoena at the proper time, it did not stop the defense from immediately raising its opposition to the plan.

Lead defense lawyer Sheila Sison cites a provision of the Constitution — the same one invoked by the impeachment court in the trial of Renato Corona in 2012 that initially prevented him from taking the witness stand.

No person shall be compelled to be a witness against himself.” Article 3 Section 17 of the 1987 Constitution

Sison cited this constitutional clause in her manifestation, saying that this right of a witness is absolute.

“This is not only a simple right or a statutory right. This is a fundamental right. This is a right emanating from the Constitution itself,” she said.

Play Video

Precedent

On the second day of the Corona trial in January 2012, the Senate impeachment court presided over by Juan Ponce Enrile junked the motion of the prosecution team to summon the chief justice, who enjoys the right against self-incrimination.

The prosecution had wanted Corona and his family to take the witness stand in connection with allegations of ill-gotten wealth.

It was not a unanimous decision: 14 senators voted to quash the motion, while six rejected it.

Interestingly, among those who voted no were senator-siblings Alan and Pia Cayetano — both senator-judges in the Duterte trial — and Manny Villar, whose children Mark and Camile are also current senator-judges.

Among those who voted yes to that motion in the Corona trial, six are incumbent senators today: Lito Lapid, Jinggoy Estrada, Tito Sotto, Kiko Pangilinan, Ping Lacson, and presiding officer Chiz Escudero.

At the Duterte trial, Escudero pointed out to the defense team that Corona still eventually testified in his own trial, but out of his own volition. He was the last witness of his own defense team.

Play Video

“Although there may seem to be…a prohibition against opposing counsel calling the respondent, nothing prevents the respondent from deciding through her counsel to also appear, should she wish to

do so, basing it on Corona and what he did,” Escudero told Sison.

“We are aware of that, your Honor, but I think the Corona event is different,” Sison replied. “Because in that case, I think the decision to testify was voluntary.”

Prosecutors’ stand

The prosecution team’s declaration to summon Duterte at some point in the trial came shortly after it announced its decision to drop remaining witnesses in their article of impeachment on her alleged misuse of confidential funds.

The prosecution presented a total of 12 personalities for the confidential fund misuse case, including three hostile witnesses: former Office of the Vice President special disbursing officer (SDO) Gina Acosta, OVP chief of staff Lemuel Ortonio, and former Department of Education chief of staff Michael Poa.

All three have claimed they don’t have personal knowledge as to how the secret funds were actually disbursed. This is because the OVP and DepEd SDOs had turned over the funds to Duterte’s security officers Raymund Lachica and Dennis Nolasco, in apparent violation of the government joint circular on confidential spending.

“The testimony elicited very clearly a pattern as one would see a chessboard. And the reason I make this metaphor is I am told that I cannot use the word sham nor mastermind, nor can I use the words illegal, improper, extravagant, immoral, unconscionable,” Kapunan said at the trial on Tuesday, September 8.

“All of these pawns and castles and horses and bishops point to only one person, and that accountable person is the Vice President,” she added.

Play Video

Potential oral arguments

Escudero did not issue a ruling on Tuesday, saying the court will await the formal manifestation of the prosecution on the matter.

“You can make your formal comment. We can open it to oral arguments if necessary, before the chair makes a ruling,” Escudero told the defense.

“We do take note, Honorable Luistro, of the constitutional provision specifically Article 3, Section 17. I hope when you make your motion that you will argue insofar as its non-applicability,” he also told lead public prosecutor Jinky Luistro.

Luistro asserted that the prosecution’s plan to call the Vice President to the witness stand after presenting all their impeachment articles is aligned with the ideals of the Constitution.

“It is important that the impeachment court, including the viewing public, witness how the

respondent Vice President answered to all these allegations because this is the spirit behind the

provision of the Constitution on transparency and accountability,” Luistro said. – Rappler.com

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

World.title: 68 Itogon families evacuate amid prolonged rains in Benguet
World.content:
Sixty-eight families (351 people) have voluntarily evacuated their homes in the Benguet municipality of Itogon as prolonged rains from a succession of weather disturbances and the enhanced southwest monsoon raised safety concerns in several communities.

BAGUIO CITY – Sixty-eight families (351 people) have voluntarily evacuated their homes in the Benguet municipality of Itogon as prolonged rains from a succession of weather disturbances and the enhanced southwest monsoon raised safety concerns in several communities.

As of Monday, a total of 227 families, or 874 individuals, have been affected by the continued rains across Itogon’s nine barangays, according to the Municipal Social Welfare and Development Office (MSWDO). It said 81 houses were also reported damaged.

The evacuations were carried out as residents in high-risk areas responded to government advisories to seek safer locations amid weeks of rainfall brought by weather disturbances Luis, Maymay, Neneng, Obet, and Pilandok, as well as the monsoon.

Article continues after this 

READ: Benguet in Cordillera under state of calamity

Barangay Ampucao recorded the highest number of affected families at 65 (256 individuals, followed by Loacan with 47 families (211 people). Gumatdang reported 46 affected families, while Poblacion had 44 families (134 individuals).

The MSWDO distributed 238 family food packs and hygiene kits to affected residents. The provincial government also provided 200 five-kilogram rice packs, while the Office of Civil Defense in the Cordillera provided nonfood items and fuel assistance for emergency response operations.

The Department of Social Welfare and Development also extended cash assistance to affected families in Gumatdang, Virac, Tuding, and Tolibeng in Loacan. The Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office provided additional nonfood items to families in Tolibeng.

Mayor Bernard Waclin, together with the MSWDO and disaster risk reduction councils, led the assessment and relief efforts. The municipal government said no casualties had been reported in Itogon amid the prolonged rains and successive weather disturbances. Maureen Matayew / Contributor/coa

World.title: Zamboanga City marks ‘Day of Remembrance’ for bloody 2013 siege
World.content:
File photo of soldiers standing guard on a street as the battle raged on during the three-week 2013 Zamboanga City siege. Photo by Bong S. Sarmiento

PAGADIAN CITY, Zamboanga del Sur – The Zamboanga City government observed a “Day of Remembrance” on Wednesday for the 2013 bloody Zamboanga Siege that killed hundreds and displaced tens of thousands of residents.

Mayor Khymer Adan Olaso issued Executive Order KHYM 183- 2026 on Tuesday, declaring Wednesday a “Day of Remembrance” to honor the lives lost and the sacrifices made during the 2013 Zamboanga Siege.

The order recognizes the heroism of the security forces who defended the city and remembers the civilians caught in the crossfire during the three-week conflict 13 years ago.

Article continues after this 

READ: PH Army pays tribute to ‘fallen heroes’ in fight to stop 2013 MNLF siege of Zambo City

Olaso highlighted the selflessness of the military, police, and emergency personnel who stood on the frontlines to safeguard the city’s democratic ideals and way of life.

Pursuant to Sangguniang Panlungsod Resolution No. 1019, dated Sept. 2, 2014, the declaration formalizes Sept. 9 as an annual day of commemoration.

The mayor urged local businesses—including major department stores, restaurants, public conveyances, entertainment centers, and resorts—to observe the occasion by offering customers a 20% discount every September 9, with special emphasis on active security personnel, as a gesture of solidarity and appreciation.

The September 2013 siege remains one of the darkest chapters in the city’s history.

Article continues after this 

READ: Never again, Zamboanga City’

Sparked by an influx of Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) fighters identified with the Nur Misuari faction, the three-week standoff directly affected six barangays and displaced 22,196 families—or 122,226 individuals.

Article continues after this 

The urban armed conflict claimed the lives of 25 military and police personnel, alongside 13 civilians, while 266 others were wounded. Rebel casualties were reported at 153 killed in action, with 278 individuals arrested.

The physical and economic destruction was massive.

At least 9,722 homes were burned or destroyed, causing an estimated P200.83 million in damages, while the closure of the city’s airport and seaport paralyzed trade links across Basilan, Sulu, Tawi-Tawi, and the broader Zamboanga Peninsula, resulting in an estimated P331 million in daily economic losses.

Despite the lingering scars, local officials emphasized the resilience of the city’s constituents. Rebuilding and recovery efforts have relied heavily on support from the national government, non-governmental organizations, civil society groups, and international partners.

World.title: Intent to nab dela Rosa not waning amid ‘negotiations’ – PNP
World.content:
Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa faces the media on August 2, 2022 to express his support to the decision of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. not to rejoin the International Criminal Court. (File photo from Albert Calvelo and Bibo Nueva España / Senate PRIB)

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) maintained that its efforts to arrest Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa were not waning despite purported ongoing negotiations with “protectors” for his surrender.

“It will take as long as it will take,” PNP public information chief Col. Allen Rae Co said in a press briefing in Camp Crame on Wednesday.

“Our efforts did not wane, will not wane, and we will not deviate from serving the warrant of arrest,” he insisted.

Article continues after this 

READ: Remulla: Negotiations underway with Bato dela Rosa’s ‘protectors’

Dela Rosa was ordered arrested by the International Criminal Court in a warrant issued last November.

The warrant was only publicized in May and it was in connection with his alleged involvement in former President Rodrigo Duterte’s war against illegal drugs.

On Tuesday, Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla said that the government was in negotiations with dela Rosa’s “protectors,” whom he only identified as “powerful people.”

The senator’s legal counsel, Israelito Torreon, however, denied any personal knowledge of the supposed negotiations nor the protectors.

Article continues after this 

For its part, Co said the PNP’s search for dela Rosa are continuous, but the spokesperson refused to provide further details, citing operational matters.

He further noted that 91 of the 117 firearms registered to dela Rosa are still unaccounted for.

Article continues after this 

“Our FEO is continuously coordinating with the family for the surrender of the guns. Legal police action will be initiated,” Co explained.

The PNP FEO revoked dela Rosa’s firearms license and gun registrations in June as part of the bid to capture him.

Dela Rosa was last seen leaving the Senate premises and was supposedly dropped off in Makati City in the early hours of May 14, after a shooting in the chamber.

World.title: Iloilo City mayor secures power pledges to strengthen local grid
World.content:
In response to recurring power interruptions across Panay Island, Iloilo City Mayor Raisa Treñas has secured critical commitments from energy providers to boost power capacity and build grid redundancy for the fast-growing city. NGCP file photo

ILOILO CITY — In response to recurring power interruptions across Panay Island, Iloilo City Mayor Raisa Treñas has secured critical commitments from energy providers to boost power capacity and build grid redundancy for the fast-growing city.

In a statement released on Wednesday from South Korea, where she is currently on official travel, Treñas said the city government is proactively pursuing long-term solutions to safeguard local power stability despite regional supply challenges.

“We know how frustrating these continuing interruptions and rotational brownouts are for our people,” Treñas noted.

Article continues after this 

READ: Iloilo City mayor: No quick fix to power woes

She added: “Even while the manual load shedding implemented by the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) is not directly within the control of the city government, we will not just wait around.”

To address Panay Island’s vulnerability as it sits at the tail end of the national power grid, the mayor outlined three major power generation projects to strengthen the island’s electricity supply.

The mayor said Panay Energy Development Corporation (PEDC) has committed to expanding its generation capacity, with the additional power targeted to become fully operational by 2028. Meanwhile, cleaner energy provider PH Natural Gas is preparing to establish operations in Iloilo City, which is expected to help diversify the local energy mix.

In nearby Guimaras, MORE Power is also set to operate a 40-megawatt (MW) floating power barge by the first quarter of 2027. The facility is expected to provide immediate backup power and help improve the reliability of electricity supply in Panay.

Article continues after this 

Treñas noted that building redundancy—having multiple, independent sources of electricity—is essential to sustaining Iloilo’s rapid economic expansion and insulating it from wider grid failures.

READ: Visayas power woes highlight need for gridwide upgrade

Article continues after this 

“These are the investments we must continuously pursue because we cannot depend on just one source of power,” Treñas stressed. “Especially here in Panay, being at the tail end of the grid, having more generation, more sources, and more redundancy is vital.”

To ensure these projects proceed without unnecessary delays, the mayor called on the national government and regulatory bodies to fast-track the required permits and approval processes so construction can begin immediately.

World.title: Ombudsman opposes Romualdez’s bid for continued hospital arrest
World.content:
Former House Speaker and Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez is served the warrant for his arrest by the CIDG at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City on Monday night, Sept. 7. INQUIRER / Jason Sigales

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman on Wednesday said it will oppose the motion of former House Speaker Martin Romualdez for extended hospital confinement after his arrest, adding that it will request a team of government doctors to assess whether his declared illnesses could be managed outside the hospital.

READ: Romualdez asks court to extend hospital confinement after arrest

This was the response of Assistant Ombudsman Mico Clavano after Romualdez on Monday filed a Manifestation of Hospital Confinement and Urgent Motion ad Cautelam for Continued Hospital Confinement for continuous lawful custody at the hospital “for so long as inpatient confinement remains medically necessary, certified by his attending physical, until he is medically cleared for transfer.”

Article continues after this 

“The prosecutors will strongly oppose the motion. In fact, the prosecutors will ask that not just one doctor but a team of government doctors assess whether or not the illnesses declared need confinement or can be managed outside of the hospital,” Clavano said in a statement.

Clavano also said that if Romualdez’s illnesses could be managed outside the hospital, the prosecutors would move for his transfer to a regular detention facility, including the other co-accused in the charges.

READ: Martin Romualdez arrested in hospital for plunder

The Sandiganbayan Third Division issued an arrest warrant against Romualdez, former lawmaker Zaldy Co, and two others last Monday for plunder over allegations that they received more than P7 billion in kickbacks from government projects between 2022 and 2025.

Romualdez was arrested in the hospital and he is currently confined at Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City.

Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla on Monday said that according to the former House Speaker’s doctors, he suffered from a cardiovascular event, and was having an anxiety attack and unstable blood pressure. /jpv

World.title: Northern Mindanao cops seize P19-M contraband, net 126 drug pushers
World.content:
FIRST REPORT. Newly installed PRO-10 director Brig. Gen. Nestor Babagay Jr. delivers an opening statement during his first press briefing at Camp 1Lt. Vicente Alagar in Lapasan, Cagayan de Oro City on Tuesday, September 8, 2026. Photo by Cong B. Corrales

CAGAYAN DE ORO CITY — The Police Regional Office-10 (PRO-10) seized around P19 million from alleged illegal activities and netted 126 suspected drug pushers in a span of about two weeks.

Brig. Gen. Nestor Babagay Jr, newly installed PRO-10 director, shared the achievement as he marked 12 days in office during his first press briefing on Tuesday at Camp 1Lt. Vicente Alagar in Barangay Lapasan here.

He sent a message to criminals that “they will not find any breathing room” in the region.

Article continues after this 

READ: Cops net P138-M illegal drugs in Northern Mindanao

“Our provincial and city directors are very good. These first days have set the direction for my leadership of PRO-10,” Babagay told reporters in mixed Filipino and English.

He noted that consistent with the priority agenda of PNP Chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. and the directives of Interior and Local Government Secretary Juanito Victor “Jonvic” Remulla Jr., PRO-10 will remain focused, visible, intelligence-driven, responsive, and accountable.

“We will prioritize sustaining efforts to make Northern Mindanao peaceful,” Babagay said.

Under the Enhanced Managing Police Operations framework, PRO-10’s anti-narcotics campaign chalked the biggest haul, confiscating 1,141 grams of suspected shabu valued at an estimated P7.7 million and arresting 126 drug suspects across 104 operations.

Article continues after this 

Babagay said P6.7 million worth of suspected smuggled cigarettes and P4.4 million worth of equipment and minerals from alleged illegal mining activities were seized in just about two weeks.

The region-wide campaign also curbed loose weapons and underground betting. Under Oplan Kontra Boga, police carried out 73 operations, arresting eight individuals and seizing 71 firearms. In contrast, 10 anti-illegal gambling operations resulted in 18 arrests and the recovery of P5,911 in proceeds and gambling paraphernalia.

Article continues after this 

Manhunt operations accounted for 107 wanted individuals, including 32 classified as most wanted persons. On the counterinsurgency front, Babagay reported that five communist personalities surrendered, turning over three firearms to authorities.

READ: Northern Mindanao cops join global hunt vs cross-border syndicates

Babagay also highlighted urban order under the “Safer Cities Initiative,” which logged 10,030 ordinance violators, with 4,853 individuals fined and 4,897 issued warnings. He said that PRO-10 will maintain maximum visibility patrols, checkpoints, Oplan Bakal, Oplan Sita, Oplan Bandillo, and other area-specific policing interventions.

World.title: ‘No executive suite for Romualdez if transferred to PNP hospital’
World.content:
Former House Speaker and incumbent Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez is served a warrant for his arrest at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City. (INQUIRER.net / Jason Sigales)

MANILA, Philippines — Former House Speaker and incumbent Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez will not be confined in an executive suite if he is transferred to the Philippine National Police General Hospital (PNPGH) in Camp Crame.

“May room nang naka-ready sa kanya,” PNP public information chief Col. Allen Rae Co explained in a press briefing at Camp Crame.

(There is a room waiting for him already.)

Article continues after this 

“Wala ditong executive suite. Rooms are rooms. Ordinary rooms,” he stressed.

(There is no executive suite here. Rooms are rooms. Ordinary rooms.)

READ: DILG chief: ‘We won’t allow’ Romualdez to stay at private hospital

Romualdez was arrested on plunder charges on Monday night while confined at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City for various purported ailments.

On Tuesday, however, Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla said the PNP will ask the Sandiganbayan to transfer Romualdez to the PNPGH to show that the former speaker is not receiving special treatment.

Article continues after this 

“Our doctors have been coordinating with the doctors of Cardinal Santos for practicing rights so we can assess him independently,” Co said.

“And then, they will confer for us to be able to assess if the former Speaker will be physically fit to face the Sandiganbayan,” he added.

Article continues after this 

Romualdez has since requested the Sandiganbayan to allow his continued hospital confinement.

But earlier on Wednesday, the Office of the Ombudsman opposed the motion while asking that another team of government doctors assess whether he needed to be confined.

“We welcome them to erase any doubts or suspicions of special treatment,” Co said.

“The more, the merrier. We very much welcome additional doctors to assess the situation or the health status of our former speaker,” he added.

World.title: Yellow rainfall warning up in Metro Manila, 5 areas in Luzon
World.content:
Image from Pagasa

MANILA, Philippines — The state weather bureau placed Metro Manila and five other areas in Luzon under a yellow rainfall warning on Wednesday due to the effects of the southwest monsoon or habagat.

In its Heavy Rainfall Warning No. 18 issued at 11 a.m., the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) said the following areas were under the yellow warning level:

Metro Manila: Caloocan, Malabon, Navotas, Valenzuela, Quezon City, Makati, Mandaluyong, San Juan, Pasay, Marikina, and Manila

Bataan

Rizal: Rodriguez and San Mateo

Zambales: Olongapo, Subic, Castillejos, San Marcelino, San Narciso, San Antonio, Iba, Botolan, Cabangan, Palauig, San Felipe, Masinloc, and Candelaria

Bulacan: Meycauayan and Obando

Pampanga: Floridablanca and Lubao

Areas under yellow warning tend to experience rainfall between 7.5 mm and 15 mm within one hour and can continue in the next two hours.

Article continues after this 

The yellow warning level likewise indicates a need for the public to “be alert,” with flooding in flood-prone areas identified as its associated hazard, Pagasa said.

Several local government units have already suspended in-person afternoon classes this Wednesday due to the forecast rains.

READ: Walang pasok: Class suspensions on Wednesday, Sept. 9

Meanwhile, according to Pagasa, light to moderate rains with occasional heavy rains were expected within the next three hours over Laguna, portions of Rizal, Bulacan, Tarlac, Batangas, and Quezon.

World.title: Experts: Kazakhstan’s AI Balancing Could Challenge Old Logic of Geopolitical Rivalry
World.content:
ASTANA – For decades, Kazakhstan has built its foreign policy around a principle central to its place in the world: maintaining productive relations with competing powers without becoming dependent on any one of them. This has allowed Astana to work with Russia, China, the United States (US), the European Union and others, even as those powers have competed for influence in Eurasia. AI may be about to test that model in an entirely new way.

But the question may not be whether Kazakhstan will eventually be forced to choose between Washington and Beijing. A more consequential question is whether AI could encourage a different way of organizing international relations in the first place, one in which cooperation, interoperability, transparency and trust become as strategically important as alignment.

Kazakhstan is already at the center of that debate. It is participating in both the U.S.-led Pax Silica initiative and China’s World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), two frameworks that reflect different approaches to the emerging AI landscape.

The overlap has already attracted attention in Washington. Reuters reported in August that the U.S. State Department was preparing to tell countries participating in both Pax Silica and China’s competing AI framework that they would have to choose one side. According to a draft letter reviewed by Reuters, countries seeking to participate in Pax Silica would be expected to commit exclusively to the U.S.-led initiative, although Washington had not decided whether or when to send the letter. Kazakhstan was among the countries identified as participating in both.

That possibility reflects a familiar logic of great-power competition: as a strategic technology becomes more important, major powers seek trusted partners and become less comfortable with those partners maintaining deep ties to their rivals. AI, however, may ultimately make that logic harder to sustain.

Two visions of the AI era

Pax Silica is broader than an AI organization. Launched by the US in late 2025, it is built around securing supply chains that underpin the AI economy, extending from critical minerals and energy to semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, computing infrastructure and logistics. It emphasizes resilience, trusted partners and the protection of sensitive technologies.

WAICO, established in Shanghai on July 16 by 29 founding countries including Kazakhstan, presents itself differently. Beijing describes it as an international intergovernmental organization focused on AI cooperation and global governance.

At a July 17 press briefing, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said China would work with other countries on the basis of “extensive consultation and joint contribution for shared benefit” and seek greater coordination on AI development strategies, governance rules and technical standards. He said China was ready to work with all parties to respond to AI’s opportunities and challenges.

The wording is significant. Pax Silica emphasizes building a trusted technology ecosystem. WAICO is being presented as a platform for broader international participation and coordination. Neither approach is free of geopolitics. Both clearly serve national interests. But they suggest two different ways of thinking about the future of AI: one centered on technological security and trusted supply chains, the other on international cooperation and governance. The question for countries such as Kazakhstan is whether these approaches must ultimately become mutually exclusive.

AI is not simply another strategic industry. There is a temptation to compare AI with oil, gas or telecommunications, all of which have at different times become arenas of strategic competition. The comparison is useful, but incomplete. Oil was a strategic resource. Telecommunications infrastructure created long-term dependencies. AI increasingly encompasses both, while adding another layer: computing, data, software, research and models that can affect almost every sector of the economy.

The AI “stack” begins with critical minerals and energy and extends through chips, computing capacity, data, models and applications. That means competition over AI is simultaneously competition over infrastructure, supply chains, standards, investment and technological capabilities.

But the same characteristics also make AI unusually dependent on cross-border cooperation. No country is likely to control the entire AI ecosystem alone. Research, capital, talent, energy, data and hardware move across borders, while AI applications are increasingly integrated into global industries. That creates a paradox. AI’s strategic importance gives governments a reason to build separate, trusted ecosystems. Its inherently interconnected nature gives them a reason to preserve interoperability between those systems. Kazakhstan is now sitting directly in the middle of that tension.

Kazakhstan’s position

For Astana, participation in both Pax Silica and WAICO fits a foreign policy built on preserving options rather than narrowing them. Kazakhstan needs access to advanced technologies, computing infrastructure, investment, expertise and markets. It also possesses resources and geographic advantages that make it relevant to the emerging AI supply chain.

Alexander Dergay, founder and managing partner of Orbis Nova, has described WAICO as part of China’s broader effort to expand AI cooperation and capacity building across the Global South. He says that the organization is designed around openness and inclusivity while also helping Beijing deepen technological ties with participating countries.

That combination is important. China does not necessarily need countries to make dramatic declarations of political allegiance if its companies, infrastructure, technologies and standards are already becoming embedded in their economies. Temur Umarov, a fellow at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center who focuses on Central Asian countries’ domestic and foreign policies and China’s relations with Russia and Central Asia, says Kazakhstan is unlikely to make a clean choice even if Washington puts pressure on Astana.

“If the US puts Astana in front of an ultimatum in the spirit of the Cold War, it will be a step backwards for American foreign policy in Central Asia,” he wrote on his Telegram channel.

For Umarov, this would run against the region’s basic logic, where successful external partners have historically had to coexist with Russia and China rather than try to displace them.

“Instead of ultimatums in the face of a ban on cooperation with the United States or anyone else, Beijing usually uses the tools it already has,” he said.

Those tools, he says, include Chinese corporations, technology, investment and digital infrastructure, making a sharp technological break with China difficult and, from Kazakhstan’s perspective, unnecessary. His conclusion is deliberately unsentimental.

“Astana and its neighbors in the region will simply do what they are good at — quietly feeding each of the great powers the illusion of their exclusive loyalty while cooperating with everyone,” he said.

That may be precisely what Kazakhstan has done successfully for years. But AI could require something more sophisticated than strategic ambiguity.

The American dilemma

A senior fellow at the Hudson Institute Ken Moriyasu offers a different reason for why Washington may ultimately find it difficult to force Kazakhstan into a binary choice. He describes Kazakhstan as one of the most important “swing states” in the U.S.-China competition and argues that its flexibility is itself strategically valuable to the US.

“This very flexible stance of Kazakhstan is very beneficial for the US strategy,” he said to the Astana Times.

From that perspective, forcing Kazakhstan to choose could undermine one of the very characteristics that makes the country useful to Washington.

“And if the US tries to force Kazakhstan to choose sides, then that really goes against the multi-vector foreign policy, the balancing act, which keeps Kazakhstan very relevant,” he said.

Moriyasu notes that Kazakhstan’s ability to maintain influence with China can itself serve American interests in Eurasia.

“Keeping Kazakhstan a trusted ally and partner in this endeavor is more important than forcing it to choose sides in Pax Silica,” he said.

His argument raises an important question for Washington. Is the objective to build an exclusive American technological bloc, or to preserve a wider strategic balance in which countries such as Kazakhstan can engage China while maintaining close ties with the US? Those two goals may not always lead to the same policy.

The real issue may be bigger than Pax Silica or WAICO

The deeper issue is not formal membership but whether competing AI ecosystems can coexist. Can Chinese models run on U.S.-designed infrastructure? Can data move between systems without creating risks of leakage, surveillance or technology transfer? And who decides what qualifies as a trusted system?

Those questions may matter more than Kazakhstan’s continued membership in both frameworks. AI could therefore force governments to rethink strategic autonomy. Great-power rivalry will remain, but the technology also creates a need for rules that preserve interoperability between competing systems. China’s language around WAICO reflects that logic, emphasizing coordination on AI strategies, governance rules and technical standards. Beijing’s approach is clearly geopolitical, but it also shows how cooperation can become a tool of influence without requiring exclusive blocs.

A new geopolitics of AI

Kazakhstan could translate its balancing diplomacy into a new model of technological governance: neither treating every Chinese technology as a threat nor opening strategic systems indiscriminately, but setting transparent rules for foreign technology, data access, system isolation and security standards.

That would allow Astana to work with competing ecosystems on its own terms and give Washington and Beijing a different basis for competition: whose technologies are more secure, innovative, accessible and trusted. For Kazakhstan, the goal would no longer be to prove loyalty by choosing one side, but competence by managing relations with both.

However, the stakes extend beyond Kazakhstan. AI depends on a network of minerals, energy, chips, computing, data, models and applications. Dividing that network into exclusive spheres could reduce its value. That does not eliminate the need for restrictions around critical infrastructure, advanced chips, sensitive data and dual-use technologies. But it does challenge the assumption that major-power rivalry must force smaller countries into one camp.

Kazakhstan may be an early test of whether a middle power can connect competing technological systems while maintaining enough transparency, security and trust to keep them compatible. Its objective would not simply be to maintain good relations with everyone, but to create rules under which everyone can work with Kazakhstan without requiring exclusive allegiance.

For Washington, that means choosing between treating Kazakhstan as a prize in a contest for technological loyalty and recognizing its value as a connector. For Beijing, it means showing that openness and cooperation can produce trust rather than dependence. And for Astana, the opportunity is to demonstrate that strategic autonomy is not about staying outside the system. It may be about becoming the country in the middle that knows how to make different systems work together.

World.title: Kazakhstan Expands Air Links to Southeast Asia with New Singapore Route
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is continuing to broaden its aviation network across Asia, with SCAT Airlines set to launch flights from Shymkent to Singapore via China’s Sanya on Oct. 20. The new service comes amid a wider expansion of routes by Kazakh carriers to China and other Asian destinations.

Via Sanya

The Shymkent-Sanya flight will take around 6.5 hours, followed by an approximately two-hour transit in Sanya. Passengers will remain in the airport’s sterile transit zone and continue their journey without passing through Chinese passport control.

The Sanya-Singapore segment will take nearly three hours, the airline reported on Sept. 7.

The new route comes as Kazakhstan’s airlines continue to expand connectivity with China and other Asian destinations.

Growing Asian Connectivity

The Air Astana Group reported an 81% increase in capacity to China during the 2026 summer season, reaching 49 flights per week across seven destinations.

The group launched new services from Almaty to Shanghai and Xi’an, from Astana to Guangzhou and from Aktau to Urumqi. FlyArystan is also scheduled to launch twice-weekly flights between Almaty and Chongqing on Sept. 23.

Across the wider network, the group increased services to Central Asia, the Caucasus, Europe, Türkiye and Asia during the summer season.

Passenger Advisory

FlyArystan has advised passengers traveling to or from China to arrive at the airport at least three hours before departure following updated entry and exit procedures that will take effect on Sept. 15.

The airline said immigration checks may take longer and advised passengers to check passport validity and current entry requirements in advance.

The visa-free regime between Kazakhstan and China remains in effect, allowing Kazakh citizens to stay in China for up to 30 calendar days per trip.

World.title: Expert: Kazakhstan Residents See Infrastructure Gains, Demand Further Development
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan residents are largely positive about improvements in their towns and villages, but their expectations are shifting toward further development of everyday infrastructure and services, according to a nationwide survey presented on Sept. 7.

National Analytical Center expert Roza Tleukhan said the findings show that people continue to expect the development course to move forward.

“The survey clearly shows that people retain a strong demand for further development – they notice the changes, value them and expect this course to continue,” Tleukhan said.

Conducted in July-August among 1,000 adult residents through telephone interviews, the survey found that 68% believe conditions in their settlements have improved over the past three years. 82% are satisfied with their current living conditions, while 68% expect further improvement over the next three years.

Visible improvements shape expectations

Residents most often notice improvements in areas they encounter in daily life. Roads were identified by 32% of respondents, followed by landscaping and public amenities (29%), parks and greenery (22%), schools and kindergartens (18%), and new housing (15%).

The results show that public perceptions of infrastructure development are shaped not only by the scale of investment, but also by how visible and usable its results are. The survey reflects residents’ perceptions rather than the actual volume of completed work.

A clear urban-rural distinction also emerged. City residents were more likely to notice improvements in parks, greenery, new housing and public transport, while rural residents more often pointed to roads and utilities.

The next demand is broader

Future priorities indicate where expectations remain high. Roads and landscaping ranked joint first at 26% each, followed by hospitals and clinics (21%), internet and mobile connectivity (20%), schools and kindergartens (19%), utilities (17%), and parks and greenery (16%).

Roads and landscaping rank highly both among recent improvements and future priorities, suggesting that progress has not reduced demand for continued investment.

Meanwhile, healthcare, connectivity and utilities feature more prominently among future priorities than among areas where residents have noticed major improvements. This indicates that public expectations are increasingly focused on service quality and accessibility.

Expectations will test implementation

Confidence in further progress remains relatively strong, with 70% of urban residents and 63% of rural residents expecting conditions to improve over the next three years. Among respondents aged 18-35, the share rises to 76%.

The findings suggest that infrastructure policy will increasingly be judged not only by new construction, but by whether projects improve access to healthcare, connectivity, utilities and other essential services.

For policymakers, the key measure will be whether visible infrastructure gains translate into improvements in the areas where demand remains highest.

The survey therefore points to a positive public assessment while setting a higher benchmark for the next three years: development is expected to remain continuous, visible and relevant to everyday life.

World.title: EDB: Kazakhstan Maintains Growth, Strengthens Position Amid Tighter Global Financing Conditions
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s resilient economic growth, moderate public debt and strong external buffers are strengthening its ability to access global capital markets despite tighter borrowing conditions worldwide, according to the Eurasian Development Bank (EDB) September Macroeconomic Outlook.

The EDB experts said the economy continued to expand this year, with GDP growing 4.1% year-on-year in January-July, while the non-oil sector increased by 5.4%. Construction rose 15.3%, manufacturing 9%, transport and warehousing 7.4%, and trade 5.9%.

“The key factor behind economic growth was the increase in output in the non-resource sector by 5.4% year-on-year,” the report said.

Investment activity also remained strong. Fixed capital investment increased 7.7% year-on-year to 11.5 trillion tenge (US$25.3 billion), supported by state-backed manufacturing projects and growing investment in electricity, information and communications.

At the same time, oil production fell 8.9% to 53.2 million tons in January-July, underscoring the need for continued economic diversification.

Annual inflation slowed to 9.8% in August from a peak of 12.9% in September 2025. The EDB expects inflation to moderate to 9.7% by the end of 2026, while the National Bank’s base rate stood at 16.25% in September.

“The strengthening of the tenge against the dollar by 8.5% since the beginning of the year reduces imported price pressure, while tight monetary conditions limit domestic demand,” the report said.

The report noted that Kazakhstan’s fiscal deficit widened to 1.7% of GDP in January-July, reflecting higher government spending and continued fiscal support for economic activity.

Kazakhstan’s external position remains a key strength. Gross international reserves stood at $63.3 billion as of Aug. 1, while National Fund foreign assets reached $66 billion.

The EDB also highlighted Kazakhstan’s improved sovereign credit standing. On Aug. 21, S&P Global Ratings upgraded Kazakhstan’s sovereign rating from BBB- to BBB with a stable outlook, citing the country’s economic resilience, substantial foreign exchange reserves and expectations of a declining non-oil deficit.

According to the EDB, Kazakhstan’s average public debt stood at 24% of GDP in 2023-2025, significantly below the average for selected A-rated economies. The bank projects the country’s gross public debt to rise moderately to 32% of GDP by 2031.

“Maintaining sustainable economic growth in a complex and rapidly changing external economic environment is another pillar of Kazakhstan’s investment attractiveness,” the report said.

According to the EDB experts, Kazakhstan retains the possibility of regularly accessing global capital markets “in the medium term on comfortable terms.” It added that the transition to the “A” category will depend on “the success of ongoing institutional reforms and the pace of economic diversification.”

The EDB’s regional outlook showed that the economies in its region of operations grew 1.5% year-on-year in the first half of this year, while Central Asian economies expanded by 6%. Domestic demand, investment activity and infrastructure projects remain key drivers of growth.

World.title: Kazakhstan Takes Lead as Central Asia Expands Space Cooperation
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan is positioning itself as a Central Asian space hub as the nation expands its satellite and spacecraft capabilities and deepens regional cooperation, including discussions on a proposed Central Asia Space Agency.

The ambitions were highlighted at Space Days Kazakhstan 2026, an international forum taking place in Astana on Sept. 7–9. The event brings together government representatives, space agencies, international organizations, scientists, technology companies and investors to discuss satellite communications, Earth observation, artificial intelligence and new space technologies.

Speaking at the opening, Deputy Prime Minister – Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev said Kazakhstan’s priority is to strengthen its space industry while making greater use of the country’s space infrastructure.

“Our task is to use the unique legacy of Baikonur to develop a modern and competitive space industry,” Madiyev said.

Kazakhstan is currently modernizing its satellite infrastructure and expanding its capabilities in Earth observation and spacecraft manufacturing.

By 2030, the nation plans to create an international Earth remote sensing satellite constellation comprising nine spacecraft. It will include six satellites from Kazakhstan, as well as spacecraft from Mongolia, the Republic of the Congo and Nigeria. Madiyev said Kazakhstan is open to cooperation with new partners and sees potential to expand the constellation to 14 satellites.

The country is also working to replace KazSat-3 with a new KazSat-3R spacecraft to maintain the stability of Kazakhstan’s national satellite communications system and meet modern technological requirements.

In July, the government allocated 10.4 billion tenge ($22.8 million) from its reserve fund for the creation of KazSat-3R. The new spacecraft is intended to enter service as KazSat-3’s expected service life ends in 2029.

At the same time, Kazakhstan is expanding its domestic space capabilities. A spacecraft assembly and testing center in Astana allows the country to build and test satellites, train engineers and participate in international space projects.

Kairzhan Kozhayev, chairman of Kazakhstan Gharysh Sapary, Kazakhstan’s national operator for Earth remote sensing and high-precision satellite navigation systems, said the country is building the capabilities needed to strengthen its role in the regional space industry.

“We are gradually positioning ourselves as a kind of Central Asian space hub,” Kozhayev told The Astana Times.

Kozhayev also highlighted Kazakhstan’s spacecraft assembly, integration and testing center in Astana and the growing pool of young engineers as important advantages for the country’s space industry. The Astana Times visited the facility in December 2025 to see how Kazakhstan’s spacecraft are assembled and tested.

“We have a lot of brave, smart and unique minds, new generations of engineers growing up so fast,” he said, emphasizing the importance of involving younger specialists in major space projects.

Regional cooperation gains momentum

The forum also highlighted efforts to build an integrated Central Asian and Turkic space ecosystem.

Uzbekistan is exploring closer cooperation with Kazakhstan in Earth observation and space-based monitoring, particularly for water management, agriculture, land use and environmental protection.

Shukhrat Kadirov, director of the Space Research and Technology Agency under Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Digital Technologies, said the two countries were also discussing an initiative to establish a Central Asia Space Agency.

“I believe Central Asia has significant potential to become an active regional hub for the space industry, connecting East and West, and creating new opportunities for innovation, business, international cooperation, and investment,” Kadirov said.

He noted that common regional challenges, including water scarcity, climate change, land degradation and desertification, require solutions that extend beyond national borders.

Deputy Secretary General of the Organization of Turkic States Merey Mukazhan said space cooperation was becoming an important part of the organization’s broader technological agenda.

The OTS has held five meetings of the heads of space agencies, alongside technical consultations and working groups. One of the most concrete outcomes is the joint OTS-SAT satellite project, which will support Earth observation, technology demonstrations in orbit and the development of joint space capabilities.

Mukazhan said the project shows how regional countries can combine expertise and resources to develop capabilities that would be difficult to build independently.

“We are determined to ensure that the Turkic world is not merely a consumer of new technologies but an active contributor to their development,” he said.

From satellites to practical applications

For Kazakhstan, the development of the space sector is increasingly tied to practical applications on Earth.

Madiyev stressed that satellites and launches should not be viewed as an end in themselves. Satellite data are used in Kazakhstan for emergency response and monitoring climate and environmental changes.

The next step, he said, is to move from individual satellite images toward integrated data analysis and practical digital services.

“Artificial intelligence allows us to process space data faster, detect changes earlier, and improve the accuracy of forecasting,” Madiyev said.

This approach is particularly relevant to water management, agriculture and environmental monitoring, areas where Kazakhstan and other Central Asian countries face common challenges.

The European Union is also supporting the development of satellite ground infrastructure and digital connectivity in Central Asia. Ambassador of the European Union to Kazakhstan Aleška Simkić highlighted the EU’s cooperation with Kazakhstan in satellite infrastructure and Earth observation.

She noted that satellite data can increasingly support farmers and improve water management across the region.

“This is space technology working best for farmers, for water management, and for us,” Simkić said.

Madiyev said Kazakhstan’s space strategy would continue to combine infrastructure development with international partnerships. Baikonur Cosmodrome, a major space launch facility in southern Kazakhstan, is expected to remain an active launch site while also developing as an international center for space technology, science, education and tourism.

He identified three priorities for the development of Kazakhstan’s space industry: data, technology and people.

These include improving analytical products based on satellite data, expanding the use of AI, integrating space data into government and sectoral digital platforms, attracting investment and commercializing technologies, as well as strengthening education and international training programmes.

For Kazakhstan, Space Days Kazakhstan is intended to become part of that longer-term effort.

“This forum is only the beginning of this journey,” Madiyev said, adding that Kazakhstan expects concrete agreements and joint projects to emerge from the event and plans to make Space Days Kazakhstan a regular international forum.

World.title: Caspian Sea’s Decline Raises Water Security Concerns As Kazakhstan Strengthens Management
World.content:
ALMATY – The rapid decline of the Caspian Sea is emerging as one of Kazakhstan’s most complex water and environmental challenges, with falling water levels threatening ecosystems, fisheries, coastal infrastructure and communities. As the country strengthens its broader water management system, the changing Caspian is adding urgency to efforts to improve how Kazakhstan monitors and uses its water resources.

The scale of the challenge is becoming visible along Kazakhstan’s Caspian coast. A newly emerged island, already referred to locally as Rybachy, has become a visible sign of the sea’s retreat, while scientists have warned of potentially significant ecological consequences.

Experts have compared some aspects of the current situation with the deterioration of the Aral Sea, although the two water bodies have very different causes and dynamics.

Vadim Ni, founder of the Save the Caspian Sea movement and director of the Social and Environmental Fund, said the consequences are already being felt in several sectors, including shipping, cargo transportation, fisheries, tourism and drinking water supplies in Aktau.

At the same time, speaking with the Inbusiness agency, he noted that the full economic cost of the Caspian’s decline has yet to be systematically assessed.

A changing sea creates economic risks

The Caspian is particularly important for Kazakhstan because its economic role extends far beyond the coastline. The sea supports fisheries, ports and tourism, while Kazakhstan’s ports form part of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, linking China and Europe.

A continued decline in water levels could therefore create additional costs for maritime transportation and port infrastructure. Shallowing waters can restrict access for larger vessels and require adjustments to navigation channels and coastal facilities.

Economist and financial adviser Arman Baiganov said declining water levels could disrupt port infrastructure because deep-draft vessels may no longer be able to access and dock at some facilities. However, the exact economic impact remains difficult to calculate because it will depend on the speed and extent of the decline, as well as the measures taken to adapt infrastructure.

The same uncertainty applies to tourism. Kazakhstan has invested heavily in developing Aktau and other Caspian destinations, but a retreating shoreline could eventually change the location and viability of existing recreation facilities.

“If the water significantly retreats from the shore, tourist bases and recreation areas located today along the coast may have to be relocated or rebuilt closer to the sea,” Baiganov said.

Fisheries face a double pressure

The reduction of shallow-water areas in the northern Caspian affects habitats that are important for fish feeding and reproduction. This is particularly significant for sturgeon species, historically associated with the Caspian ecosystem.

Ni noted that declining water levels are already making fishing more difficult in parts of northeastern Kazakhstan, including the Atyrau region. The geography of the industry has also changed. In 2006, Atyrau accounted for around 13,650 tonnes, or nearly 40%, of total fish catches, according to Ni. By 2024, its share had fallen to just over 20%, with catches of about 9,480 tonnes.

At the same time, Mangystau’s catch increased substantially, from 315 tonnes in 2006 to almost 5,000 tonnes in 2025. But the sea’s decline is only one factor affecting fisheries. Overfishing and poaching also place pressure on fish populations, making it difficult to attribute changes in catches to water levels alone. This mix of environmental and human pressures means adapting to the changing Caspian will require more than infrastructure measures.

Scientists warned about climate change

According to a forecast cited by Ni from researchers at universities in Bremen, Giessen and Utrecht, under a lower-emissions climate scenario the Caspian’s surface area could decline by 23% and its level fall by about nine meters by the end of the century. Under a more severe warming scenario, the area could decline by 34%, with a similar fall in water level.
