World.title: President Emomali Rahmon - three decades of stability and development in Tajikistan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 9. On September 9, Tajikistan marks State Independence Day. In 2026, the country commemorates 35 years since the declaration of independence, a milestone of particular significance in the republic’s modern history.

Over the past decades, Tajikistan has experienced a complex period that included civil war, the restoration of state institutions, the consolidation of peace and national unity, and the subsequent pursuit of large-scale infrastructure development, energy advancement, industrialization, and expanded international cooperation.

A key role in Tajikistan's development process has been attributed to the policy pursued by President Emomali Rahmon. His period of leadership coincided with the most challenging stage of Tajikistan’s post-civil-war recovery and the subsequent consolidation of the country’s modern system of public administration.

One of the principal outcomes of this period has been the preservation of national unity and the establishment of conditions conducive to long-term development. A significant milestone in this process was the signing of the General Agreement on the Establishment of Peace and National Accord in Tajikistan on June 27, 1997. The agreement paved the way for the cessation of armed confrontation and the restoration of stability.

President Emomali Rahmon has repeatedly underscored the historical significance of independence for Tajikistan. “Indeed, independence and freedom are our greatest historical achievement and the foundation for the development of national statehood,” President of Tajikistan Emomali Rahmon said.

Following the end of the civil war, state policy gradually shifted toward economic recovery, infrastructure development, and the creation of conditions conducive to improving living standards. In parallel, Dushanbe began implementing long-term strategies focused on achieving energy independence, ensuring food security, overcoming the country’s communications isolation, and accelerating industrialization.

The outcomes of these policy priorities can now be assessed through a range of economic indicators. According to figures presented by Ambassador of Tajikistan to Azerbaijan Ilhom Abdurahmon during a speech in Baku marking the 35th anniversary of Tajikistan’s state independence, the country’s GDP increased 3.4-fold over the past decade, while average annual economic growth reached 7.6%. In 2025, Tajikistan’s GDP amounted to 173 billion somoni ($18.77 billion), while real economic growth stood at 8.4%.

Over the same period, the country’s population increased from 5.3 million in 1991 to 10.7 million in 2026, while the poverty rate declined to 19%. “Over the years since gaining independence, our country has achieved significant progress in socio-economic development under the leadership of the Leader of the Nation, President of the Republic of Tajikistan, respected Mr. Emomali Rahmon,” Ambassador of Tajikistan to Azerbaijan Ilhom Abdurahmon said.

Energy remains among the principal priorities of Tajikistan’s economic policy. Over the past decade, 60 billion somoni ($6.51 billion) has been invested in the sector, while power generation capacity has increased by more than 1,000 MW. The largest project in this sector remains the Rogun Hydropower Plant. Its construction is viewed by Dushanbe as a strategic project that could strengthen the country’s energy independence, create additional opportunities for industrial development and increase Tajikistan’s export potential.

At the same time, the country is accelerating industrial development. During seven years of implementing its industrialization policy, more than 2,600 new industrial enterprises have been established and commissioned, creating more than 87,000 jobs. During this period, industrial production increased 2.5 times.

Another important factor is infrastructure development. As part of preparations for the 35th anniversary of independence, 29,000 facilities were initially planned for construction. However, more than 31,000 social, industrial, and infrastructure facilities have already been commissioned across the country. More than 70% of them were built with funding from domestic investors and donors.

The transformation has been particularly significant in the regions. More than 8,360 facilities of various types have been commissioned in Khatlon region over the past five years. The development of roads, social facilities, industrial enterprises and urban infrastructure is gradually changing the economic profile of the regions.

Tajikistan’s economic policy is also increasingly focused on human capital, including education, healthcare, culture, sports and expanding opportunities for young people. In his address marking the 35th anniversary of independence, Emomali Rahmon separately emphasized the responsibility of the younger generation for the country’s future.

Alongside domestic development, Tajikistan is consistently expanding its foreign economic and diplomatic ties. One of the most notable areas is cooperation with Azerbaijan. On May 23, 2024, Azerbaijan and Tajikistan signed a Declaration on Strategic Partnership in Baku. The document covers a broad range of areas, from trade and investment to transport, energy, industry, education, and culture.

According to Ilhom Abdurahmon, Azerbaijan currently holds a special place in Dushanbe’s foreign economic strategy. “Azerbaijan is one of Tajikistan’s most important and close partners, with whom we maintain sincere and friendly relations,” Ambassador of Tajikistan to Azerbaijan Ilhom Abdurahmon said.

Economic statistics also point to the intensification of bilateral ties. In 2025, trade turnover between Tajikistan and Azerbaijan increased by 84%, while the volume of strategically important transit transportation increased by 50%. At the same time, the potential for cooperation extends far beyond trade. Dushanbe is considering opportunities to use Azerbaijan’s transport and logistics infrastructure and further develop routes, including the Middle Corridor. Four direct flights per week also operate between Baku and Dushanbe, creating additional opportunities for business and tourism contacts.

Going forward, the combination of energy, industry and transport infrastructure could become one of the key factors in Tajikistan’s further economic development. For a landlocked country, expanding transport links with external markets is of strategic importance. The development of transit routes through Azerbaijan could expand access for Tajik producers to international markets while increasing Tajikistan’s role in regional logistics.

Energy remains an equally important area. The completion of major projects, development of renewable energy sources and modernization of infrastructure could strengthen domestic power supplies and create additional opportunities for electricity exports. Against this backdrop, the 35th anniversary of independence is becoming not only an opportunity for Tajikistan to assess its achievements, but also a starting point for a new stage of development. The country’s authorities have already outlined long-term priorities, including industrialization, energy independence, food security, transport development, digitalization and improving the quality of human capital.

Speaking to military personnel ahead of the anniversary, Emomali Rahmon linked the preservation of the achievements made to the responsibility of the state and society. “Therefore, compliance with the law and the requirements of military regulations, continuous improvement of professional skills, responsibility and devotion to the Motherland, the state and the people of Tajikistan are the most important and sacred duties of every officer and soldier,” the president said.

The military parade held in Dushanbe on September 7, which involved more than 27,000 people, was one of the central events marking the anniversary. At the same time, the symbolism of the 35th anniversary of independence goes far beyond the celebrations. For Dushanbe, the anniversary provides an opportunity to demonstrate the results of state-building over the past decades while also outlining the country’s future direction.

The next phase could be characterized by a gradual shift from large-scale recovery and the construction of basic infrastructure toward deeper economic integration, industrial cooperation, development of the digital economy and increasing export potential. Strategic partners could play a particularly important role in this process, including Azerbaijan, which, due to its geographic position, could become an important element of Tajikistan’s external logistics strategy.

Over 35 years of independence, the country has moved from a period of acute internal crisis and armed conflict toward a development model in which statehood, infrastructure development, energy and industrial policy have become central elements of its national strategy.

The policy of President Emomali Rahmon is viewed as a foundation for maintaining stability, strengthening independence, and creating conditions for the country’s further development.

World.title: Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan to resume passenger ferry services on Caspian Sea
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 9. Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan set to resume passenger ferry services on the Caspian Sea.

This was announced by Ambassador of Kazakhstan to Azerbaijan Alim Bayel. According to the diplomat, the Kazakh side had proposed to Azerbaijan resuming passenger ferry services on the Kuryk Port – Baku Port – Kuryk Port route. The service operated until 2020, when it was suspended due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

Alim Bayel noted that before the service was suspended, approximately 1,500 passengers per year used the ferry connection across the Caspian Sea. He expressed confidence that even more people would be interested in travelling along this route in the coming period. The resumption of the ferry service will give impetus to the development of passenger connectivity between the two countries, increase tourism exchanges, and expand the opportunities offered by the Middle Corridor.

The Ambassador said that the Azerbaijani side has supported Kazakhstan’s proposal. The transport authorities of the two countries have now begun work aimed at restoring passenger services as soon as possible.

Today, 37 air flights are carried out between Baku and Kazakh cities of Astana, Almaty, Shymkent, Aktau and Atyrau.

World.title: TOYO set to join Japan-Turkmenistan committee meeting in Tokyo (Exclusive)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 9. TOYO Engineering expects to participate in the upcoming Japan-Turkmenistan Economic Committee meeting in Tokyo.

The Japanese company made the remarks in an exclusive interview with Trend about the role of the bilateral committee platform in advancing industrial cooperation with Turkmenistan.

"TOYO is a member of the Japan–Turkmenistan Economic Committee and will most probably participate in the forthcoming joint meeting in Tokyo as a member of the Committee," the company said.

According to TOYO, the meeting is expected to bring together government institutions, state-owned enterprises and Japanese companies to discuss industrial priorities and identify practical areas for cooperation.

"We understand that the meeting is intended to provide an opportunity for government organizations, state-owned enterprises and Japanese companies to exchange views on industrial priorities and identify concrete areas of cooperation," the company noted.

TOYO described the committee framework as an important mechanism for expanding bilateral industrial cooperation.

"We regard the bilateral committee framework as a valuable platform for promoting industrial cooperation," the company said.

The company also reaffirmed its interest in contributing to Turkmenistan's industrial development, particularly in gas-chemical and fertilizer projects.

"TOYO remains interested in contributing to Turkmenistan's industrial development, particularly in the gas-chemical and fertilizer sectors, while evaluating each future opportunity on its technical and commercial merits," the company added.

TOYO Engineering Corporation is one of Japan's leading engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) companies, founded in 1961 and positioning itself globally under the concept of "Engineering for Sustainable Growth of the Global Community." The company specializes in gas processing, petrochemicals, fertilizers, power infrastructure, hydrogen, carbon management, and other industrial projects, while also expanding digital engineering and sustainability-oriented solutions across its international operations.

Turkmenistan has become one of TOYO's longest-standing markets in Central Asia. In 2018, the company completed the Kiyanly Polymer Plant for Turkmengaz, delivering a gas separation unit, a 400,000-ton-per-year ethylene plant and an 80,000-ton-per-year polypropylene plant using its proprietary COREFLUX technology. Since 2025, TOYO has been carrying out a major overhaul of the Kiyanly complex together with Türkiye's Rönesans Endüstri Tesisleri, while in February 2026 the partners signed a second-phase cooperation memorandum with Turkmenhimiya. Earlier this year, TOYO President and CEO Eiji Hosoi described Turkmenistan as one of the company's main partners during talks with President Serdar Berdimuhamedov.

World.title: Georgia’s business sector sees wages rise in 2Q2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 9. Average wages in Georgia's business sector increased in the second quarter of 2026, with average remuneration for male employees exceeding the figure recorded for women.

This was reported by Trend in its calculations, based on data released by the National Statistics Office of Georgia (Geostat).

According to Geostat, average monthly remuneration across the business sector reached 2,471.5 lari ($942), up 153.8 lari ($58.6) year-on-year, while remuneration for women employees stood at 1,944.9 lari ($742), up 161.4 lari ($61.5). Women accounted for 43.8% of the 828,400 people employed in the sector, while men represented the remaining 56.2%.

Trend's calculations, based on the overall average and the female-specific figure, show that the implied average monthly remuneration for male employees was approximately 2,882 lari ($1,099). This was around 937 lari ($357), or 32.5%, above the average remuneration for women.

By enterprise size, medium-sized businesses recorded the highest average remuneration, at 2,918.9 lari ($1,113), followed by large businesses at 2,622.8 lari ($1,000) and small businesses at 1,972.3 lari ($752), according to Geostat.

Total personnel costs across the business sector rose 10.3% year-on-year to 5.83 billion lari ($2.22 billion). Trend's calculations show that the change was associated with both a 3.1% increase in the number of employees and a 6.6% rise in average wages.

For reference, Geostat's quarterly enterprise survey does not break down remuneration by gender at the sectoral level. Currency conversions are based on the National Bank of Georgia's exchange rate of 1 lari to $0.3813 as of early August 2026.

World.title: Turkmenistan’s banking system becomes increasingly credit-oriented
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 9. Lending by Turkmenistan’s credit institutions continued to expand in 2026, with loans accounting for more than 81% of the banking system’s total assets by August 1.

The shift reflects a broader reallocation of bank resources toward credit rather than an expansion of the banking system itself. According to consolidated data published by the Central Bank of Turkmenistan, loans provided by credit institutions to other credit institutions, enterprises, organizations and individuals amounted to 136.2 billion Turkmen manats ($38.9 billion) as of August 1, 2026. Trend's calculations based on the data show the figure increased by 2.2% compared with 133.4 billion Turkmen manats ($38.1 billion) at the beginning of 2026, and by 7% compared with 127.4 billion Turkmen manats ($36.4 billion) a year earlier.

Over the same period, total assets of the country's credit institutions stood at 167.4 billion Turkmen manats ($47.8 billion), essentially flat since January 1 but 5.1% higher than a year earlier. As a result, the share of lending in consolidated assets rose to 81.4% by August 1, compared with 79.4% at the beginning of the year and 80% a year earlier.

Trend's analysis indicates that this rising share reflects a continued shift toward credit allocation as the main use of bank resources, rather than a broad expansion of the banking system's balance sheet. Total assets declined slightly from the beginning of 2026, while outstanding loans increased, pushing their share of assets higher - meaning lending is absorbing a growing proportion of available banking resources rather than being fueled by fresh balance-sheet growth.

The remaining components of the asset structure moved modestly: correspondent and reserve accounts with the Central Bank stood at 16.1 billion Turkmen manats ($4.6 billion), down from 19.4 billion Turkmen manats ($5.6 billion) at the start of the year; cash and cash equivalents were roughly stable at 741.5 million Turkmen manats ($211.9 million); fixed assets and investments totaled 1.6 billion manats ($464.9 million); and other assets stood at 11.7 billion Turkmen manats ($3.3 billion) - all broadly consistent with prior periods.

The development is consistent with Turkmenistan's broader policy of using the banking system to support economic activity and priority sectors. The World Bank has earlier noted that state-directed lending remains a major feature of the country's financial sector, particularly for import substitution, export promotion and other priority areas. At the same time, the IMF has argued that directed lending has weakened monetary-policy transmission and distorted credit allocation, calling for a gradual move toward more market-based lending.

The composition of lending will therefore be more important than its headline growth rate. Recent data indicate that credit to the private sector has also been expanding: outstanding loans to private businesses reached 20.2 billion Turkmen manats ($5.8 billion) by February 2026, up 36.4% year-on-year - still a modest fraction of the 136.2 billion Turkmen manats ($38.9 billion) in total lending, but one of the faster-growing segments of the credit book. This suggests that at least part of the increase in lending is reaching private economic activity rather than being driven solely by state institutions.

Overall, the latest figures point to a banking system that is becoming increasingly credit-oriented. If the growing loan share is accompanied by a sustained increase in financing for private companies, productive investment and non-hydrocarbon sectors, it could support Turkmenistan's economic diversification. The longer-term significance of the trend will therefore depend less on the 81% figure itself than on where the expanding volume of credit is ultimately directed.

World.title: Prince George arrives at Eton College: Inside its elite and controversial fame
World.content:
There are very few schools that can guarantee its graduating cohort will be future prime ministers, royals or esteemed stars.

Britain's Eton College may just be the exception.

The exclusive boy's school — just a stone's throw away from Windsor Castle — boasts itself a venerable list of alumni.

More than one in three British PMs including Boris Johnson and David Cameron attended the college, as did author George Orwell, actor Hugh Laurie and adventurer Bear Grylls.

But perhaps the most noted figures to walk the hallowed halls are its generations of British royals.

That includes Prince William and Prince Harry.

And now William's eldest, Prince George, who started his first day at the school this week.

But behind its 586-year history also lies unbending tradition, royal upset and controversy.

Prince George will become the latest royal to enrol at Eton. (X: KensingtonRoyal)

An expensive education — if you can get it

The school was founded in 1440 by Henry VI to provide free education and a gateway to Cambridge for 70 poor boys.

Its noble origins didn't last long.

The charity mission was soon scrapped by Edward IV who annulled the school's grants and transferred a large number of its assets and treasures to St George's Chapel, Windsor.

Today, Eton is one of the UK's most expensive schools — with tuition costing about of 65,000 British pounds ($121,000) a year.

That is if you can pass its enrolment interviews, tests and references.

Admission tests where, as recently as 2011 prospective students were asked to imagine they were prime minister and write a speech arguing that employing the army against violent protesters, and killing many of them, was "both necessary and moral".

The pupils of Eton, ever the bastion of tradition, wear the uniform of a black tail coat over a black waistcoat and pinstriped trousers. (Reuters: Steve Parsons/pool)

Still, it remains one of the most coveted educations boys can acquire.

Some reports say the school sees around 1,300 registrations a year for approximately 250 spots.

And Boris Johnson — at age 16 — was quoted extolling its virtues to parents because "you will imbue your son with the most important thing, a sense of his own importance".

Two brothers, two versions of Eton

Prince William and Harry are perhaps the two Eton alumni who were born already knowing their Commonwealth importance.

While more than half a dozen royals have attended the college, very few were as hounded as the brothers, who graduated in 2000 and 2003 respectively.

At 18, Prince William posed at Eton, showing off his cooking skills, polo practice and studying. (Getty Images: Ken Goff)

On his 18th birthday, William spoke about leaving Eton.

"I'll miss my friends and Dr Gailey (housemaster) who has been a tremendous support to me," he said.

" I've really enjoyed being able to go about Eton as just another student. "

As for why he was doing a photo shoot at the college on his birthday?

"I knew there would be a lot of media interest in my 18th and I didn't want a whole host of media involved," he answered.

"Neither did I want any distractions as I was revising for my A-levels."

While Prince William faced his first day at Eton with Princess Diana at his side, Prince Harry entered the school freshly grieving. (Getty Images: Stefan Rousseau/ PA Images)

His brother's experience wasn't quite the same.

In his memoir Spare, Harry wrote William wanted him to pretend they didn't know each other at school.

The Duke of Sussex also called the school a "profound shock", though soon clung onto the school's strong rugby traditions.

"Sport held me together," he told Time in June.

"I was one of those kids at school who did not enjoy classroom work.

" If it wasn't for the sports field and the amount of sports that were on offer, there's no way I would have stayed in school. "

Further controversy also engulfed Harry's Eton years in 2006, when he was embroiled in cheating allegations.

Dismissed teacher Sarah Forsyth said she had ghostwritten the prince's A-level art project — though Harry was later cleared of the allegations by the exam board.

Prince Harry with his teammates, the Oppidans, after competing in the traditonal Eton wall game. (Getty Images: Pool Photograph/Corbis/Corbis)

A storied history of scandal

And as Prince George begins his Eton journey, the school faces a fresh challenge: escaping further scandal.

For an institution cloaked in tradition, it has also repeatedly been the perpetuator of institutional cover-up.

Dating as far back as the 1920s, MI5 investigated allegations US actress Tallulah Bankhead seduced its students while headmaster Cyril Alington fought to keep the scandal from headlines.

"He wants to do everything possible to keep Eton out of the scandal," an investigator noted.

In recent years moves to progress the school have been met with both outrage and encouragement. (Reuters: Eddie Keogh )

Several teachers have also been convicted of child sexual abuse.

As recently as 2020, former teacher Matthew Mowbray was jailed after abusing boys in the dorms, with the pretext of discussing schoolwork.

The same year, teacher Will Knowland was dismissed for teaching students male aggression was a biological fact and that "saying smash the patriarchy … amounts to saying smash human nature and biological reality".

A letter asking for his reinstatement later gathered thousands of signatures.

In 2022, girls visiting from a nearby state school were also reportedly subjected to misogynistic language and racial slurs.

Eton's traditions, even including the joyful Fourth of June Day celebrations, face increasing scepticism. (Reuters: Eddie Keogh)

Increasingly, Eton faces a world sceptical of its archaic elitism.

Oxford and Cambridge admitted more Etonians each year than the country's entire pool of boys poor enough to get free school meals, The Economist cited in 2009.

It has also been accused of rorting the EU's farm subsidies, scoring £2,652 ($4,979) in funding.

Even Australian venture capitalist Mark Carnegie noted Eton's above-average influence in Sonia Purnell's 2012 book about Boris Johnson

"It became clear to me how powerful Eton is as a manufacturer of cultural capital," he remarked about Mr Johnson's education.

World.title: Coal workers back strike action at heart of WA's energy grid
World.content:
Industrial action is set to hit the heart of Western Australia's power grid after talks between unionised staff and management at one of the state's struggling coal mines broke down.

Premier Coal is the main supplier to state-owned power provider Synergy's Muja and Collie power plants, 200km south of Perth.

The mine is owned by Yancoal Australia, which is controlled by Chinese state-backed miner Yankuang Energy Group.

Workers are pushing for better pay and clarity on their redundancies as part of their final enterprise agreement, with WA's state-owned coal power plants set to be shuttered by 2030.

Final talks on Wednesday morning failed to reach a resolution, setting the scene for strike action, according to Australian Manufacturing Workers' Union (AMWU) state secretary Steve McCartney.

Steve McCartney has been in negotiations with Premier Coal. (ABC News: Courtney Withers )

"The arrogance of that company — they just treat [the workers] with contempt," he said.

"They weren't listening to anything."

Mr McCartney said WA energy consumers should brace for grid disruption if the dispute leads to protracted industrial action.

The ABC has contacted Yancoal Australia for comment.

Strike at the heart of energy grid

The state government said any strike action would not affect power supplies, as Synergy had already stockpiled coal.

The industrial unrest follows confirmation taxpayers would help cover costs of the rehabilitation at the mine, with the government pushing Premier Coal to merge with Indian-owned competitor Griffin Coal.

"What Premier Coal is doing is acting like a hedge fund and trying to work out how much money they can milk out of the government without spending their own; that's a disgrace," Mr McCartney said.

Workers recently picketed at the state parliament, calling for more clarity around the transition away from coal. (ABC News: Nic Perpitch)

He said workers will meet over the next two days to discuss potential dates and lengths for the stop-work action, with support for stoppages longer than 12 hours.

"[Workers] need to make a solid decision so that the company understand we aren't going to tolerate getting pushed around," he said.

More than 90 per cent of the workforce at Premier Coal are unionised.

The vast majority of Mining and Energy Union (MEU) and AMWU workers backed a strike in a recent ballot.

A seam of coal at Premier Coal's Collie mine (ABC South West: Anthony Pancia)

Clarity on the end of coal

The protection against future reductions to workers' redundancy payments are a central sticking point in the negotiations.

MEU state secretary Greg Busson said workers were growing increasingly anxious about the 2030 deadline, and wanted clarity as the company winds down operations.

"[Workers] just want certainty about what their last couple of years at Premier Coal are going to look like," he said.

Greg Busson says workers are increasingly anxious about the 2030 deadline for shuttering state-owned coal power plants. (ABC News: Daniel Mercer)

In April, Premier Coal announced the loss of between 70 and 100 jobs at its mine site near Collie, citing slowing demand for coal-fired power.

Shadow Energy Minister Steve Thomas said workers at the state-owned power stations were receiving better support than the mine workers.

"There is a quiet desperation creeping into the coalfields at Collie as the Labor government closes their industry down, and this industrial action is just the next step," he said.

" There is no certainty for these workers, and it is no wonder that they are pushing for a better deal in the final three years of their job tenure. "

"The government doesn't need to end coal by the end of 2029, and it shouldn't shaft non-Synergy workers in the process."

Premier Coal has been negotiating with workers. (ABC South West WA: Madigan Landry)

A Cook government spokesperson said workers had a right to bargain for wages, and it had supported the Collie transition with more than $700 million in funding.

The spokesperson said the funds included $3.2 million to support Premier Coal workers and contractors impacted by the recent shutdown.

World.title: Late payment from fugitive developer left ICAC witness 'worried' about Porsche
World.content:
A NSW corruption inquiry has heard that a key person of interest was "frustrated" with fugitive property developer Jean Nassif over a large payment he was waiting to receive to fund the purchase of a Porsche.

The Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) is investigating whether people linked to the NSW Liberal Party solicited funds from prohibited donors and other sources to advance the interests of the right-wing NSW Reformers faction.

It is also examining whether donations linked to Mr Nassif were exchanged for political favours.

Jeremy Greenwood arrives at ICAC on Wednesday. (ABC News)

ICAC is probing allegations lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood's company was used to conceal political donations as payments for lobbying and government relations work.

Counsel assisting the commission Peggy Dwyer SC questioned Mr Greenwood about disputes with Mr Nassif over large payments owed to him and his business partner Christian Ellis through their lobbying company Beckington.

"I want it f***ing paid, I'm sick of it. It's actually embarrassing," Mr Greenwood, a former NSW Liberal Party operative, wrote to Mr Ellis.

When Mr Ellis suggested they should receive $400,000, Mr Greenwood replied: "Good, because the Porsche comes in January and I'm getting worried."

"But it's also just really disrespectful from him … Not good if that f***wit doesn't pay."

Dr Dwyer: The f***wit you're talking about there or suggesting somebody who is a f***wit is Jean Nassif, is that right? Mr Greenwood: Probably, yes. Dr Dwyer: You're calling him that name because he hasn't paid you a lump sum that you say you're due? Mr Greenwood: Oh, yeah. I was very frustrated.

Mr Nassif, who is set to give evidence from Lebanon next week. (Supplied)

Dr Dwyer suggested Mr Greenwood was extracting the money from Mr Nassif by promising political outcomes, which Mr Greenwood denied.

"I have no doubt that there was always this constant need to reassure Jean that the right [faction] was strong and growing as a way of him not abandoning Beckington," Mr Greenwood replied.

ICAC is examining allegations that Mr Greenwood, Mr Ellis and Charles Perrottet, brother of former premier Dominic Perrottet, expected to receive a combined $2 million from Mr Nassif.

Dominic Perrottet has not been accused of wrongdoing.

Campaign to remove building commissioner

ICAC also heard evidence of an alleged campaign to damage the reputation of the former NSW building commissioner David Chandler, including attempts to push negative stories about him in the media.

Counsel assisting has alleged political favours for Mr Nassif included removing Mr Chandler as building commissioner.

The inquiry was shown text messages between Mr Greenwood and Toplace executive Sharangan Maheswaran discussing material about Mr Chandler, including a parliamentary process used to obtain government documents.

Mr Maheswaran sent Mr Greenwood a video of Mr Chandler appearing at a budget estimate hearing along with a transcript and asked whether it could be passed to a journalist.

Mr Maheswaran: Bombs away Mr Greenwood: Excellent. Haha I like that, "bombs away".

Mr Chandler has not been accused of any wrongdoing.

Mr Maheswaran then urged Mr Greenwood to involve then-fair trading minister Eleni Petinos.

"Mate, you've got to get Eleni to stick him," Mr Maheswaran wrote.

The key figures in ICAC investigation Eight weeks of public hearings by the ICAC that could change the NSW Liberal Party forever begin on Monday.

Ms Petinos has not been accused of wrongdoing and previously told the inquiry she felt "used" in efforts to remove Mr Chandler.

The inquiry also heard Mr Greenwood told Mr Maheswaran he wanted media stories to portray Mr Chandler as a "loose cannon f***ing up."

On Monday, Mr Greenwood gave evidence that the only written record of an alleged agreement with Beckington for $1 million payments per fast-tracked development project was written on a pink piece of paper by a Toplace employee.

Dr Dwyer suggested that no-one else involved in the alleged arrangement had previously mentioned the note, nor did Mr Greenwood raise it in a private ICAC hearing.

Dr Dwyer: That's because it was a recent invention that you came up with on Monday or prior to Monday to explain that arrangement, isn't it? Mr Greenwood: No, that's absolutely incorrect.

On Monday, Mr Greenwood told the inquiry that Charles Perrottet was also a part of the discussion.

The hearings continue.

World.title: Influential NT cultural and religious leader dies aged 91
World.content:
A pioneer within the Anglican church has been remembered by her family as a “strong cultural woman”, after she passed away this week in the Northern Territory.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the names and images of an Indigenous person who has died, used with the permission of her family.

Reverend Y. Nunggumajbarr died on Monday at Gove District Hospital in the Northern Territory's north-east Arnhem Land after a cancer diagnosis.

Reverend Y. Nunggumajbarr, the first Aboriginal woman to become an ordained priest with the Anglican church, appeared on the ABC program Compass in 2011. (ABC News)

Reverend Y. Nunggumajbarr was ordained as an Anglican priest in 2009 at a ceremony in her home community of Numbulwar, on the Gulf coast in south-east Arnhem Land.

In 2011 Reverend Y. Nunggumajbarr was featured on the ABC's Compass program for her work as the "Arnhem Land priest".

The Reverend told the program that she was born on her "motherland" of Wuyagiba, and as a girl travelled with her parents to live at what was then the Roper River Mission, which after flooding was moved to a site that is now the community of Ngukurr.

It was there she began her life in the church.

A young Y. Nunggumajbarr reading in church. (Supplied)

"Every Sunday we were going to the church, listening to the word of God," she said.

In 1974, she began her training towards priesthood at Nungalinya College in Darwin where she studied theology and linguistics.

"I said to myself I know that God want me to go to Nungalinya college," the Reverend said.

Reverend Y. Nunggumajbarr performing a baptism in her role as a priest for the Anglican church. (Supplied: Josh Mckenzie)

In an email sent to members of the Anglican Dioceses, Bishop Greg Anderson said Reverend Y. Nunggumajbarr had ministered services in nearby Angurugu and Numbulwar for more than a decade, prior to her retirement from the ministry in 2023.

"Her constant focus was on the work of the gospel, and what needed to happen to make it spread," Bishop Anderson wrote.

In her later years Reverend Y. Nunggumajbarr practised pandanus weaving and painting at the Numbulwar Numburindi Art Centre.

Reverend Y. Nunggumajbarr with Anglican Bishop Greg Thompson. (Supplied: Mick and Diamain Uibo)

"She was well known through her cultural side," her daughter Hilda Ngalmi said.

In a video published by the art centre in 2021, Reverend Y. Nunggumajbarr said she began selling her pandanus weavings during the first years of the Numbulwar Mission in the 1950s and 1960s.

"We do weaving because we want to talk about things for ourself and for our children, who we are and where we come from," she said.

'Much more than artworks'

Numbulwar Numburindi Arts centre manager Adélaïde Keraldy said the news of Reverend Y. Nunggumajbarr's passing had come "with great sadness and a very heavy heart".

"[Reverend Y. Nunggumajbarr] was one of those people whose presence shaped the life of our art centre," she said.

" She was a strong woman, an artist, a storyteller, and an important part of our community. "

Ms Keraldy said there was "something very special in the way [Reverend Y. Nunggumajbarr] made art" and "something special about her".

Y. Nunggumajbarr was an integral part of her local arts centre. (Supplied: Numbulwar Numburindi Arts)

"Her work was never separate from life," she said.

"It came from what she knew, what she had seen, what she felt, the places she belonged to and the stories she carried with her.

"We feel incredibly lucky to have spent time with her, to have listened to her stories, to have seen her dance and sing, to have watched her create, and to have helped her artworks travel far beyond Numbulwar."

But Ms Keraldy said Reverend Y. Nunggumajbarr left behind "much more than artworks".

Y. Nunggumajbarr has left a legacy of memories, knowledge and stories. (Supplied: Anglican Diocese NT)

"She leaves a legacy, memories, knowledge, stories and a presence that will remain with us," she said.

"Numbulwar Numburindi Arts will not feel the same without her."

Bush uni creates pathway to Sydney It's a university like no other, in one of the remotest places in Australia, where less than 1 per cent of Indigenous students go on to higher education.

Australian Anglican primate Mark Short said the church thanked God for Reverend Y. Nunggumajbarr's "long and faithful ministry".

"That ministry impacted not just her community at Numbulwar but the whole church through her membership of the National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Anglican Council," he said.

"As a female Aboriginal priest she was a pioneer and I pray many others will be inspired to follow in her footsteps."

Reverend Y. Nunggumajbarr is survived by her six children, 17 grandchildren and according to her daughter, "heaps" of great-grandchildren.

World.title: Australia breaks from international pack on Israeli sanctions
World.content:
It's almost 12 months since Prime Minister Anthony Albanese joined 10 other countries in recognising the state of Palestine at the United Nations General Assembly.

The move was dismissed by some critics as too late, or only symbolic, at the time.

And at that time, the prospects of a Palestinian state ever emerging were already pretty grim, with Gaza largely reduced to rubble and Israel in the process of expanding settlements in the West Bank at a record pace.

In the intervening year, with the world's attention distracted by the conflict with Iran, and by Israel's invasion of a vast swathe of Lebanon, the Israeli cabinet has defied growing criticism from the international community by only escalating its efforts to make a Palestinian state a physical impossibility.

The overnight move by the international community, spearheaded by the United Kingdom but including Canada, France and other European nations, is a significant escalation of attempts to stop Israel from doing that.

The move is not just significant because it escalates penalising actions into trade sanctions.

It is important because of what goes with that, as well as the changing context of Israel's actions.

Israel believes the West Bank 'belongs to us'

In the past, Israel has justified many of its moves to clear Palestinians from their homes — in Gaza, in Jerusalem or the West Bank — on specific security grounds: that houses and the people who lived in them were responsible for, or represented, a security threat.

Even many Israelis who are not fans of the settlement movement will say that, while they don't like them, their presence makes them feel more secure.

But settlers themselves tend to justify their takeover of Palestinian land in the West Bank on the grounds of an assertion of sovereignty, based in the Bible, rather than any immediate security threats emanating from any particular village.

Those past security concerns, and UK Labour's fraught history of allegations of antisemitism, have been part of the reason why Westminster has hesitated to adopt findings against Israel in the international criminal system.

Three G7 countries ban imports from settlements Britain, France and Canada are banning imports from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank in a move that has prompted swift retaliation and could spark a broader geopolitical storm.

As British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Tuesday, "For too long, we have been hesitant to act, fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel."

On Tuesday, local time, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told the House of Commons that the British government "agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank — perpetrated by settler terrorists".

"And all too often the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this and worse, members of it have made statements and taken actions to support the forced displacement of Palestinians," he added.

"Now for a long time, the British government has rightly said settlements are illegal.

"But we have remained silent on the question of the legality of the occupation as a whole, which in 2024 the International Court of Justice concluded was unlawful.

"Today I announce that the official view of the British government is that the occupation is unlawful."

Loading...

The significance of this is that the UK — along with countries like Australia — previously legally separated the status of the settlements from the status of the military occupation of the West Bank as a whole.

The occupation was viewed as a temporary, unresolved political dispute — even though it has been in place since 1967 — to be settled via bilateral negotiations.

Miliband also foreshadowed the likelihood of the International Court of Justice making a finding of genocide against Israel, and that the UK would accept such a finding, and the possibility of further actions at the UN General Assembly in New York later this month.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu repeated his pledge at the time of the UN move last September, saying his government was "going to fulfil our promise that there will be no Palestinian state".

"This place belongs to us," he said.

Benjamin Netanyahu addressed the 80th United Nations General Assembly in New York City last September. (Reuters: Jeenah Moon)

In March this year, Israel announced another 34 settlements in the West Bank, as well as allocating billions of shekels to fast-track infrastructure, roads, and security connectivity for these sites.

In August, it provocatively pushed ahead with a development that Miliband described to the House of Commons on Tuesday as "crossing a long-standing red line": the issuing of tenders for more than 1,200 homes in a 12-square-kilometre tract of land immediately east of Jerusalem known as E1.

The proposed housing development would start to cut the West Bank — Palestinian territory — in half, and also cut it off from Jerusalem, destroying the prospect of a viable Palestinian state.

Sanctions significant, but may be difficult to implement

While settlements — and the increasing violence shown by settlers towards Palestinian landowners (tolerated or even sometimes perpetrated by the Israeli military) — are the most visible signs of Israeli actions in the West Bank, it is also in a state of virtual war on the West Bank economy.

While settlers physically attack Palestinians, they also uproot their trees and divert the water supplies of villages, which make them viable.

But on a larger scale, Israel has increasingly made economic life impossible.

Inside Israel's 'doomsday' development World leaders have fought this Israeli "doomsday" settlement plan in the West Bank for decades. But some fear the war in Gaza could change everything.

Israel has withheld tariffs and revenue it collects on behalf of the Palestinian Authority — which is supposed to fund its provision of day-to-day services. It leaves the Palestinian banking system in a perpetual state of uncertainty by refusing to guarantee it will offer exchange services with the Israeli banking system.

It puts strict limits on how much paper money — even though it is Israeli shekels — can be exchanged between the Palestinian and Israeli economies.

The settlements themselves are often economically unviable. They are not just the odd caravan on a hill but often mini cities.

Though the Israeli government does consider informal settlements, known as outposts, illegal, they often later authorise them as formal settlements.

The Israeli government doesn't just tolerate the violence; it provides massive subsidies to encourage people to move to the settlements, including reduced income tax rates, security gear for unauthorised or "young" outposts as well as funds to purchase vehicles, drones, security cameras, generators, electric gates, and perimeter fences.

That's what makes the various economic trade sanctions announced overnight by the UK, France, Canada and 12 European countries both so significant and also so potentially difficult to implement.

They are also one of the reasons Australia has, on this occasion, broken from the pack of other nations in not adopting the trade sanctions against West Bank businesses.

Australia remains exposed, but may act further

The argument goes that it will be almost impossible for international companies to distinguish between Palestinian businesses in the West Bank and settler businesses, or between sanctions that only hurt settlers and those that might also hurt the Palestinian economy.

The Albanese government knows it remains exposed by its position, which one Labor source described as "rhetorically less impressive", but there are signs it may act further in the coming weeks and months.

Foreign Minister Penny Wong told the Senate on Tuesday that the "Netanyahu government's actions in the West Bank, the rapid expansion of settlements, the proposed E1 settlement development and flagrant settler violence are extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution".

Australia is "not, at this time, pursuing a blanket style import ban", she said, because "we have concerns about the implementation of a blanket ban and unintended consequences for Australian businesses, for Palestinians and for Israelis".

Loading...

The real effectiveness of any blanket bans is likely to be in the realm of finance, rather than sanctions on, say, date farms in the West Bank.

A particular issue for the UK in recent months has been investor "expos" inviting people in Britain to come along and find out how they could invest in the West Bank, in illegally occupied land.

The UK signalled action "against specific companies and individuals who provide services such as construction, infrastructure, financing, or real estate for settlement expansion", Mr Miliband said.

It will also ban the advertising in the UK of illegal settlements.

Just what specific actions France and Canada will take in support of the UK position are unclear, although they have said they will also ban the import of goods from illegal settlements.

The Netherlands, Ireland, Belgium, Spain and Norway have already either banned goods or are in the process of doing so, while Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Poland, Portugal, and Sweden also pledged to take further action overnight.

Loading

To date, the US has been notably quiet about the UK actions, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio not condemning the UK action but saying the US would "obviously" not be going along with it either.

"Obviously, we're not going to do what the UK did. We saw their announcement today, but I don't have any comment on it right now," Rubio told reporters in Miami.

The US does not want to see "anything destabilising going on right now in the West Bank with so much going on in the region", he added.

"We were made aware that they were going to make this decision," he said.

"We heard their arguments as to why. But we share the goal of stability. We don't want to see some uptick in violence or an uptick in conflict or tensions in the West Bank at a very tenuous time in the region."

Loading...

But there already has been more than an "uptick" in conflict on the West Bank, and little sign that the US-led peace initiative for Gaza is making any progress.

Some analysts have expressed concern that the Israeli government would be quite happy to see a full-scale uprising on the West Bank ahead of next month's Israeli elections.

And that raises another aspect of this story: that international actions against Israel often galvanise public opinion in favour of the government.

The UK-led actions this week come just as Netanyahu's standing with voters came under huge new pressures this week with revelations that he had been warned by the United Arab Emirates of the likelihood of a major Hamas attack in the days leading up to October 7, 2023, but failed to pass this intelligence on.

The man who has emerged as the greatest challenge to Netanyahu at next month's elections is Gadi Eisenkot.

While he supports maintaining established settlement blocs in the West Bank and opposes Palestinian statehood, he has also opposed unilateral annexation, criticised provocative outposts, settler violence and controversial construction plans like the E1 development, in part because of the diplomatic toll such moves impose on Israel's international standing.

In the Israeli landscape of 2026, that is quite a different position from that of the current government. But it's unclear whether it would be enough of a change to satisfy an increasingly frustrated international community.

World.title: Black dust pollution sparks push to change Chinese-owned miner's licence
World.content:
Western Australia's environmental regulator says it will look to change the operating licences of a Chinese-owned mining company and the Mid West Ports Authority after months of investigation into dust pollution around Geraldton.

Investigators from the Department of Water and Environmental Regulation (DWER) began examining the nature and source of dust earlier this year, after a surge in complaints of red, black and pink dust from residents and businesses around the city, with complaints localised around its port.

Uncovered trains filled with black iron ore enter the Geraldton Port daily. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Iron ore is the port's main export, with Chinese‑owned Karara Mining, which ships magnetite concentrate, and WA‑based Fenix Resources, which exports hematite, the two key players.

In a statement released today, DWER said its investigation of the "black dust" complaints found magnetite dust emitted from "certain industrial activities" was a contributor to overall dust pollution around the city.

"As a result of this investigation, the department is engaging with Karara Mining Limited and the Mid West Ports Authority in relation to potential licence amendments to deliver improved dust management outcomes," a DWER spokesperson said.

DWER did not disclose the changes it would ask the port and miner to make.

Karara Mine is a large iron ore project in Western Australia's Mid West region, majority-owned and operated by China's Ansteel Group. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Long-running community concern

There have been consistent calls from Geraldton residents and community leaders for wagons pulled by Karara's trains, which carry its iron ore from mine to port, to be fully covered.

In a region known for its strong southerly winds, the path from mine to port loops to the south of schools, hospitals and houses.

Residents have previously told the ABC that black dust picked up by the winds was coating their homes and businesses, and costing thousands of dollars to clean.

A Karara train loaded with iron ore being delivered to Mid West Ports. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

DWER said its investigation into the separate complaints around pink and red dust were ongoing, but nearing completion.

"While substantial information has been assessed, further technical analysis is needed before conclusions can be reached regarding other dust sources or potential regulatory action," DWER said.

"Such investigations can take time to ensure evidence is thoroughly assessed, findings are supported by evidence and processes are fair and defensible."

Iron ore is the main export from the Geraldton Port. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Both Karara Mining and Mid West Ports have been contacted for comment.

World.title: Auditor-general finds nearly half of Victoria's road in very poor condition
World.content:
A new report from Victoria's auditor-general has found almost half of Victoria's road network in poor condition and is crumbling faster than the government can repair it.

The report, tabled in parliament this morning, examined more than 23,000 kilometres of state roads and found that about 48 per cent of the network was in poor or very poor condition in 2024 compared to 39 per cent in 2021.

Newly-appointed Roads Minister Paul Hamer said the government accepted that the roads were not good enough, promising the government would fix the way it deals with roads if re-elected.

"I didn't need a report to tell me the condition of our roads in Victoria need to be improved," Mr Hamer said.

Paul Hamer says the government is working to make road repairs a priority. (ABC News)

Late last month the government announced an extra $352 million of funding to double the number of potholes fixed this year.

"That includes bringing road maintenance back in-house," he said.

"It meets higher standards, it means more accountability, it means more transparency, and it means more local delivery and local expertise."

This figure is in addition to the $1.04 billion allocated to road asset management in this year's budget, bringing the total funding to $1.39 billion.

The report found that the government's current funding commitment falls short of completing the maintenance required to fix the state's roads properly.

According to the auditor-general the funding shortfall led to a focus "more on reactive and safety-critical repairs rather than preventative works".

The Department of Transport and Planning's 2026–27 road maintenance business case, which informs the state budget process, estimated it would cost more than $3 billion per year to maintain road pavement condition at existing levels, while replacing aging assets.

Mr Hamer would not be drawn on whether he would ask Premier Ben Carroll to boost funding.

"We've had record investment over the last few years in each of those financial years, but we need to do more. We are not shying away from that," he said.

More than half of the state roads in the Loddon Mallee region were in very poor condition. (Supplied: Victorian Auditor-General's Office)

Regional communities hit hardest

State roads account for about 15 per cent of the Victorian road network by length, but carry most of Victoria's traffic.

Around 82 per cent of state roads are in regional Victoria.

The report found increasing road use and traffic is adding to the pressure on the network, with growth expected to continue.

The Loddon Mallee region recorded the highest proportion of roads as being in poor or very poor condition, with 69.1 per cent of the region's state roads receiving the rating.

The report found the Loddon Mallee region had the highest proportion of state roads in a poor or very poor condition. (Supplied: Victorian Auditor-General's Office)

Coalition pledge to tackle roads

Victorian opposition roads spokesperson and Nationals leader Danny O'Brien said the findings were damning.

"This is an indictment on the Labor government's inability to look after our roads, to maintain them properly," he said.

Danny O'Brien says the government is not doing enough for the road network. (ABC News )

Mr O'Brien said the Coalition's promise to reinstate the $288 million Country Roads and Bridges Program if it wins government in November would help address the issue.

The Coalition has also promised $5 billion to fix the state's potholes.

It also plans to spend $288 million over four years by providing funds to rural and regional councils to spend on road repairs.

"I believe if we actually do the preventative maintenance, we get on top of it after a couple of years, that will require less money in the longer run," Mr O'Brien said.

The report also highlighted that Victoria has a large and growing road maintenance backlog where the network is deteriorating faster than the pace of repairs.

Based on defect job records, which includes potholes or hazards such as structural failure, the gap between the number of defects identified and the number of defects rectified more than doubled between January 2025 and June 2026.

Call for greater investment and transparency

RACV head of public policy James Williams said the report confirmed what the agency was hearing from motorists.

James Williams says there should be greater transparency around how funding for road repairs is spent. (Supplied: RACV)

"It's no surprise for RACV that the state of the roads in Victoria is not good and probably not a surprise for most Victorian motorists," he said.

So we've seen our road network crumbling and that's after many years of a lack of investment in road resurfacing and that has a direct impact on both safety and productivity."

RACV says it has received a significant increase in reports of damage caused by potholes, with 112,000 tyre punctures recorded last year.

"This causes not only an inconvenience issue, but a safety and productivity issue as well," Mr Williams said.

Mr Williams said a key takeaway from the report was that decision-making around repairs was being conducted by four major contractors who were outsourced to by the government, and not the government or the department.

He said there needed to be greater transparency around how government funding for repairs was spent.

"RACV is very concerned that the decision maker is not the government, it's not the department and therefore there is a lack of transparency there," he said.

World.title: Iceland condemns Trump map showing dozen nations as star-spangled territories
World.content:
Iceland has become the latest nation embroiled in a diplomatic row with the United States, after Donald Trump shared a map online that showed the Nordic nation as part of American territory.

The Arctic island's foreign minister this week summoned the newly appointed US ambassador to explain the image, and its prime minister labelled it as "an insult to Icelanders".

The altercation follows a series of other heated clashes between the leaders of countries Mr Trump has suggested the US should seize or annex in a bid to demonstrate growing American influence.

One of the last encounters between the two leaders occurred at a NATO summit held in the Netherlands in 2025. (Reuters: Toby Melville)

What did Trump's map show?

In a post on his Truth Social media platform, Mr Trump shared a graphic that showed the US and other countries in its region emblazoned with the star and stripes of the American flag.

An image shared online by Donald Trump shows Canada, Mexico, Greenland, Iceland and parts of the Caribbean as US territories emblazoned with the country's flag. (Supplied: Truth Social/@realDonaldTrump)

Among those other nations were the US's immediate neighbours, Mexico and Canada, as well as Greenland, Iceland, Cuba, Guatemala, Belize, El Salvador, Honduras Jamaica, Haiti, Dominican Republic, The Bahamas, Turks and Caicos Islands and other parts of the Antilles archipelago.

The image was posted without a caption or explanation.

The post followed months of Mr Trump voicing plans to seize more territory in the western hemisphere, in a move his administration has attributed to the bolstering of American national security.

Mr Trump has repeatedly spoken of plans to make Canada the "51st state" of the US, and angered authorities in Greenland by suggesting he could launch a takeover of the country.

He has signed executive orders renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America and changing Lake Ontario to Lake America, and in March suggested he could "take" Cuba.

Executive orders in the US are only set out as presidential directives to shape or rewrite American government policy or national laws, and are therefore not legally binding abroad.

Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong has remained tight-lipped about Mr Trump's territorial decisions and comments, but has said: "The future of Greenland is a matter for Denmark and the people of Greenland."

The latest Truth Social post also came hours after the European Commission announced a 200 million euro ($321.9 million) investment in Greenland during a visit by commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

How did Iceland respond?

A day after Mr Trump's post, Icelandic Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir called in the country's US ambassador, Billy Long, who only formally took up the post last month, according to the Icelandic national broadcaster RUV.

"The position was clearly expressed that the post was completely inappropriate," the Icelandic foreign ministry told RUV.

The foreign minister then later told the outlet the move aimed to show the Trump administration that "Iceland is a sovereign, independent state that is responsible for its own destiny".

Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir summoned the US ambassador to Iceland over the image. (Reuters: Caitlin Ochs)

Icelandic Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir also condemned the image.

"There's nothing funny or normal about making fun of the sovereignty of states, especially today when it's not a given," she said at a press conference.

Mr Long did not comment publicly about Mr Trump's post, RUV reported.

The image also attracted the condemnation of Danish leaders, who have repeatedly criticised Mr Trump over his commentary about Greenland, an autonomous territory within the kingdom of Denmark.

Billy Long has not yet publicly commented on Donald Trump's post. (Reuters: Greg Nash)

"This is of course alarming and in many ways inappropriate. These are, of course, signs that the US president still has some grandiose ideas in his head," Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lökke told RUV.

The US State Department, the US embassies in Copenhagen and Reykjavik, and the US consulate in Nuuk have not publicly commented on the post.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, speaking to Danish news agency Ritzau in Nuuk, said the message from Greenland's government and people had been consistent.

The Arctic nation of Greenland has also been in Donald Trump's sights, with the president voicing plans to attempt a takeover of the island. (AP: Evgeniy Maloletka)

"The Greenlandic government and the Greenlandic people have said again and again that they do not want to be American," she said.

"I hope no-one is in any doubt about that, either in the United States or the rest of the world."

In Mexico, President Claudia Sheinbaum also took aim at the post and reiterated the country's independence.

"We reaffirm that Mexico is not nor will be a colony or protectorate of any foreign country," she said in a post on X.

"We are proudly a free, independent and sovereign country."

Is this Trump's first mention of Iceland?

No.

Iceland, which is located 290 kilometres away from the US, first became alarmed when Mr Trump mistakenly named the country four times while speaking about his designs on Greenland.

The country relies on the US for its security because the island has not had a military since gaining independence in 1944. It also has a 1951 bilateral defence agreement with the US.

But the gaffe led its left-leaning coalition government to bring forward the date of a referendum, originally planned for next year, on whether the country should resume long-stalled negotiations to become a member of the European Union.

Loading...

Voters last month rejected the measure, which was partly promoted as an effort to strengthen ties with Europe to better insulate the country from geopolitical instability.

Thousands of Icelanders also signed a petition urging the prime minister to reject Mr Long — a former US congressman for Missouri — as ambassador after he suggested earlier this year that Iceland could become the 52nd US state, with him elected as governor.

Mr Long later apologised for the comments.

ABC/wires

World.title: Glad Max: The headline-grabbing recruit happy with pressure of the NSW No.10
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Glad Max: The headline-grabbing recruit happy with pressure of the NSW No.10 Iain Payten September 9, 2026 — 3:24pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Max Burey already knows a week is a long time in football, let alone a year. Seven days ago, the Waratahs recruit was stuck in the middle of a contract standoff between the Force and NSW, and for no good reason, Burey looked likely to miss the Super Rugby AUS competition. The Waratahs’ new signing Max Burey, posing at the NSW Rugby headquarters. Wolter Peeters Fast-forward a week and Burey has been named at No.10 for the Waratahs opening round clash with the Brumbies on Sunday, after Rugby Australia cut the right-sized cheque and resolved the problem. “It was good to hear,” Burey said. “I was a bit of floating in no-man’s land there for a bit. I had kept training and kept ticking along, making sure I was ready in case. Then I got the green light when (Waratahs interim coach) Locky (McCaffrey) messaged me.



“It’s just good to know what you’re doing so you can start to plan and build off that. Obviously, I’m excited to play footy.” Burey will take his place in a NSW side with a mixture of existing Super Rugby stars, recruits and developing players drawn from the Waratahs pathways and Shute Shield. Last year Sid Harvey, James Hendren and Apolosi Ranawai won full-time contracts via strong form in Super Rugby AUS. Max Burey was the player of the tournament in the Super Rugby AUS competition in 2025. Getty Images McCaffrey has called up several players from the premiership-winning Easts side, including highly-rated outside centre Otto Serfontein, prop Edwin Langi, former Highlanders winger Freedom Vaha’akolo and 18-year blindside flanker Justice Taumoepeau, who will start. Taumoepeau, the son of former Tahs forwards coach Pauli, is also still in the Australian Schools and under 18 squad. The Tahs backrow will also contain 34-year-old Pete Samu and rising Norths openside flanker Marshall Le-Maitre, 20, who is smoky to debut in Super Rugby next season.



Burey will partner in-form Tahs and Easts halfback Teddy Wilson, and he’s keen to make a similar impact on the competition as he did last year, when the 27-year-old was exceptional for the Force. NSW beat the WA side in the final but Burey was named player of the tournament. The Wagga product was approached by the Tahs thereafter. “The coaches here saw me play rugby at a higher level, and to be honest, that’s probably why I ended up here — it was based off that,” he said. Burey’s deal to join NSW as a five-eighth followed, as per a year being an even longer time in rugby than a week, so did plenty of other roster change at the Tahs.



Including the Waratahs signing Bernard Foley, the veteran five-eighth, for 2027. Far from being miffed, Burey was stoked to hear the news. He and Foley have been friends for several years, after first meeting when Burey was with the Australian sevens team in 2022 and Foley trained with the squad. Max Burey will make his NSW debut on Sunday against the Brumbies in Bungendore. Wolter Peeters Burey said he has leaned on Foley as a mentor, including getting advice just ahead of the fateful Super Rugby AUS competition last year. “Around this time last year, I was chatting to him over the phone to get advice, so it ended up being a full-circle moment now that we’ve both ended up at the Waratahs” Burey said. “The conversations I had with him really helped me play well in that tournament, so it will be very beneficial.



”With him, it’s not so much, “This is how I do it, so this is how you have to do it.” He empowers you, asks questions, and makes you think more about the game. I already know what I know; I want to learn what he knows, see how he views the game, and that’s how you grow.” Foley and Burey share similarities; both are short, skilled utility types who came up through sevens and settled at five-eighth. Burey has much to do to reach Foley’s heights in the game, of course, but he says he’s excited to learn from his new teammate. The Tahs’ five-eighth stable of Foley, Burey and rookie Joey Fowler - with all three at different stages - is a “blueprint for how it should work in Aussie rugby”, Burey says. Nick Phipps (right) will play in Super Rugby AUS but Bernard Foley won’t start until November. Sam Mooy “That’s how it should work, almost like a conveyor belt,” he said.



Related Article Force ‘Knocked on the head pretty quickly’: Why Lomax chose Force over potential Storm move “It’s outstanding. Obviously, we have coaches around, but having a guy [like Foley] who’s right in the heat of it, with all his experience, it lets you have one-on-one time to sit down, watch film, and go through things on the field. It’s great.” No Super Rugby jersey in Australia has a brighter spotlight on it than the Waratahs No.10. But Burey, who has played 37 Super games over four years, says he isn’t concerned about the pressure. “You have to lean into it. If you’re playing 10, you’re happy to be wearing the jersey and you don’t want to shy away from it,” he said. “I don’t believe there’s extra pressure. Whether at the Force or anywhere else, whatever jersey you wear, you have to perform.



“Sure, there might be a bit more media coverage, but I have the perfect guy here to help handle that. I don’t see any extra pressure; I see a great opportunity. You want time in that 10 jersey. It will be awesome.” Burey said he is similarly stoked about the chance to play under returning coach Michael Cheika. “He knows what it takes to win Super Rugby. He has a big reputation for being tough, but if you’re going to win Super Rugby, that’s what you need,” Burey said. “He is a world-class coach, and I’m looking forward to being in that environment and learning from him.”

World.title: ‘Cowardly’: Wong slammed by former colleague for dodging Israeli settlement trade ban
World.content:
PoliticsFederalIsraeli-Palestinian conflict ‘Cowardly’: Wong slammed by former colleague for dodging Israeli settlement trade ban Matthew Knott September 9, 2026 — 3:20pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Israel has applauded the Albanese government for declining to join a United Kingdom-led push to crack down on imports from settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories, a move former Labor foreign minister Bob Carr has branded astonishing and cowardly. Australians will continue to be able to buy wine, dates and other products cultivated in Israeli settlements, considered illegal under international law, after the Albanese government declined to join the UK, France, Canada and other nations implementing an import ban. Foreign Minister Penny Wong. Dominic Lorrimer Foreign Minister Penny Wong revealed the government was pursuing new, targeted measures “in coordination with international partners to deter illegal settlements and settler violence” on Tuesday, but would not implement a blanket ban on imports at this time. Asked about the decision, Israel’s ambassador to Australia Hillel Newman said: “We appreciate it very much”.



“It was a wise decision on behalf of Australia. It was a mistake of Britain to go down that path. There is no logic to it, it is based on false assumptions and it’s a dead end,” he said. Israel’s Ambassador to Australia Hillel Newman applauded the government for not imposing an import ban on goods produced in Israeli settlements. Dominic Lorrimer Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar responded with fury to the UK push, announcing he would close the British consulate in East Jerusalem, among other measures. While it would be a decision for the highest levels of the Israeli government, Newman said he could only assume similar measures would have applied to Australia had it joined the UK. By contrast, Carr, who served as foreign minister from 2012 to 2013, said he was “utterly astonished” Australia had not joined the 11 nations who signed up to the joint statement spearheaded by the UK.



Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Israel targets UK in response to sanctions on settlements in West Bank “The government has sanctioned violent settlers in the West Bank. Why then are we not addressing the root cause of the crisis that is currently spiking? Namely, the turbocharging of Israeli settlement activity, all illegal under international law and pursued with one objective: to make a Palestinian state impossible,” he said. Carr, a longtime critic of Israel’s conduct in Gaza and the West Bank, said: “We could have perfect diplomatic comfort about taking such a position because our ‘like-mindeds’ have all moved. Instead we look cowardly and intimidated.” Israel seized the West Bank, home to around 3 million Palestinians, from Jordan in 1967, but it has not formally annexed the territory. Around 700,000 Israeli settlers live in the West Bank and East Jerusalem.



The International Court of Justice said in a 2024 advisory opinion that Israel should stop settlement activity in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, and end its “illegal” occupation of those areas and the Gaza Strip as soon as possible. Loading Newman said it was often difficult to make a distinction between products produced in Israel proper and the West Bank. Banning imports from the Palestinian territories could also have negative consequences for Palestinians, he said. Hundreds of Palestinian workers lost their jobs when SodaStream relocated a factory from the West Bank to Israel in 2016 after an international boycott campaign. Wong alluded to this in a Senate speech by saying: “We have concerns about the implementation of a blanket ban and unintended consequences for Australian businesses, for Palestinians and Israelis.”



Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has been a passionate opponent of the boycott, divestment and sanctions campaign against Israel. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Penny Wong prepares new sanctions against Israel but no trade ban Australians are not believed to purchase large quantities of goods produced in the West Bank, with the main imports being wine, fruit and vegetables and cosmetics from the Dead Sea region. The Australia Palestine Advocacy Network has been running a boycott campaign of Israeli medjool dates on the grounds that many of the dates are likely to have originated from Israeli settlements in the West Bank. Wines made by the Psagot Winery, located in an Israeli settlement close to the de facto Palestinian capital of Ramallah, can be purchased online in Australia.



The provenance of such wines is commonly listed as Israel, meaning consumers would not easily know they originated in settlements considered illegal by the Australian government. Wines and liquors made by companies based in the Israeli-controlled Golan Heights are also widely sold by mainstream Australian retailers. Israel has administered the Golan Heights since seizing it from Syria in the 1967 Six-Day War, but the international community, including Australia, considers it occupied territory. Former Labor cabinet minister Ed Husic had urged Australia to join the UK’s “seismic” move, saying: “I just don’t think we can be left dragging the chain on something as big as this.” UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the British government “agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank perpetrated by settler terrorists”.



Britain’s new policy states that products made in illegal Israeli settlements will no longer be allowed to be imported into the UK, and that the government will have powers to sanction individuals and companies that support, facilitate or profit from illegal settlement activity.
