World.title: Sarah, 7, was just recognised as student of the week. She died on the drive home from school
World.content:
Sarah El Hawli had just won the student of the week award. Hours later, the handwriting star of her year 1 class died in a car accident near a quiet country road. John Bibby checking his fence. Eddie Jim The young girl – described as the “smartest kid in her school” – was picked up along with six other children from Melton South’s Al Iman College on Tuesday afternoon. Among them was her 11-year-old cousin Ossama, who also died after the crash. Police are not sure exactly what caused the four-wheel-drive carrying the children to veer off a road near Parwan and roll onto a steep, dirt nature strip.



Detective Sergeant Tony Gentile described the events that followed as “hectic”. “People [were] everywhere. Witnesses who witnessed it, they stopped and rendered assistance,” he said. “Obviously, with seven children, they were distressed, and they were cared for by paramedics, members of the public and police.” Two air ambulances and nine emergency crews were sent to help, while witnesses rushed to assist paramedics. Sarah was pronounced dead on the scene. Not much is known yet about the young girl’s family, but a close relative said it was difficult to believe she was gone.



Major Collision Investigation Unit detectives are investigating a fatal single-vehicle rollover in Parwan which occurred on Tuesday afternoon. Nine News “She was an angel … she is an angel now,” they said. Ossama died overnight after he was flown to hospital. On Wednesday morning, shards of windscreen glass from the car remained sprawled across the roadside. A single black sneaker, belonging to a child, lay nearby. The scene of the fatal crash near the intersection of Parwan-Exford Road and Exford Road. Eddie Jim



Local farmer John Bibby picked at his wire fence after it was cut by emergency services during the rescue. He got a late night call from the local fire commander about the crash that happened a few metres from his paddock. “It’s just horrible – especially when kids are involved,” he said, glancing down at the dirt. Locals said the road the group travelled on was considered one of the safer routes in the area, which is known for potholes and speeding. The scene on Wednesday morning. Eddie Jim



Richy, a parent at the nearby Exford Primary School, wondered if fencing would be placed along the road, which is near the site of a separate bus crash in May 2023. “There are a few rough spots further up – but right here where it happened, the road’s perfect,” he said. Local communities are in deep grief following Tuesday’s tragic accident. The Australian Islamic Centre said it was supporting the family and assisting with funeral arrangements for the children in what was an “incredibly difficult time”.



“Their loss has deeply affected our entire [...] community. Our hearts are with their parents, family and loved ones as they face an unimaginable loss,” a statement said. A spokesperson from Al Iman College has asked the community to respect the family’s privacy as they grieved. Loading Three boys – one in critical condition – are recovering at the Royal Children’s Hospital. A further three children – a female toddler with minor injuries, and a teenage boy and primary school-aged boy – are in Sunshine Hospital, all in a stable condition.



The 34-year-old female driver was taken to the Royal Melbourne Hospital for observation. Intensive paramedic crews and advanced life support crews were at the scene. Nine News Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: I was blessed to call Blanche d’Alpuget a friend. What an extraordinary life
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsBlanche D'Alpuget Opinion I was blessed to call Blanche d’Alpuget a friend. What an extraordinary life Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author September 9, 2026 — 3:00pm

September 9, 2026 — 3:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Blanche d’Alpuget, who has just died after a brief illness, was a whole lot more than Bob Hawke’s second wife, even though she was the first to note that our former prime minister was ever and always the most important thing in her own life. Her final message released by her family was “our highest calling and greatest achievement is love, the rule of life,” and she surely had Hawke in mind when enunciating it. Blanche d’Alpuget photographed at Chiswick restaurant, Woollahra, in October 2025. Jessica Hromas They met briefly in Indonesia in the mid-70s when he was leading the ACTU and she was living in Jakarta, married to an Australian businessman. On their third meeting, in Australia, shortly afterwards, she later detailed how she felt such a pull towards his charisma that there was, just a “wordless understanding that we were going to sleep together”. “Now it’s none of my damn business,” I asked her when interviewing her last year, “and I deserve to be told to get back in my box and stop being so impertinent, but did it start again before he left The Lodge, or after he left The Lodge?” “Oh, before!” she exulted.



Blanche d'Alpuget with Bob Hawke in 2014. Sireshan Kander. Already an accomplished journalist, she would go on, shortly after beginning her affair with Hawke, to write one of Australia’s most acclaimed biographies of all time, Robert J. Hawke: A Biography, release in 1982. She added to it in 2010, covering his years as prime minister, and then in 2019, after his death released Bob Hawke: The Complete Biography. The first book, particularly, was a masterpiece, often hailed as the country’s first psycho-bio, where she was genuinely “in the head” of her subject, as she knew him so well. After Hawke left The Lodge in 1991, he shortly thereafter left his first wife Hazel, to live with Blanche, and they were married in 1995, for another happy quarter-century before he began ailing badly in 2019. When I asked her what were Bob Hawke’s last words, she replied: “His last words were, ‘This is killing me. I’m dying’. It was, and he was. I have a great belief in the spiritual world, and I believe the spiritual governs the material. The angel of death – for want of a better term – had come and taken a great bite out of him, taking his spleen when he was 17. And now the angel of death had returned, in exactly the same spot where he was seized with excruciating pain. The doctor, whom I called, who’d been treating him before, had no explanation.” That was Blanche. She always felt that her love with Hawke was completely “other-worldly”.



Related Article Opinion

Five Minutes with Fitz Why I turned to crime: Blanche d’Alpuget, six years after losing Bob Hawke Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author I had got to know her in the course of writing Kim Beazley’s biography in the late ’90s, and she was wonderfully generous to me in her advice before publication on how to try and capture him, and always great fun to see ever afterwards. She had an impish sense of humour, mixed with velvet steel in her character which said: “I might be in my 80s, but I am NOT to be messed with.” Blanche was confident and sure of herself. Ten days after Anthony Albanese was elected PM, I happened to be present when she took Jodie Haydon aside to give her full box and dice on what to expect, and how to adapt, to being the partner of the PM. Jodie listened closely, rapt. In recent years, persistent illness plagued her. Every time I saw her for lunch or dinner in the past two years particularly, she seemed a little more frail, a little more bird-like. “I’m … OK ... Yes, OK is the right word,” she told me in that same interview last year. “I’m not yet ‘good’, right? I don’t recommend having COVID and pneumonia twice. As far as I’m concerned, I’m now ... doing fine. But I’d say for the first four years after losing Bob, it was very rough.”



She was, nevertheless, always surrounded by friends, many of them denizens of the Labor Party. When I informed Beazley of her death just after the news broke, he replied: “She was a brilliant bright light. Very intelligent. Full of life. She was a source of joy in Bob’s last years. I did think she would go on a lot longer, she was full of life. Hard to think she is gone.” I will remember her exactly like that. A woman full of life, who had lived an extraordinary one, and documented a great one. Vale, dear Blanche. All of us blessed to know you, were proud to do so. Peter FitzSimons is an author and columnist.

World.title: First look: How the MCG has been transformed into the NFL’s field of dreams
World.content:
SportNFLMelbourne major events First look: How the MCG has been transformed into the NFL’s field of dreams Jon Pierik September 9, 2026 — 2:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The transformation of the MCG into an NFL field of dreams is almost complete, but one of the sport’s more “scary” sights will be missing from Friday’s historic clash. Ahead of the sell-out game between the Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers, the home of AFL and cricket has the full NFL vibe, complete with all the on-field markings required for a rectangular field of almost 110 metres long and 49m wide, vertical posts and painted end zones and team logos. First look: The MCG has been transformed into the home of the NFL on Friday when the Rams and 49ers clash. AP Photo/Asanka Brendon Ratnayake The field is not perfectly central, for the 49ers and Rams wanted the AFL coaches’ boxes they will use to be at the midfield line. The completed field also features the familiar yard lines, numbers and hash marks, helping to deal with yardage measurements. There is dead spacing between the outside line of the field and bottom tier of seating of the oval-shaped venue, NFL officials opting not to fill these areas with seats because of potential beverage and amenity issues.



NFL-mandated camera positions have been installed around the ground, while media have been shifted from the customary press box at centre-wing of the MCC members side to high in the stands. Related Article NFL 2026 ‘Hit even harder’: The viral video that shows the 49ers’ quarterback is in for a torrid time at the MCG Senior event architect Todd Barnes of Populous, the company employed by the NFL to get the MCG ready for the game, said the MCG was spectacular, but suggested it could have more LED lighting inside the venue. “This is probably one of the best international stadiums that I’ve been in. But one of the things I’ve noticed in the NFL marketplaces is that the more LED [lighting] that you have, it just seems like it’s a really big deal,” he said. Barnes also believes the ground’s two high-definition LED scoreboards, which are 25.24 metres wide and 13.1 metres high , should be larger.



“It just seems like it’s the way of the world, is just like getting the fans more integrated with more video type of stuff,” he said. As ground works continue, including extended security areas outside the venue, the 49ers and Rams continue their pre-game preparations. The 49ers were bracing for the Rams to unleash defensive duo Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald for the first time at the MCG on Friday, with Donald, a 185-centimetre, 127-kilogram, three-time defensive player of the year, beast, emerging from retirement on August 30 after two years out. But the Rams coach Sean McVay revealed on Wednesday that Donald, a defensive end, was not ready to play.



“He’s doing a great job. I think he’ll be ready to go sooner rather than later, but we’re making a decision that we think is best for him and for our team,” McVay said in Los Angeles, hours before his team boarded a chartered flight for Melbourne. Related Article NFL 2026 Incredible food, great coffee – and no crocs: Why the 49ers changed their tune on Melbourne “He’s attacked this the right way, but it would have been a really quick turnaround.” Defensive end Garrett has also been under a fitness cloud, in his case swelling in a knee, but McVay insisted he will be “ready to go” at the MCG. “He’s looked great. We’ve been smart with Myles … but his impact has been tremendous,” McVay said.



Ahead of training at AAMI Park on Wednesday, San Francisco coach Kyle Shanahan delivered a priceless response when asked about Donald’s absence. “Very excited. I told you guys last time I talked to you guys, he was definitely playing. So I’ve never been more excited to be wrong about something,” said Shanahan, who has won 11 of 18 games against McVay-led sides. Not ready: Star Los Angeles Rams defensive powerhouse Aaron Donald won’t take to the field at the MCG. Getty Images Donald’s absence means those attending on Friday won’t have the chance to watch Donald and Garrett targeting 49ers quarter-back Brock Purdy through their ruthless “sacking” – tackling a player to the ground with force. NFL great Jeff Saturday, now an ESPN analyst, dubbed that prospect one of the sport’s most “scary” sights. The 49ers have had injury issues of their own to address, for Shanahan said defensive tackle Alfred Collins had torn his patellar tendon in practice on Tuesday, and would miss the entire season.



The Rams will not arrive in Melbourne until Thursday, when they will have their only practice, at Marvel Stadium, late in the afternoon. There has been much debate about the contrasting travel plans of each side. But Shanahan said these would be no excuse for any poor on-field play. “I’m sure it will be a good case study for anybody in the future to sit there and overthink which one helped and not. But the real thing that’s going to help this game … is who plays better football, and whoever doesn’t,” Shanahan said. Prominent ESPN personality Stephen A. Smith warned on Wednesday that “if the Los Angeles Rams get rolling, very few teams, if anybody, is going to be able to stop ’em”. Led by veteran quarter-back Matthew Stafford, the Rams boast elite playmakers, including pass catchers Puka Nacua and Davante Adams.

World.title: Auric adds 102koz shovel-ready gold kicker to WA Coolgardie ambitions
World.content:
Auric Mining has pulled the trigger on another gold acquisition near Coolgardie, snapping up the 102,000-ounce Union Jack gold project in a deal that boosts its global resource inventory by a hefty 51 per cent to 301,000 ounces and strengthens its strategy of becoming a fully integrated gold producer.

The company has signed binding agreements to buy the project for an upfront $6.6 million in cash and $3 million in Auric shares, with further milestone payments tied to future resource growth. The deal hands Auric control of an initial inferred resource of 3.12 million tonnes grading 1.02 grams per tonne (g/t) gold for 102,000 ounces.

Auric Mining’s Burbanks processing facility, subject to a refurbishment study, just 15km from its newest Union Jack project near Coolgardie, WA.

Importantly, Union Jack sits just 15 kilometres by road from Auric’s Burbanks processing plant, putting it firmly within trucking distance and dovetailing neatly with the company’s strategy of snapping up mineable ounces that could ultimately feed its planned processing hub.

The project has all the hallmarks of a classic Goldfields opportunity, with a raft of historic mine shafts and shallow workings, leaving a solid 102,000 ounces at surface with plenty of potential for modern exploration to delve deep. The company says its current resource is based on just 241 drill holes and, importantly, remains open along strike and at depth.

World.title: It has all the right ingredients for a gripping thriller, but this Australian drama is stuck in the wrong gear
World.content:
★★ CultureTV & radioReview It has all the right ingredients for a gripping thriller, but this Australian drama is stuck in the wrong gear Jared Richards September 9, 2026 — 2:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Last Seen ★★ After the emotional cramp that was Amazon Prime Video’s The Runner, where Gal Gadot played a woman sprinting across London in a dull, drab attempt to find her kidnapped son, I was hopeful Last Seen would hit all the hallmarks of the Taken sub-genre. There was promise; the six-part series is Apple TV’s first Australian production, and the next in their stream of new thrillers this year alone, ranging from slick (Lucky), to the overwrought (Cape Fear) and funny (Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed), but always engaging. Patrick Brammall in Last Seen, in which he plays a father whose daughter goes missing. The premise is immediate: 11 years after his daughter Maggie went missing, triple-zero operator Ian (Colin From Accounts co-creator Patrick Brammall) receives a call on-duty and is immediately convinced it’s her.



Related Article Review What to stream this week: Sharehouse comedy returns better than ever, plus five more picks Stopping at nothing to find her, Ian – a former cop who lost his job and marriage in the haze of grief – is soon chasing after cars, roughing up teens for leads and casing suspects up down and through Victoria’s dense, foreboding rainforests that made an eerie backdrop in The Dry 2. Add in an ensemble filled with actors able to tap into intense, dark depths – including Daniel Henshall (Snowtown), Brendan Cowell (Plum) and Maxine Peake (Say Nothing) – and Last Seen has all the ingredients for a gripping thriller. Strange, then, for Last Seen to continually undercut its tension with sluggish flashbacks and poorly placed left-turns just as a scenario is building. There is also, fundamentally, no mystery within the show’s six episodes, with the who and why established for the audience by the second episode. That is a carry over from its source material, US crime-novelist Ryan David Jahn’s The Dispatcher, which establishes early if Maggie is alive and, if she is, who kidnapped her. But an airport thriller is a fast, furious read, while Last Seen’s script from Kris Mrksa stretches out these non-relevations. Loading That might work for some people. It certainly gives Brammall a lot to work with to establish how hollowed-out Ian is by Maggie’s disappearance, a crack often making it through to his voice.



But if The Runner lacked any emotion, Last Seen might be overwhelmed by it. Take the pilot, which opens with the discovery of a toddler’s body that the audience knows – via the show’s well-publicised premise – cannot be Maggie’s. Of course, there’s immense pain witnessing Ian and now ex-wife Debbie (Jessica Wren) find a false resolution, with the latter hoping to lay her daughter (and grief) to rest while Ian fixates on revenge. That the dispatch call doesn’t arrive until the end of episode two is indicative of Last Seen’s reluctance to move forward – a stasis that mirrors Ian, but isn’t particularly interesting to watch. Last Seen is now streaming on Apple TV. Want more TV? We’ve got you.

World.title: Golden Dragon breathes fire with high-grade WA gold hits
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Golden Dragon breathes fire with high-grade WA gold hits Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward September 9, 2026 — 2:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Golden Dragon Mining has hit high-grade gold at its Behring Bore and Coodardy prospects at its Cue project in Western Australia’s Murchison region, with a new quartz lode at Behring Bore returning four metres at a solid 6.98 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from just 44m. The result comes as re-assays of previous drilling at the nearby Coodardy prospect, just 400m away, also delivered a suite of spectacular high-grade hits including an 11-metre intersection grading 6.42g/t gold from 45m, containing a bonanza 1-metre section going an eye-watering 59.2 g/t gold. Golden Dragon Mining is drilling its Cue gold project in Western Australia’s prolific Murchison region. The company’s ground sits in a well-endowed part of the world, with WA’s Murchison region hosting a litany of major gold deposits. Golden Dragon previously pegged new ground right next door to Westgold Resources’ formidable 2.3-million-ounce Big Bell mine, highlighting the golden pedigree of the neighbourhood. Golden Dragon’s latest reverse circulation (RC) drilling campaign at Coodardy was designed to test for extensions to mineralisation, successfully stretching the known system to a strike length of 500m. The system remains open to the north, south and northeast.



‘Importantly, mineralisation remains open along strike and at depth at both prospects.’ Golden Dragon Mining managing director Simon Buswell-Smith Re-assaying one-metre intervals from previous 4m composite samples at Coodardy further defined the high-grade nature of the mineralisation. In addition to the stunning 1m at 59.2g/t gold, other standout re-assay results included a 6-metre intercept grading 5.02g/t gold from a shallow 28m, which hosted a higher-grade one-metre slice at a hefty 28.1g/t. The company says the results have helped define a high-grade, northeast-trending orientation within the broader mineralised system at Coodardy, providing a priority target for follow-up drilling. Over at the Behring Bore prospect, the new high-grade intersection of 4m at 6.98g/t gold has added another dimension to the broader system. The company says gold mineralisation there is hosted within an altered, pyritic quartz dolerite, a rock type recognised as a host for significant gold mineralisation in Western Australia. Golden Dragon says it has identified a strong correlation between rich gold and increased alteration intensity within the dolerite, providing an important geological pointer for targeting further mineralisation.



Previous drilling at Behring Bore has already served up some impressive numbers, with re-assays confirming 7m grading 4.35g/t gold from 44m, including 1m at an eye-catching 25.3g/t gold, and a wide 19-metre zone grading 1.72g/t gold from 41m, containing a 3-metre section at 7.42g/t gold. Golden Dragon Mining managing director Simon Buswell-Smith said: “At Behring Bore, the new high-grade quartz lode intersection of 4m @ 6.98g/t gold from 44m in one hole is an exciting result and adds a new high-grade component to the broader mineralised system. At Coodardy, the resampling and re-assaying of previous drilling has returned exceptional high-grade results, including 1m @ 59.20g/t gold within 11m @ 6.42g/t gold.” The company recently lit up a mouthwatering three-kilometre-long gold-in-soil anomaly at the Cue project, effectively stitching together four previously separate prospects, including Behring Bore, Curtis Find, Coodardy and Piston into what looks to be a single, large, mineralised corridor. The newly defined three-kilometre-long corridor adds considerable weight to the string of high-grade reverse-circulation drilling hits the company has already clocked up at the individual prospects now potentially linked by the new soil anomalies. Importantly, mineralisation remains open along strike and at depth at both prospects, with the company moving quickly to follow up its success. A larger RC rig has now been mobilised to the site to test the systems at depth, chasing extensions and continuity of the high-grade zones. Notably, Golden Dragon also recently secured a significant $2.2 million cornerstone investment at a 17.65 per cent premium to its previously traded share price. The deal saw Shanghai-listed heavyweight Chengtun Mining Group, via Chengtun Gold, bag a 19.89 per cent stake in the junior explorer, a move that suggests a significant vote of confidence in the company’s strategy.



With a larger rig now spinning the rods and a swag of high-grade targets to chase, Golden Dragon looks to be well-placed to build on its early exploration success. In a part of the world where proximity to a major mine can mean everything, having two high-grade prospects just 400m apart and open in all directions could get very interesting very quickly. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.title: Glad Max: The headline-grabbing recruit happy with pressure of the NSW No.10
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Glad Max: The headline-grabbing recruit happy with pressure of the NSW No.10 Iain Payten September 9, 2026 — 3:24pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Max Burey already knows a week is a long time in football, let alone a year. Seven days ago, the Waratahs recruit was stuck in the middle of a contract standoff between the Force and NSW, and for no good reason, Burey looked likely to miss the Super Rugby AUS competition. The Waratahs’ new signing Max Burey, posing at the NSW Rugby headquarters. Wolter Peeters Fast-forward a week and Burey has been named at No.10 for the Waratahs opening round clash with the Brumbies on Sunday, after Rugby Australia cut the right-sized cheque and resolved the problem. “It was good to hear,” Burey said. “I was a bit of floating in no-man’s land there for a bit. I had kept training and kept ticking along, making sure I was ready in case. Then I got the green light when (Waratahs interim coach) Locky (McCaffrey) messaged me.



“It’s just good to know what you’re doing so you can start to plan and build off that. Obviously, I’m excited to play footy.” Burey will take his place in a NSW side with a mixture of existing Super Rugby stars, recruits and developing players drawn from the Waratahs pathways and Shute Shield. Last year Sid Harvey, James Hendren and Apolosi Ranawai won full-time contracts via strong form in Super Rugby AUS. Max Burey was the player of the tournament in the Super Rugby AUS competition in 2025. Getty Images McCaffrey has called up several players from the premiership-winning Easts side, including highly-rated outside centre Otto Serfontein, prop Edwin Langi, former Highlanders winger Freedom Vaha’akolo and 18-year blindside flanker Justice Taumoepeau, who will start. Taumoepeau, the son of former Tahs forwards coach Pauli, is also still in the Australian Schools and under 18 squad. The Tahs backrow will also contain 34-year-old Pete Samu and rising Norths openside flanker Marshall Le-Maitre, 20, who is smoky to debut in Super Rugby next season.



Burey will partner in-form Tahs and Easts halfback Teddy Wilson, and he’s keen to make a similar impact on the competition as he did last year, when the 27-year-old was exceptional for the Force. NSW beat the WA side in the final but Burey was named player of the tournament. The Wagga product was approached by the Tahs thereafter. “The coaches here saw me play rugby at a higher level, and to be honest, that’s probably why I ended up here — it was based off that,” he said. Burey’s deal to join NSW as a five-eighth followed, as per a year being an even longer time in rugby than a week, so did plenty of other roster change at the Tahs.



Including the Waratahs signing Bernard Foley, the veteran five-eighth, for 2027. Far from being miffed, Burey was stoked to hear the news. He and Foley have been friends for several years, after first meeting when Burey was with the Australian sevens team in 2022 and Foley trained with the squad. Max Burey will make his NSW debut on Sunday against the Brumbies in Bungendore. Wolter Peeters Burey said he has leaned on Foley as a mentor, including getting advice just ahead of the fateful Super Rugby AUS competition last year. “Around this time last year, I was chatting to him over the phone to get advice, so it ended up being a full-circle moment now that we’ve both ended up at the Waratahs” Burey said. “The conversations I had with him really helped me play well in that tournament, so it will be very beneficial.



”With him, it’s not so much, “This is how I do it, so this is how you have to do it.” He empowers you, asks questions, and makes you think more about the game. I already know what I know; I want to learn what he knows, see how he views the game, and that’s how you grow.” Foley and Burey share similarities; both are short, skilled utility types who came up through sevens and settled at five-eighth. Burey has much to do to reach Foley’s heights in the game, of course, but he says he’s excited to learn from his new teammate. The Tahs’ five-eighth stable of Foley, Burey and rookie Joey Fowler - with all three at different stages - is a “blueprint for how it should work in Aussie rugby”, Burey says. Nick Phipps (right) will play in Super Rugby AUS but Bernard Foley won’t start until November. Sam Mooy “That’s how it should work, almost like a conveyor belt,” he said.



Related Article Force ‘Knocked on the head pretty quickly’: Why Lomax chose Force over potential Storm move “It’s outstanding. Obviously, we have coaches around, but having a guy [like Foley] who’s right in the heat of it, with all his experience, it lets you have one-on-one time to sit down, watch film, and go through things on the field. It’s great.” No Super Rugby jersey in Australia has a brighter spotlight on it than the Waratahs No.10. But Burey, who has played 37 Super games over four years, says he isn’t concerned about the pressure. “You have to lean into it. If you’re playing 10, you’re happy to be wearing the jersey and you don’t want to shy away from it,” he said. “I don’t believe there’s extra pressure. Whether at the Force or anywhere else, whatever jersey you wear, you have to perform.



“Sure, there might be a bit more media coverage, but I have the perfect guy here to help handle that. I don’t see any extra pressure; I see a great opportunity. You want time in that 10 jersey. It will be awesome.” Burey said he is similarly stoked about the chance to play under returning coach Michael Cheika. “He knows what it takes to win Super Rugby. He has a big reputation for being tough, but if you’re going to win Super Rugby, that’s what you need,” Burey said. “He is a world-class coach, and I’m looking forward to being in that environment and learning from him.”

World.title: ‘Cowardly’: Wong slammed by former colleague for dodging Israeli settlement trade ban
World.content:
PoliticsFederalIsraeli-Palestinian conflict ‘Cowardly’: Wong slammed by former colleague for dodging Israeli settlement trade ban Matthew Knott September 9, 2026 — 3:20pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Israel has applauded the Albanese government for declining to join a United Kingdom-led push to crack down on imports from settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories, a move former Labor foreign minister Bob Carr has branded astonishing and cowardly. Australians will continue to be able to buy wine, dates and other products cultivated in Israeli settlements, considered illegal under international law, after the Albanese government declined to join the UK, France, Canada and other nations implementing an import ban. Foreign Minister Penny Wong. Dominic Lorrimer Foreign Minister Penny Wong revealed the government was pursuing new, targeted measures “in coordination with international partners to deter illegal settlements and settler violence” on Tuesday, but would not implement a blanket ban on imports at this time. Asked about the decision, Israel’s ambassador to Australia Hillel Newman said: “We appreciate it very much”.



“It was a wise decision on behalf of Australia. It was a mistake of Britain to go down that path. There is no logic to it, it is based on false assumptions and it’s a dead end,” he said. Israel’s Ambassador to Australia Hillel Newman applauded the government for not imposing an import ban on goods produced in Israeli settlements. Dominic Lorrimer Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar responded with fury to the UK push, announcing he would close the British consulate in East Jerusalem, among other measures. While it would be a decision for the highest levels of the Israeli government, Newman said he could only assume similar measures would have applied to Australia had it joined the UK. By contrast, Carr, who served as foreign minister from 2012 to 2013, said he was “utterly astonished” Australia had not joined the 11 nations who signed up to the joint statement spearheaded by the UK.



Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Israel targets UK in response to sanctions on settlements in West Bank “The government has sanctioned violent settlers in the West Bank. Why then are we not addressing the root cause of the crisis that is currently spiking? Namely, the turbocharging of Israeli settlement activity, all illegal under international law and pursued with one objective: to make a Palestinian state impossible,” he said. Carr, a longtime critic of Israel’s conduct in Gaza and the West Bank, said: “We could have perfect diplomatic comfort about taking such a position because our ‘like-mindeds’ have all moved. Instead we look cowardly and intimidated.” Israel seized the West Bank, home to around 3 million Palestinians, from Jordan in 1967, but it has not formally annexed the territory. Around 700,000 Israeli settlers live in the West Bank and East Jerusalem.



The International Court of Justice said in a 2024 advisory opinion that Israel should stop settlement activity in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, and end its “illegal” occupation of those areas and the Gaza Strip as soon as possible. Loading Newman said it was often difficult to make a distinction between products produced in Israel proper and the West Bank. Banning imports from the Palestinian territories could also have negative consequences for Palestinians, he said. Hundreds of Palestinian workers lost their jobs when SodaStream relocated a factory from the West Bank to Israel in 2016 after an international boycott campaign. Wong alluded to this in a Senate speech by saying: “We have concerns about the implementation of a blanket ban and unintended consequences for Australian businesses, for Palestinians and Israelis.”



Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has been a passionate opponent of the boycott, divestment and sanctions campaign against Israel. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Penny Wong prepares new sanctions against Israel but no trade ban Australians are not believed to purchase large quantities of goods produced in the West Bank, with the main imports being wine, fruit and vegetables and cosmetics from the Dead Sea region. The Australia Palestine Advocacy Network has been running a boycott campaign of Israeli medjool dates on the grounds that many of the dates are likely to have originated from Israeli settlements in the West Bank. Wines made by the Psagot Winery, located in an Israeli settlement close to the de facto Palestinian capital of Ramallah, can be purchased online in Australia.



The provenance of such wines is commonly listed as Israel, meaning consumers would not easily know they originated in settlements considered illegal by the Australian government. Wines and liquors made by companies based in the Israeli-controlled Golan Heights are also widely sold by mainstream Australian retailers. Israel has administered the Golan Heights since seizing it from Syria in the 1967 Six-Day War, but the international community, including Australia, considers it occupied territory. Former Labor cabinet minister Ed Husic had urged Australia to join the UK’s “seismic” move, saying: “I just don’t think we can be left dragging the chain on something as big as this.” UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the British government “agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank perpetrated by settler terrorists”.



Britain’s new policy states that products made in illegal Israeli settlements will no longer be allowed to be imported into the UK, and that the government will have powers to sanction individuals and companies that support, facilitate or profit from illegal settlement activity. World.title: Sarah, 7, was just recognised as student of the week. She died on the drive home from school
World.content:
Sarah El Hawli had just won the student of the week award. Hours later, the handwriting star of her year 1 class died in a car accident near a quiet country road. John Bibby checking his fence. Eddie Jim The young girl – described as the “smartest kid in her school” – was picked up along with six other children from Melton South’s Al Iman College on Tuesday afternoon. Among them was her 11-year-old cousin Ossama, who also died after the crash. Police are not sure exactly what caused the four-wheel-drive carrying the children to veer off a road near Parwan and roll onto a steep, dirt nature strip.



Detective Sergeant Tony Gentile described the events that followed as “hectic”. “People [were] everywhere. Witnesses who witnessed it, they stopped and rendered assistance,” he said. “Obviously, with seven children, they were distressed, and they were cared for by paramedics, members of the public and police.” Two air ambulances and nine emergency crews were sent to help, while witnesses rushed to assist paramedics. Sarah was pronounced dead on the scene. Not much is known yet about the young girl’s family, but a close relative said it was difficult to believe she was gone.



Major Collision Investigation Unit detectives are investigating a fatal single-vehicle rollover in Parwan which occurred on Tuesday afternoon. Nine News “She was an angel … she is an angel now,” they said. Ossama died overnight after he was flown to hospital. On Wednesday morning, shards of windscreen glass from the car remained sprawled across the roadside. A single black sneaker, belonging to a child, lay nearby. The scene of the fatal crash near the intersection of Parwan-Exford Road and Exford Road. Eddie Jim



Local farmer John Bibby picked at his wire fence after it was cut by emergency services during the rescue. He got a late night call from the local fire commander about the crash that happened a few metres from his paddock. “It’s just horrible – especially when kids are involved,” he said, glancing down at the dirt. Locals said the road the group travelled on was considered one of the safer routes in the area, which is known for potholes and speeding. The scene on Wednesday morning. Eddie Jim



Richy, a parent at the nearby Exford Primary School, wondered if fencing would be placed along the road, which is near the site of a separate bus crash in May 2023. “There are a few rough spots further up – but right here where it happened, the road’s perfect,” he said. Local communities are in deep grief following Tuesday’s tragic accident. The Australian Islamic Centre said it was supporting the family and assisting with funeral arrangements for the children in what was an “incredibly difficult time”.



“Their loss has deeply affected our entire [...] community. Our hearts are with their parents, family and loved ones as they face an unimaginable loss,” a statement said. A spokesperson from Al Iman College has asked the community to respect the family’s privacy as they grieved. Loading Three boys – one in critical condition – are recovering at the Royal Children’s Hospital. A further three children – a female toddler with minor injuries, and a teenage boy and primary school-aged boy – are in Sunshine Hospital, all in a stable condition.



The 34-year-old female driver was taken to the Royal Melbourne Hospital for observation. Intensive paramedic crews and advanced life support crews were at the scene. Nine News Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: I was blessed to call Blanche d’Alpuget a friend. What an extraordinary life
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsBlanche D'Alpuget Opinion I was blessed to call Blanche d’Alpuget a friend. What an extraordinary life Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author September 9, 2026 — 3:00pm

September 9, 2026 — 3:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Blanche d’Alpuget, who has just died after a brief illness, was a whole lot more than Bob Hawke’s second wife, even though she was the first to note that our former prime minister was ever and always the most important thing in her own life. Her final message released by her family was “our highest calling and greatest achievement is love, the rule of life,” and she surely had Hawke in mind when enunciating it. Blanche d’Alpuget photographed at Chiswick restaurant, Woollahra, in October 2025. Jessica Hromas They met briefly in Indonesia in the mid-70s when he was leading the ACTU and she was living in Jakarta, married to an Australian businessman. On their third meeting, in Australia, shortly afterwards, she later detailed how she felt such a pull towards his charisma that there was, just a “wordless understanding that we were going to sleep together”. “Now it’s none of my damn business,” I asked her when interviewing her last year, “and I deserve to be told to get back in my box and stop being so impertinent, but did it start again before he left The Lodge, or after he left The Lodge?” “Oh, before!” she exulted.



Blanche d'Alpuget with Bob Hawke in 2014. Sireshan Kander. Already an accomplished journalist, she would go on, shortly after beginning her affair with Hawke, to write one of Australia’s most acclaimed biographies of all time, Robert J. Hawke: A Biography, release in 1982. She added to it in 2010, covering his years as prime minister, and then in 2019, after his death released Bob Hawke: The Complete Biography. The first book, particularly, was a masterpiece, often hailed as the country’s first psycho-bio, where she was genuinely “in the head” of her subject, as she knew him so well. After Hawke left The Lodge in 1991, he shortly thereafter left his first wife Hazel, to live with Blanche, and they were married in 1995, for another happy quarter-century before he began ailing badly in 2019. When I asked her what were Bob Hawke’s last words, she replied: “His last words were, ‘This is killing me. I’m dying’. It was, and he was. I have a great belief in the spiritual world, and I believe the spiritual governs the material. The angel of death – for want of a better term – had come and taken a great bite out of him, taking his spleen when he was 17. And now the angel of death had returned, in exactly the same spot where he was seized with excruciating pain. The doctor, whom I called, who’d been treating him before, had no explanation.” That was Blanche. She always felt that her love with Hawke was completely “other-worldly”.



Related Article Opinion

Five Minutes with Fitz Why I turned to crime: Blanche d’Alpuget, six years after losing Bob Hawke Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author I had got to know her in the course of writing Kim Beazley’s biography in the late ’90s, and she was wonderfully generous to me in her advice before publication on how to try and capture him, and always great fun to see ever afterwards. She had an impish sense of humour, mixed with velvet steel in her character which said: “I might be in my 80s, but I am NOT to be messed with.” Blanche was confident and sure of herself. Ten days after Anthony Albanese was elected PM, I happened to be present when she took Jodie Haydon aside to give her full box and dice on what to expect, and how to adapt, to being the partner of the PM. Jodie listened closely, rapt. In recent years, persistent illness plagued her. Every time I saw her for lunch or dinner in the past two years particularly, she seemed a little more frail, a little more bird-like. “I’m … OK ... Yes, OK is the right word,” she told me in that same interview last year. “I’m not yet ‘good’, right? I don’t recommend having COVID and pneumonia twice. As far as I’m concerned, I’m now ... doing fine. But I’d say for the first four years after losing Bob, it was very rough.”



She was, nevertheless, always surrounded by friends, many of them denizens of the Labor Party. When I informed Beazley of her death just after the news broke, he replied: “She was a brilliant bright light. Very intelligent. Full of life. She was a source of joy in Bob’s last years. I did think she would go on a lot longer, she was full of life. Hard to think she is gone.” I will remember her exactly like that. A woman full of life, who had lived an extraordinary one, and documented a great one. Vale, dear Blanche. All of us blessed to know you, were proud to do so. Peter FitzSimons is an author and columnist.

World.title: First look: How the MCG has been transformed into the NFL’s field of dreams
World.content:
SportNFLMelbourne major events First look: How the MCG has been transformed into the NFL’s field of dreams Jon Pierik September 9, 2026 — 2:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The transformation of the MCG into an NFL field of dreams is almost complete, but one of the sport’s more “scary” sights will be missing from Friday’s historic clash. Ahead of the sell-out game between the Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers, the home of AFL and cricket has the full NFL vibe, complete with all the on-field markings required for a rectangular field of almost 110 metres long and 49m wide, vertical posts and painted end zones and team logos. First look: The MCG has been transformed into the home of the NFL on Friday when the Rams and 49ers clash. AP Photo/Asanka Brendon Ratnayake The field is not perfectly central, for the 49ers and Rams wanted the AFL coaches’ boxes they will use to be at the midfield line. The completed field also features the familiar yard lines, numbers and hash marks, helping to deal with yardage measurements. There is dead spacing between the outside line of the field and bottom tier of seating of the oval-shaped venue, NFL officials opting not to fill these areas with seats because of potential beverage and amenity issues.



NFL-mandated camera positions have been installed around the ground, while media have been shifted from the customary press box at centre-wing of the MCC members side to high in the stands. Related Article NFL 2026 ‘Hit even harder’: The viral video that shows the 49ers’ quarterback is in for a torrid time at the MCG Senior event architect Todd Barnes of Populous, the company employed by the NFL to get the MCG ready for the game, said the MCG was spectacular, but suggested it could have more LED lighting inside the venue. “This is probably one of the best international stadiums that I’ve been in. But one of the things I’ve noticed in the NFL marketplaces is that the more LED [lighting] that you have, it just seems like it’s a really big deal,” he said. Barnes also believes the ground’s two high-definition LED scoreboards, which are 25.24 metres wide and 13.1 metres high , should be larger.



“It just seems like it’s the way of the world, is just like getting the fans more integrated with more video type of stuff,” he said. As ground works continue, including extended security areas outside the venue, the 49ers and Rams continue their pre-game preparations. The 49ers were bracing for the Rams to unleash defensive duo Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald for the first time at the MCG on Friday, with Donald, a 185-centimetre, 127-kilogram, three-time defensive player of the year, beast, emerging from retirement on August 30 after two years out. But the Rams coach Sean McVay revealed on Wednesday that Donald, a defensive end, was not ready to play.



“He’s doing a great job. I think he’ll be ready to go sooner rather than later, but we’re making a decision that we think is best for him and for our team,” McVay said in Los Angeles, hours before his team boarded a chartered flight for Melbourne. Related Article NFL 2026 Incredible food, great coffee – and no crocs: Why the 49ers changed their tune on Melbourne “He’s attacked this the right way, but it would have been a really quick turnaround.” Defensive end Garrett has also been under a fitness cloud, in his case swelling in a knee, but McVay insisted he will be “ready to go” at the MCG. “He’s looked great. We’ve been smart with Myles … but his impact has been tremendous,” McVay said.



Ahead of training at AAMI Park on Wednesday, San Francisco coach Kyle Shanahan delivered a priceless response when asked about Donald’s absence. “Very excited. I told you guys last time I talked to you guys, he was definitely playing. So I’ve never been more excited to be wrong about something,” said Shanahan, who has won 11 of 18 games against McVay-led sides. Not ready: Star Los Angeles Rams defensive powerhouse Aaron Donald won’t take to the field at the MCG. Getty Images Donald’s absence means those attending on Friday won’t have the chance to watch Donald and Garrett targeting 49ers quarter-back Brock Purdy through their ruthless “sacking” – tackling a player to the ground with force. NFL great Jeff Saturday, now an ESPN analyst, dubbed that prospect one of the sport’s most “scary” sights. The 49ers have had injury issues of their own to address, for Shanahan said defensive tackle Alfred Collins had torn his patellar tendon in practice on Tuesday, and would miss the entire season.



The Rams will not arrive in Melbourne until Thursday, when they will have their only practice, at Marvel Stadium, late in the afternoon. There has been much debate about the contrasting travel plans of each side. But Shanahan said these would be no excuse for any poor on-field play. “I’m sure it will be a good case study for anybody in the future to sit there and overthink which one helped and not. But the real thing that’s going to help this game … is who plays better football, and whoever doesn’t,” Shanahan said. Prominent ESPN personality Stephen A. Smith warned on Wednesday that “if the Los Angeles Rams get rolling, very few teams, if anybody, is going to be able to stop ’em”. Led by veteran quarter-back Matthew Stafford, the Rams boast elite playmakers, including pass catchers Puka Nacua and Davante Adams.

World.title: Auric adds 102koz shovel-ready gold kicker to WA Coolgardie ambitions
World.content:
Auric Mining has pulled the trigger on another gold acquisition near Coolgardie, snapping up the 102,000-ounce Union Jack gold project in a deal that boosts its global resource inventory by a hefty 51 per cent to 301,000 ounces and strengthens its strategy of becoming a fully integrated gold producer.

The company has signed binding agreements to buy the project for an upfront $6.6 million in cash and $3 million in Auric shares, with further milestone payments tied to future resource growth. The deal hands Auric control of an initial inferred resource of 3.12 million tonnes grading 1.02 grams per tonne (g/t) gold for 102,000 ounces.

Auric Mining’s Burbanks processing facility, subject to a refurbishment study, just 15km from its newest Union Jack project near Coolgardie, WA.

Importantly, Union Jack sits just 15 kilometres by road from Auric’s Burbanks processing plant, putting it firmly within trucking distance and dovetailing neatly with the company’s strategy of snapping up mineable ounces that could ultimately feed its planned processing hub.

The project has all the hallmarks of a classic Goldfields opportunity, with a raft of historic mine shafts and shallow workings, leaving a solid 102,000 ounces at surface with plenty of potential for modern exploration to delve deep. The company says its current resource is based on just 241 drill holes and, importantly, remains open along strike and at depth.

World.title: It has all the right ingredients for a gripping thriller, but this Australian drama is stuck in the wrong gear
World.content:
★★ CultureTV & radioReview It has all the right ingredients for a gripping thriller, but this Australian drama is stuck in the wrong gear Jared Richards September 9, 2026 — 2:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Last Seen ★★ After the emotional cramp that was Amazon Prime Video’s The Runner, where Gal Gadot played a woman sprinting across London in a dull, drab attempt to find her kidnapped son, I was hopeful Last Seen would hit all the hallmarks of the Taken sub-genre. There was promise; the six-part series is Apple TV’s first Australian production, and the next in their stream of new thrillers this year alone, ranging from slick (Lucky), to the overwrought (Cape Fear) and funny (Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed), but always engaging. Patrick Brammall in Last Seen, in which he plays a father whose daughter goes missing. The premise is immediate: 11 years after his daughter Maggie went missing, triple-zero operator Ian (Colin From Accounts co-creator Patrick Brammall) receives a call on-duty and is immediately convinced it’s her.



Related Article Review What to stream this week: Sharehouse comedy returns better than ever, plus five more picks Stopping at nothing to find her, Ian – a former cop who lost his job and marriage in the haze of grief – is soon chasing after cars, roughing up teens for leads and casing suspects up down and through Victoria’s dense, foreboding rainforests that made an eerie backdrop in The Dry 2. Add in an ensemble filled with actors able to tap into intense, dark depths – including Daniel Henshall (Snowtown), Brendan Cowell (Plum) and Maxine Peake (Say Nothing) – and Last Seen has all the ingredients for a gripping thriller. Strange, then, for Last Seen to continually undercut its tension with sluggish flashbacks and poorly placed left-turns just as a scenario is building. There is also, fundamentally, no mystery within the show’s six episodes, with the who and why established for the audience by the second episode. That is a carry over from its source material, US crime-novelist Ryan David Jahn’s The Dispatcher, which establishes early if Maggie is alive and, if she is, who kidnapped her. But an airport thriller is a fast, furious read, while Last Seen’s script from Kris Mrksa stretches out these non-relevations. Loading That might work for some people. It certainly gives Brammall a lot to work with to establish how hollowed-out Ian is by Maggie’s disappearance, a crack often making it through to his voice.



But if The Runner lacked any emotion, Last Seen might be overwhelmed by it. Take the pilot, which opens with the discovery of a toddler’s body that the audience knows – via the show’s well-publicised premise – cannot be Maggie’s. Of course, there’s immense pain witnessing Ian and now ex-wife Debbie (Jessica Wren) find a false resolution, with the latter hoping to lay her daughter (and grief) to rest while Ian fixates on revenge. That the dispatch call doesn’t arrive until the end of episode two is indicative of Last Seen’s reluctance to move forward – a stasis that mirrors Ian, but isn’t particularly interesting to watch. Last Seen is now streaming on Apple TV. Want more TV? We’ve got you.

World.title: Golden Dragon breathes fire with high-grade WA gold hits
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Golden Dragon breathes fire with high-grade WA gold hits Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward September 9, 2026 — 2:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Golden Dragon Mining has hit high-grade gold at its Behring Bore and Coodardy prospects at its Cue project in Western Australia’s Murchison region, with a new quartz lode at Behring Bore returning four metres at a solid 6.98 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from just 44m. The result comes as re-assays of previous drilling at the nearby Coodardy prospect, just 400m away, also delivered a suite of spectacular high-grade hits including an 11-metre intersection grading 6.42g/t gold from 45m, containing a bonanza 1-metre section going an eye-watering 59.2 g/t gold. Golden Dragon Mining is drilling its Cue gold project in Western Australia’s prolific Murchison region. The company’s ground sits in a well-endowed part of the world, with WA’s Murchison region hosting a litany of major gold deposits. Golden Dragon previously pegged new ground right next door to Westgold Resources’ formidable 2.3-million-ounce Big Bell mine, highlighting the golden pedigree of the neighbourhood. Golden Dragon’s latest reverse circulation (RC) drilling campaign at Coodardy was designed to test for extensions to mineralisation, successfully stretching the known system to a strike length of 500m. The system remains open to the north, south and northeast.



‘Importantly, mineralisation remains open along strike and at depth at both prospects.’ Golden Dragon Mining managing director Simon Buswell-Smith Re-assaying one-metre intervals from previous 4m composite samples at Coodardy further defined the high-grade nature of the mineralisation. In addition to the stunning 1m at 59.2g/t gold, other standout re-assay results included a 6-metre intercept grading 5.02g/t gold from a shallow 28m, which hosted a higher-grade one-metre slice at a hefty 28.1g/t. The company says the results have helped define a high-grade, northeast-trending orientation within the broader mineralised system at Coodardy, providing a priority target for follow-up drilling. Over at the Behring Bore prospect, the new high-grade intersection of 4m at 6.98g/t gold has added another dimension to the broader system. The company says gold mineralisation there is hosted within an altered, pyritic quartz dolerite, a rock type recognised as a host for significant gold mineralisation in Western Australia. Golden Dragon says it has identified a strong correlation between rich gold and increased alteration intensity within the dolerite, providing an important geological pointer for targeting further mineralisation.



Previous drilling at Behring Bore has already served up some impressive numbers, with re-assays confirming 7m grading 4.35g/t gold from 44m, including 1m at an eye-catching 25.3g/t gold, and a wide 19-metre zone grading 1.72g/t gold from 41m, containing a 3-metre section at 7.42g/t gold. Golden Dragon Mining managing director Simon Buswell-Smith said: “At Behring Bore, the new high-grade quartz lode intersection of 4m @ 6.98g/t gold from 44m in one hole is an exciting result and adds a new high-grade component to the broader mineralised system. At Coodardy, the resampling and re-assaying of previous drilling has returned exceptional high-grade results, including 1m @ 59.20g/t gold within 11m @ 6.42g/t gold.” The company recently lit up a mouthwatering three-kilometre-long gold-in-soil anomaly at the Cue project, effectively stitching together four previously separate prospects, including Behring Bore, Curtis Find, Coodardy and Piston into what looks to be a single, large, mineralised corridor. The newly defined three-kilometre-long corridor adds considerable weight to the string of high-grade reverse-circulation drilling hits the company has already clocked up at the individual prospects now potentially linked by the new soil anomalies. Importantly, mineralisation remains open along strike and at depth at both prospects, with the company moving quickly to follow up its success. A larger RC rig has now been mobilised to the site to test the systems at depth, chasing extensions and continuity of the high-grade zones. Notably, Golden Dragon also recently secured a significant $2.2 million cornerstone investment at a 17.65 per cent premium to its previously traded share price. The deal saw Shanghai-listed heavyweight Chengtun Mining Group, via Chengtun Gold, bag a 19.89 per cent stake in the junior explorer, a move that suggests a significant vote of confidence in the company’s strategy.



With a larger rig now spinning the rods and a swag of high-grade targets to chase, Golden Dragon looks to be well-placed to build on its early exploration success. In a part of the world where proximity to a major mine can mean everything, having two high-grade prospects just 400m apart and open in all directions could get very interesting very quickly.
