Not air conditioners. Not power tools. The ‘wattage arms race’ has been optimizing for the 20% edge cases while the 80% majority pays a premium for capability they never use.”

For fridges specifically, you need to consider that they’re intermittent loads. That means they cycle on and off, drawing power heavily for short periods and then entering a low-power standby mode. Because of this, a power station’s inverter efficiency and self-consumption (idle draw) matter more than just battery size. That’s why a portable power station such as the Fossibot F3600 Pro can beat something like the Oupes Mega 5, which looks larger on paper in terms of capacity.

The Jackery HomePower 3600 has a huge amount of capacity for fridge backup. But despite winning a lab award, it surprisingly wasn’t our top performer. Jackery/CNET

“We generally recommend a 1kw or 2kw power station for common kitchen appliances such as refrigerators, microwaves and coffee makers,” said Brian Essenmacher, head of North American business development for EcoFlow. “These mid-sized units can typically power a fridge for a half day or full day.”

“A smaller 10- to 15-cubic foot refrigerator during a short four-hour outage may only require around a 1kWh power station,” said Marc Deng, R&D manager at Bluetti, concurring with the power estimate, though he pointed out that for US consumers, the requirement may be on the higher end. “But the reality for many American households is different. Larger French-door and side-by-side refrigerators are often in the 18- to 28-cubic-foot range, with typical power consumption around 80 to 190W. For families preparing for longer outages caused by hurricanes, winter storms or grid failures, around 2kWh becomes a much more practical starting point.”

What you need to know before buying a power station for a fridge

“The biggest trap is looking at capacity alone,” said Tan. “Capacity tells you how much energy is stored, not how much actually reaches the device.” He points to two things that matter more: light-load efficiency and idle consumption. “A home fridge runs at 100–200W, cycling on and off. Most of the time the power station is operating well below its rated output. Efficiency at these light loads varies dramatically between units.” As more idle consumption, “When the fridge compressor is off, the power station is essentially sitting idle, but still burning power. Industry typical idle draw is 15–20W. That adds up fast.”

Those looking for a reliable emergency fridge backup should prioritize low idle power consumption and high small-load efficiency over buying the largest, heaviest battery available. A well-optimized 2,000Wh unit can easily outlast a poorly optimized over 3,000Wh unit, as our data shows. By default, all portable power stations waste some energy; the key is to find the one that wastes the least, while also providing stable power.

Bluetti/CNET

Ideally, you also want one with an uninterruptible power supply (or UPS), which helps maintain stable, continuous power. “Modern refrigerators often rely on electronic controls and variable-frequency compressors, which are designed to operate continuously under stable power conditions,” said Marc Deng, R&D manager at Bluetti. “A good rule of thumb is that the UPS transition time should be below 20 milliseconds, with around 10 milliseconds being ideal. If the transfer is too slow, the refrigerator’s internal electronics may reset, causing the compressor and control system to restart unnecessarily. Over time, repeated interruptions can create additional stress on the appliance.”

It’s also important not to overlook the surge power stat that many portable power stations advertise. Deng pointed out that depending on the refrigerator model, the startup surge can range from around 600W to well over 1,200W. “Surge power matters a lot,” Tan said. “Compressor startup pulls several times the running wattage. A station needs 2,500–3,000W peak to reliably handle most residential fridges.”

The FridgeGuard is thin enough that it can sit on top of a fridge or in a tight corner. Jackery

You also need to consider the percentage of energy wasted as overhead. The Anker Solix F3800 Plus wasted 46.63% of its energy just keeping itself running, which explains its short runtime. The Pecron E3600LFP had the lowest overhead loss with a tiny 15.75% reduction, while other highly efficient units included the Anker Solix C2000 Gen 2 (18.21% loss) and the Bluetti AC200L (22.16% loss). These low-loss units ensure that power actually reaches the refrigerator rather than being lost as internal heat.

In the XL category, our undisputed winner is the Fossibot F3600 Pro, which is $2,600 at full price, but frequently on sale for less. It lasted the longest and wasted the least energy in the XL category. For the large power stations, our winner is the Bluetti AC200L. It punched above its size and power capacity, offering excellent efficiency and the longest fridge runtime of any large portable power station.

Do you need a portable power station specially designed for fridges?

The FridgePower lets you pair multiple BlueCell batteries with it, giving you up to four days of runtime. Bluetti

It’s worth noting that there’s a new category of portable power stations, with slim models designed to sit on or be mounted behind a fridge. Examples include the new Bluetti FridgePower and the Jackery FridgeGuard, both of which I’m testing at home, while Anker’s Solix S2000 is a more traditional take on the capability.

Of these, we’ve only been able to run lab tests on the FridgePower, and the results are impressive. It falls into the upper tier of large portable power, keeping our test fridge running 23.43 hours (0.98 days), so it lasts nearly a full day. Of its 1,621.09Wh measured capacity, the FridgePower only lost 328.08Wh (a 20.24% reduction) to internal inverter overhead. This compares favorably with other, more efficient models.

While it won’t keep the fridge running for multiple days, even the bulky Fossibot 3600 Pro is hard-pressed to do that. The design is its biggest selling point: The FridgePower is slim, lightweight and can be out of sight and out of mind, unlike hooking up your fridge to a traditional power station. So while it’s not required to power a fridge, the FridgePower won’t look out of place in your kitchen and it provides sufficient power to get you through an outage.

Tech.title: The Best of IFA 2026, Where There’s No Such Thing as Too Many Robots
Tech.content:
After nearly a week roaming the halls of IFA 2026 in Berlin, CNET staffers have seen a lot of tech: some genuinely useful, some wonderfully strange. That includes a dishwasher and toothbrush equipped with cameras, a mom Roomba carrying a baby Roomba, and a variety of life- and voice-recording devices. Together, they offer a glimpse at how tech companies see the future.

Now that the show has come to a close, we’ve sorted through everything we saw to pick the standouts. Here’s the best tech we spotted at IFA 2026.

An all-seeing dishwasher

Miele’s Diamond G8 isn’t your average dishwasher. David Watsky/CNET

Miele’s new Diamond G8 dishwasher has an AI-powered internal camera that scans your dishes and decides how to wash them so it doesn’t miss a single spot. Though Home and Kitchen Managing Editor David Watsky, who saw the dishwasher in person, was skeptical about this feature, he was left impressed.

But the Diamond G8’s scrubbing smarts don’t stop there. If you want the Diamond G8 to run only when electricity is most affordable, it can do that, too, waiting for the hours when power costs less.

Note-taking earbuds

Plaud One: your AI note-taking assistant earbuds. Plaud/CNET

Going beyond its AI note-taking wearable pin and credit card-like device that you can attach to your phone, Plaud launched the Plaud One earbuds to capture and transcribe your conversations and calls. You can even talk to Plaud’s AI by saying, “Hey Plaud,” and then ask it your questions or give it directives.

“We’d always recommend informing people that you’re using a recording device, and it’s important to note that recording phone calls without permission from all participants can be illegal in some states,” principal writer Katie Collins wrote when covering the Plaud One announcement.

A robot vacuum that seals itself to carpet

The Roomba Max 875 Combo is all about clean carpet. iRobot

While robot vacuums are great for taking the effort out of keeping your floors clean, CNET’s testing has found that they don’t offer the same suction power as traditional vacuums. iRobot aims to improve on that with its new Roomba Max 875 Combo, which uses SealForce technology to seal itself to carpet and better suction up spots that need extra cleaning.

In a video call with Home and Robotics Editor Ajay Kumar prior to IFA 2026, Adam Pope, vice president and chief engineer at iRobot, said SealForce is like pressing harder with a traditional vacuum to thoroughly clean a specific patch of carpet, but in a robot vacuum format.

A smart ring puts contactless payments at your fingertips

Imagine how cool it will feel to use your ring for contactless payments. Circular

In addition to having the health-tracking capabilities we expect of smart rings, Circular has added contactless payments, a feature typically found on smartwatches and smartphones, to its new subscription-free Ring 3 Pro and Ring 3 Slim. When covering the launch, principal writer Vanessa Hand Orellana wrote that the company also gave both rings haptic vibration alerts, a feature previously available on its first Circular Ring, along with advanced sleep metrics, glucose trend estimates and access to its AI health coach.

A laptop built to be repaired

The Vero 16 comes with its own repair guide. Acer/CNET

With its new fourth-generation Vero 16, Acer brings the “right to repair” conversation into focus, as CNET writer Tyler Graham explained that the modular laptop is designed to let users easily upgrade its components themselves. There’s even a repair guide engraved on it to help with these swaps.

The Vero 16 didn’t come alone, as it was announced alongside Acer’s compact 14-inch Swift Blade 14 and sleek 16-inch Swift Air 16.

A speaker that lulls you to sleep

Sleep has never sounded so sweet. Katie Collins/CNET

Alongside its Sleep Earbuds 4 and Sleep Earbuds 4 Pro with a touchscreen case, Anker introduced the SleepLab Pro speaker, which uses radar to track your sleep, breathing and heart rate, then customizes its audio to help you drift off to dreamland and stay there. “It looks like a thoughtfully designed piece of kit that I know I’d be happy to have on my bedside table,” Collins wrote when describing the device. It also triples as a sunrise alarm clock and a nightlight that glows in a range of shades.

A non-Pro SleepLab has the same features, minus radar sleep tracking.

Dyson’s largest air purifier

Dyson’s new HushJet air purifiers are a total redesign. Tara Brown/CNET

The new Dyson HushJet Big+Quiet Cool Pure+Formaldehyde (try to say that five times fast) was designed to purify multiple rooms using the company’s most powerful processor. As Kumar put it, it looks like a Dune sandworm with its nozzle head that can be rotated and tilted. While operating quietly, the purifier can capture 99.99% of pollutants down to 0.01 microns for a breath of fresh air.

Lenovo’s first rollable work laptop

Lenovo is on a roll. Josh Goldman/CNET

Lenovo’s Project Swan concept is a laptop that expands horizontally at the touch of a button, transforming its display from 14 to 17 inches. But unlike the Legion Pro Rollable Graham spotted at CES 2026, this isn’t a gaming laptop – it’s for work. Perfect for work trips when you want a more compact 14-inch display for travel, but a 17-inch for getting the job done (or watching movies during your downtime).

Dyson’s first toothbrush

Plaque begone! Tara Brown/CNET

Dubbed the CameraJet, Dyson’s first toothbrush has a built-in, AI-powered camera that detects gaps between your teeth within 100 milliseconds so that it can floss while you brush. To do so, the brush has an anti-gravity tank that its charging dock fills with mouthrinse, which its jet uses to floss.

You can even use the CameraJet’s camera as an endoscope to see your teeth in the app, where brushing and flossing insights, coverage maps and guided cleaning are also available. However, this high-tech toothbrush comes at a cost: $500.

An Instant Pot-like feeder for cats

Get your cat to stop meowing at you for food, and let them meow at this machine instead. David Watsky/CNET

Pet care and home cleaning company Neakasa showed off its Riko smart wet food maker, which Watsky described as an Instant Pot for cats. All you have to do is add water to Riko’s reservoir and freeze-dried food, so refrigeration isn’t required. On demand or when feeding time is scheduled in the app, the device will prepare your feline’s feast by rehydrating and mixing the cat food. Bon appetit!

A smart radiator valve

Its high-res screen shows temperature, settings and device status in real time. Sonoff

Home Security and Smart Home Senior Editor Tyler Lacoma has been waiting for a smart thermostat that isn’t just for forced air heating and cooling, and smart home company Sonoff displayed exactly that at IFA. The TRV Smart Thermostatic Radiator Valve provides three temperature scheduling plans and frost protection and anti-calcification reminders. It even connects to window sensors to prevent energy waste. Just screw it onto your radiator’s valve pipe and let it take care of the rest.

A Roomba that carries another Roomba

A true dynamic duo. Ajay Kumar/CNET

Apparently, one Roomba is no longer enough. The Roomba Duo is a concept floor-cleaning system consisting of a large robot that vacuums and steam-mops open areas and a smaller Roomba that rides on top of it. When the Duo encounters furniture or another space it can’t squeeze beneath, a mechanical arm lowers the little robot to the floor and sends it in.

The two robots share a map and coordinate their cleaning through the Roomba app, while the larger unit also carries clean and dirty water tanks, a dust bag and enough hardware to function as its own mobile dock. It’s ambitious and ridiculous-looking, but honestly, it’s exactly the sort of thing we come to IFA to see. Because it remains a concept, iRobot hasn’t announced a price or release date.

An AI mic that writes your emails for you

Keyboards beware. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Collins got a first look at the Relay Q, which looks like a small lighter. Just hold down the top to whisper voice commands or whatever you want it to write. Then, double-press the top to send. You can even slide the top off the device, using its magnet to turn it into a wearable pin.

“What immediately impressed me about the Relay Q is its design and the tactile experience of holding the device,” Collins wrote. “I wasn’t surprised to learn the team members are Nothing alumni, responsible for helping design some of the coolest audio and mobile devices on the market.”

Home security with custom AI detection

Custom on-device AI with no extra costs? Say less. Reolink

At IFA, smart home security company Reolink showed off its AI engine, ReoNeura, which impressed Lacoma, who reviews home security tech for CNET, for several reasons. In addition to enabling users to customize its AI, ReoNeura doesn’t require a cloud or a cloud subscription. This would make it the only custom AI engine that doesn’t cost extra.

A wearable robot

You can have your robot and wear it, too. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

iKairos can be either a pendant on your necklace or a desktop robot. Currently being developed by Singaporean startup Lingverse and spotted by Collins, it tracks your conversations and environment to preserve memories and make helpful suggestions. Underneath its display with cartoon eyes, there’s also a camera you can use to take photos or videos.

Tech.title: Why Miele Put a Camera Inside Its Latest Dishwasher
Tech.content:
It seems the public wants fewer cameras, not more, but that hasn’t stopped the large appliance industry. While a fridge or oven camera almost certainly presents less of a privacy risk than a Flock surveillance unit — hey, it’s right there in the name — one could argue they’ve gone overboard.

Sensors and lenses have crept into nearly every other kitchen machine, met with a range of consumer sentiment. Smart ovens and connected refrigerators aren’t new, but a camera-equipped dishwasher? When I heard that Miele snuck one inside its latest model, the Diamond G8 unveiled at IFA 2026 in Berlin, I was suspicious. After a rep walked me through the new machine’s novel smart features, the reasoning came somewhat into focus.

A camera in Miele’s new dishwasher helps it choose the best cycle.

An AI-powered camera recognizes dish types to help pick a cycle

The small camera, fixed to the back of the dishwasher door, gets a clear shot of the dishwasher’s interior. It uses that view to take inventory of what’s inside, recognizing dozens of common kitchen items and tailoring the wash cycle and detergent volume accordingly.

The Diamond G8 is one of the smartest dishwashers we’ve encountered, and it’s easy on the eyes.

Got portable bottles or reusable straws in the dedicated slots? The dishwasher’s brain recognizes them and makes sure those items get the spritz they need. Load it up with pots and pans, and the camera identifies them, triggering a more intensive cycle so everything comes out clean. A smaller load prompts a lighter cycle, so you’re not wasting hot water or soap.

The G8 recognizes straws, flatware, silverware and cookware and adjusts its cycle for optimized cleaning.

The camera also determines how full the dishwasher is. Command the G8 to start when it reaches, say, 80% capacity, and it’ll monitor the load and automatically begin a cycle once it hits that threshold.

One of my favorite features has nothing to do with the camera

The G8 Diamond takes advantage of fluctuations in electricity prices throughout the day. Tell it to run when electricity is cheapest, and the dishwasher waits for those lower-cost hours before starting its cycle. It’s a small detail, but it points to where Miele – and kitchen appliances more broadly – seem to be headed: machines that don’t just perform a task, but figure out the best and most efficient way to do it.

The dishwasher can be programmed to run when energy costs are cheapest in your area.

Miele’s newly unveiled machine has other AI-powered features that encourage efficiency and performance. The G8 features careful water and energy monitoring, which you can track through Miele’s app. It also includes a smart detergent-dispensing system, first introduced by the brand in 2018, and a beefed-up hot-air drying system that Miele says gets dishes bone-dry every time.

The camera paired with a smart detergent dispenser doles out just the right amount of soap.

Miele plans to roll out the Diamond G8 in the European market later this year as it considers a North American strategy, according to a spokesperson.

A retail price is still under wraps, but I expect it to land in the super-premium zone. For a top-performing dishwasher you can buy today, see our list of the best models in 2026.

Editors’ note: David Watsky’s travel costs for the IFA conference were covered by IFA. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

Tech.title: Meta’s New AI Agent Wants to Get Personal With You
Tech.content:
This seems to be the year of AI agents, and Meta is diving into the game. The company on Tuesday announced a new agent program called Muse, which CEO Mark Zuckerberg describes as a “personal agent” that understands your habits and goals. It’s available now in the US.

Introducing Muse, the personal agent that understands your goals and works 24/7 to get things done for you. — Mark Zuckerberg (@finkd) September 8, 2026

Agentic AI is a type of generative AI based on a large language model where agents, or bots, are meant to take actions autonomously on your behalf. Meta’s Muse, for example, can do online shopping (with your permission), create documents, fill out forms and respond to emails.

Meta says that Muse is a more general-purpose agent, not limited to specific tasks like coding. (If you want agentic coding help, you can use Muse Code, also recently released by the company.) You have to give Muse permission to access your apps and data, which you can revoke at any time. Like a lot of agentic AI tools, the more info you give it, the more personalized your results will be.

Muse runs “on its own dedicated computer in the cloud,” according to a Meta blog post, in what the company calls a “virtual machine.” The tool also has a separate Sentinel agent — you can think of it as a virtual traffic cop, giving Muse a red or green light before letting it out onto the internet to complete tasks.

Agentic AI can be risky. Over the summer, agents from Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic each slipped out of their testing environments and hacked outside websites, casting increased scrutiny on the potentially disastrous harm AI can do to our cybersecurity.

Meta’s vice president of Superintelligence Labs, Tarek Sheasha, said in a blog post: “The harness runs in its own isolated cell, it doesn’t see real credentials, and every interaction with the outside world runs through a Sentinel which the agent can’t override.”

Muse is available now on iOS and Android and on the muse.ai website. The company says it will be bringing the AI to its controversial smart glasses soon. According to Zuckerberg, it will be free for people to use “up to 100 million tokens per week” (one token is roughly equivalent to four characters). So unless you’re constantly running Muse on complex tasks, you should be able to use it for a while before running into a paywall.

Tech.title: Dyson’s First-Ever Dryer Brush, the Airsmooth, Is Now Available
Tech.content:
At the Dyson Unveiled event at IFA 2026 in Berlin, Dyson announced a whopping 10 new products, including its first toothbrush, three robot vacuums, three air purifiers, a wet floor cleaner and two hair tools: its first dryer brush and a hair straightener designed to lessen heat damage. If you’re on the lookout for the latest tech for lustrous locks, here’s everything you need to know.

The Airsmooth

Dyson has round brush attachments for its Airwrap multistyler, but according to a press release, the Airsmooth is the brand’s first dedicated dryer brush. Designed for all hair types, it uses two different bristle types: PivotFlex bristles that bend up to 90 degrees and anti-snag bristles that collapse to release strands. Both were created to reduce uncomfortable hair-pulling. The PivotFlex bristles also have an open base that helps control and diffuse airflow, minimizing frizz.

A close-up of the Dyson Airsmooth’s bristles. Tara Brown/CNET

To further protect the hair’s natural texture and prevent damage, Airsmooth’s intelligent heat control measures temperature 100 times per second.

For those who want a dryer brush they can take with them on the go, the Airsmooth has universal voltage, making it a great hair tool for travel.

The Airsmooth’s dual-bristle design was developed with scalp comfort in mind. Dyson/CNET

“For folks who just want a drying brush and don’t want to spend over $600 on the Airwrap and all its attachments, the Airsmooth seems like a great option,” said Nasha Addarich Martínez, who tests hair tools for CNET. “This is similar to Shark, which has the FlexStyle (an Airwrap competitor), but it sells a dryer brush separately, too.”

The Corrale CoolShine

The successor to the Corrale straightener, the Corrale CoolShine includes Dyson’s first-of-its-kind cooling attachment that uses pipes containing a specific amount of water. When heat is applied to the hair, these pipes draw excess heat away from your strands to cool them and prevent damage.

You can choose from four different temperatures on the Corrale CoolShine. Tara Brown/CNET

Just like the Corrale, the Corrale CoolShine has flexing plate technology that shapes around the hair to gather it.

According to Dyson, all of this technology combined leaves your locks cooler to the touch, with results lasting up to 24 hours and with up to 154% more shine compared to untreated hair.

The Corrale CoolShine uses heat-extracting pipes to minimize damage. Dyson/CNET

Availability and price

The Airsmooth dryer brush is $250 and now available in ceramic pink through Dyson and Ulta. For $300, it’s also being sold at Sephora, but is currently out of stock.

As for the Corrale CoolShine straightener, it’s $329 and available on Sept. 15.

Tech.title: Apple’s Foldable iPhone Ultra Could Launch Tomorrow, but Arrive Later
Tech.content:
Key takeaways The foldable iPhone Ultra’s release date will likely be announced on Sept. 9, but it won’t come out that day.

Current rumors suggest it will hit store shelves later in September, or even October or November.

The first foldable iPhone will likely be a book-style format, potentially followed by a Razr-style clamshell design.

Design leaks suggest a wider, squatter look, similar to the original Google Pixel Fold.

It’s expected to cost between $2,000 and $2,500.

Apple’s fall launch event is Wednesday, and it could mean that Samsung, Google and Motorola may have to share the foldable spotlight with a new rival. After years of rumors, mounting reports suggest this could finally be the year Apple launches its first foldable iPhone, which might be called the iPhone Ultra.

But there could be a wait between announcing the foldable and getting it into people’s hands. Analyst Ming-Chi Kuo, as reported by MacRumors, says Apple could unveil the foldable alongside the iPhone 18 lineup, but the company may wait until later in the year to put it on sale, similar to the iPhone X launch in 2017. Apple sent out invites to an event on Sept. 9, where we expect the next iPhones to be unveiled — and likely the foldable as well.

That event will be a landmark for other reasons beyond the potential launch of a folding iPhone. It’s the first since outgoing CEO Tim Cook formally handed the keys to the Apple kingdom to its new head, John Ternus. To celebrate this occasion, CNET has been reliving fun and pivotal moments from our decades covering the company with our Apple a Day series.

A folding iPhone is expected to arrive at a starting price north of $2,000, with Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reporting that Apple has discussed starting prices as high as $2,200 — with larger storage configurations nearing $3,000. The name that’s stuck in the rumor mill for years, the iPhone Fold, might even change before it hits store shelves. Leaks increasingly point to “iPhone Ultra,” a label that would elevate the device above the Pro lineup and signal a new tier of Apple hardware.

Mock-ups of potential iPhone foldables, including a clamshell “iPhone Flip” on the left and a book-style foldable on the right, along with a flat iPhone for comparison on the bottom. Zain bin Awais/CNET

While the inside of the iPhone foldable will have a near tablet-sized 7.8-inch display, it may not have all the functionality of an iPad, Gurman recently told Yahoo Tech. From what he’s heard, the Mac-like multitasking that Apple added to iPadOS won’t quite be what’s in the foldable iPhone. Instead, expect side-by-side app layouts that should still let users drag and drop things between them.

We’ve gotten far more design leaks suggesting how Apple’s foldable may look. Most suggest that the iPhone Fold will be a book-style foldable that’s squat and wide, looking more like the original Pixel Fold or the new Galaxy Fold 8 than taller, thinner models, such as the Galaxy Z Fold 7 or the Pixel 10 Pro Fold.

The screen on the iPhone Fold is rumored to have little or no crease, according to a recent report by the Chinese publication UDN. Screen creases, especially on early foldable phones, have long annoyed consumers and critics, and they still remain, despite the seam getting less noticeable over the years. Even Samsung’s most advanced Galaxy Z TriFold has two screen creases, one for each of its hinges. It would be a major breakthrough if Apple were to find a way to fold a screen in half without leaving a crease.

Another report from leaker Fixed Focus Digital on Weibo suggests that Apple’s hinges could be made of liquid metal, an alloy possibly provided by Liquidmetal Technologies, with which Apple has had an exclusive contract since 2010. It’s been the topic of many rumors since then and the basis of several patent applications, but so far, no products other than the SIM ejector tool that once shipped with iPhone models.

Even days before its potential release, we’ve yet to hear any official word on a foldable iPhone from Apple.

Foldable phones represent a tiny fraction of all phones sold globally. In a recent survey, CNET found that 64% of people said they don’t want a foldable phone. But those numbers could change if Apple were to sell a foldable iPhone. As of April, IDC analysts predict that global foldable sales will jump 19% if the iPhone Fold launches in 2026, with Apple’s folding device capturing around 24% of the global market share.

A lot of hope and high expectations have been placed on Apple’s release of a foldable phone. And if rumors are correct, we won’t have to wait much longer for the company to do so.

iPhone Fold release date: It could launch on Sept. 9… or in 2027

Apple’s invite to its Sept. 9 event has the tagline “Surprise and shine.” Apple

Apple has neither confirmed the iPhone Fold nor announced a release date. But analysts and rumors have predicted that the foldable could come out in 2026 or be pushed until next year. So while the upcoming Sept. 9 Apple event is the most likely release date, as the first device of its kind released by Apple, we can’t be sure until the company shows it off.

As for timing, since the iPhone Air was released alongside the iPhone 17 models, the Fold is likely to come alongside the iPhone 18 series, which is expected to launch during the Sept. 9 event. Apple could even delay the launch of the standard iPhone 18 to the spring of 2027 to make room for the iPhone Fold in Apple’s Sept. 9 launch, according to an ET News report. Given that Samsung offsets its standard and foldable phone releases at Unpacked events months apart from each other, Apple could do the same.

Once the foldable iPhone does go on sale, it may be hard to get. Leaker Fixed Focus Digital said in a Weibo post that although the initial run of foldable iPhones will be around 10 million units, production could take three to five months to ramp up. That’s about 30% to 40% slower than the iPhone 17’s production of 5 million units per month. That could mean a supply shortage delaying people from picking up the folding iPhone for some time after its launch.

It’s been an open secret for years that Apple is working toward a foldable iPhone, but buzz and possible release dates have been floated for just as long. Early rumors pointed to 2021 as a potential target date, but the year passed with no foldable iPhone in sight, as have successive rumors for potential releases in 2023 and 2025.



iPhone Fold price

Kuo, the analyst, predicted that a book-style iPhone foldable coming in 2026 could be priced anywhere from $2,000 to $2,500, as it’s “expected to generate strong replacement demand — despite the premium price — provided quality meets expectations.”

The day before Apple is expected to reveal the foldable iPhone, Bloomberg’s Gurman reported that the company had still been discussing the price as recently as weeks before the event. It could start as high as $2,200, with higher storage configurations pushing the price north of $3,000.

A report last year found that half of American consumers are interested in buying a foldable phone, though Apple customers are slightly less willing to make the leap than Samsung or LG users. Perhaps the “Apple effect” will change those stats if and when a foldable iPhone ever becomes a reality.

Although Motorola offers one of the most affordable folding phones with its clamshell Razr at $800, most others in the category are book-style foldables, such as the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Pixel 10 Pro Fold, which cost around twice as much as most flagship phones. We don’t expect a foldable iPhone to be cheaper than its rivals, which start around $2,000.

iPhone Fold specs

There are no confirmed specs for the iPhone Fold; Apple hasn’t even confirmed one exists or is coming out. Even if we expect it to come out soon, it’s tough to predict what kind of internal specs the iPhone Fold will have. Presumably, Apple will equip it with its most powerful A-series chip, along with enough RAM to handle two or three displays (depending on whether it folds inward or outward and needs a dedicated outer screen). That could mean an A20 Pro chip, if Apple follows precedent in equipping this year’s iPhone Pro models with successors to last year’s A19 Pro silicon.

We do have some predictions for other specs, though only for the rumored book-style Fold (not the clamshell). In March 2024, Kuo predicted the larger Fold could have a 5.5-inch outer screen and a 7.8-inch inner display. When folded, it’s rumored to be 9 millimeters to 9.5mm thick and 4.5mm to 4.8mm when unfolded. Plus, a front-facing camera is also rumored to work whether the phone is folded or unfolded; the phone is also rumored to have two rear cameras.

Kuo predicted that the device would use the same high-density battery cells as used in what he referred to then as the “ultrathin iPhone 17,” which presumably meant the iPhone Air. But that trim thickness means the foldable may forgo Face ID, so the device could end up using Touch ID in a side button.

Some rumors about hardware have emerged, too. In January, an analyst note seen by MacRumors suggested Apple’s foldable could launch with 12GB of RAM, the same amount in the Galaxy Z Fold 7‘s starting configuration. That could mean Apple doesn’t need much memory to handle multiple screens or isn’t banking on large AI features that require significant RAM.

And we finally have a prediction on the iPhone Fold’s battery, with Weibo leaker Fixed Focus Digital posting that it could have a 5,500-mAh capacity, as 9to5Mac first reported. That’s larger than batteries on some other foldables. (The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, for example, has a 5,000-mAh battery, but Samsung has been in the foldable game for years and has likely improved efficiency in an effort to slim down its devices.) Yet if the Weibo leak is true, this will be the largest battery ever on an Apple handset. The iPhone 17 Pro Max has a 5,088-mAh battery.

Design: What will the foldable iPhone look like?

This illustration, according to Apple’s patent filing, shows a “device that bends along a flexible portion, such as a flexible seam associated with a hinge.” Apple/US Patent and Trademark Office

Apple seems to have taken out every patent under the sun when it comes to foldable displays, including an origami-style folding display, a flip-up display and even a wraparound display. As far back as 2021, a Bloomberg report indicated Apple already had a prototype of a foldable iPhone display, and rumors since then have bounced back and forth between suggesting Apple will opt for either a clamshell- or book-style foldable first.

In March 2025, Kuo made several specific predictions for Apple’s foldable: It would be a book-style device with a 5.5-inch outer screen that unfolds into a 7.8-inch internal display, measuring 4.5 to 4.8mm thick when unfolded and 9 to 9.5mm when folded. It would also use the same high-density battery cells as the “ultrathin iPhone 17” and include a hinge made of stainless steel and titanium alloy — a favorite material in Apple’s iPhone 16 Pro and Pro Max, as well as the Apple Watch Ultra 3.

A mock-up of the iPhone Fold based on unofficial leaked CAD renders from @SonyDIckson on X. Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

Per Kuo’s predictions, the foldable will have two rear cameras and a front-facing camera on both the external and internal displays. Most interestingly, he also expects that Apple’s book-style foldable will see the return of Touch ID as a side button, as Face ID might be left out due to space constraints — presumably for the array of depth-of-field sensors and cameras needed for the tech.

Then there are the renders, which have gone from a trickle to a steady stream through 2026. One set of 3D CAD renders from leaker Sonny Dickson (pictured above) points to a squat, wide design that looks much more like the original Pixel Fold than the tall, thin Galaxy Z Fold 7 or the Honor Magic V6 Foldable.

iPhone 2026 lineup

CNET’s Jeffrey Hazelwood created these custom renders of what an iPhone 18 Pro might look like. Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

There’s no guarantee about which phones Apple will release during its usual September window, but the safest bet is on another series of flat phones, which we expect to be the iPhone 18 line. But what else could be coming alongside the usual lineup?

There could be an iPhone Air 2, though rumors conflict over whether to expect one next year. There’s been a lot more evidence of an iPhone Fold, though whether it comes out in 2026 or later remains uncertain. If the iPhone Fold does launch next year, more rumors suggest a clamshell device has been prioritized and may come first. Given reports of Apple researching a book-style foldable, we could get one of those as well.

In mid-January, MacRumors reportedly saw a research note from analyst Jeff Pu suggesting that the iPhone Fold will pack 12GB of memory — as will the entire iPhone 18 line. Apple never discloses how much RAM its phones include, but spec sites such as GSMArena have reported that the standard iPhone 17 has 8GB of RAM, while the rest of the series (iPhone Air, 17 Pro and Pro Max) all have 12GB. If correct, that means Apple doesn’t think its foldable will need more memory than its standard flat phones; it would have more screen area but potentially no more advanced hardware than its iPhone 18 siblings.

It’s also interesting to see the standard iPhone 18 packing 12GB of memory, as the RAM shortage is predicted to hike prices on phones released in 2026 and potentially even wipe out the cheapest budget phones from the market until memory prices drop enough to make low-cost phones profitable again. Apple may be willing to absorb the costs of a more capable basic iPhone 18 model, or perhaps it’ll pass those costs on to consumers with a price hike.

Tech.title: World’s Largest Gun Aims to Shoot Satellites Into Space
Tech.content:
When a rocket launches a payload into orbit, the overwhelming majority of its weight at launch is just fuel. After decades of space travel, a company called Longshot Space hopes to unlock a more efficient way to launch satellites into orbit.

The plan: Shoot satellites into space with the world’s biggest gun. To accomplish this, Longshot is designing its cannons to accelerate payloads using compressed gas. Unlike regular guns, which use one sudden burst, Longshot uses multiple bursts of gas to accelerate its projectiles through a barrel that, in its final form, will be miles long.

Launching satellites this way also requires satellites capable of withstanding the shock. The company believes it is possible, but indicates that traveling by gunshot is probably not feasible for sensitive cargo, especially human beings.

That didn’t stop our contributor Andy Altman from climbing inside the barrel of one of these guns. To see his in-depth tour of Longshot Space, check out the video in this article.

Tech.title: Could Apple Announce Smart Glasses at ‘Surprise and Shine’ Tomorrow? CNET Readers Are Split
Tech.content:
It seems like everyone is anticipating the first foldable iPhone at Apple’s “Surprise and shine” event on Wednesday, Sept. 9. That’s not all we can expect.

Apple could show us the latest models of some of its best-known devices, like the AirPods 5, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. On top of that, we can expect at least part of the iPhone 18 series lineup. Apple’s known to surprise us with a few new features and devices, so that’s not all we’re expecting.

In the meantime, we’ve been having fun guessing what Apple’s up to while we wait for the big announcements that are now hours away. The CNET Group has been hosting the Big Guessing Game contest across its websites — CNET, Lifehacker, Mashable, PCMag and ZDNET. The first round of our game focused on Apple’s software, the second round focused on its devices, and the third round of the Apple event just wrapped up. A brand-new Apple Watch is up for grabs to the winner with the most correct guesses.

We won’t know some of the answers for certain until the big day, but here’s what CNET readers expect.

Nearly 80% expect Apple’s first foldable phone

Most CNET readers (77%) think Apple will debut its first foldable phone this year. Many leaked rumors and reports suggest it could be as soon as September.

There’s plenty of speculation around the design, price and name. Apple could name it the iPhone Fold, iPhone Ultra or iPhone Flip. It might fold like a book, resembling other foldable phones like the Pixel 10 Pro Fold and the new Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8. There’s also the rumor of a clamshell-style design like the Motorola Razr models and the just-announced Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 8.

One other big question is how much the phone will cost, given the global RAM shortage and Apple’s recent price hikes. Some rumors say the phone could start at $2,000 and go up to $2,500.

We don’t know whether Apple will unveil a foldable phone tomorrow, but in the past, it has announced new phones at its September event. For example, the iPhone 17 models and iPhone Air were announced on Sept. 9, 2025, at Apple’s “Awe Dropping” keynote. And the iPhone 16 models were released on Sept. 9, 2024, at the “It’s Glowtime” keynote.

Over 70% predict a black iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max

I was disappointed when I upgraded to the iPhone 17 Pro Max and found out it wasn’t available in black, but most readers (72%) think the color will be making a comeback with the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max models.

There are plenty of rumors about which colors the Pro model will come in — like light blue, dark cherry and dark gray. However, there aren’t any rumors of black yet.

We haven’t seen black in the Pro and Pro Max models since the iPhone 16, and the iPhone 15 came in black titanium. Before that, the iPhone 14 Pro and Pro Max came in space black. And earlier versions came in different black variants, such as the iPhone 13 and 12 Pro in graphite and the iPhone 11 Pro and Pro Max in space gray.

Most don’t expect new AirPods with cameras

AirPods with cameras sound like cutting-edge technology. Experts say the cameras would be more like AI sensors to guide Siri, not for taking high-quality photos and videos.

We know Siri’s getting a major upgrade soon with agentic AI features and a standalone app. So it wouldn’t be surprising if Apple wants those devices to work in tandem.

However, most readers (77%) don’t think Apple will unveil the new earbuds this year. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman expects AirPods with cameras to be a part of Apple’s 2027 product plan. That’s the same time we could see a 20th anniversary iPhone and the second generation of Apple’s rumored foldable phone.

Apple released the AirPods Pro 3 last September, while the AirPods 4 were released in September 2024. We may see new AirPods, but it’s unlikely Apple will announce a camera-equipped version this year.

Readers are nearly split on Apple releasing smart glasses

Just over half (51%) of readers think Apple will announce its first pair of smart glasses at its September event, while 49% don’t.

However, experts aren’t expecting Apple’s smart glasses this year. Gurman says we shouldn’t expect them until late 2027, because Apple has experienced “bumps” during development.

Gurman also says that outgoing CEO Tim Cook is a big fan of the smart glasses project and that it’s a major part of Apple’s product roadmap. The smart glasses are rumored to be led by Cook’s successor, John Ternus.

They want a cheaper iPhone, but that’s wishful thinking

If there’s one thing CNET readers could change about the iPhone, it’s the price — 16% want a lower sticker price. Currently, the iPhone 17 Pro Max starts at $1,199. The iPhone 17E, the budget-friendly model, costs half as much — $599.

The hope for better pricing is wishful thinking, since Apple raised prices on many of its products in June, including MacBooks and iPads. Many brands, including Apple and Samsung, are increasing tech prices due to a RAM shortage and rising demand for memory chips used in most personal devices. You may be able to save money by buying a refurbished iPhone, but demand for gently used smartphones is also increasing as new phones get more expensive. So you can expect higher prices for the foreseeable future.

The other most requested change to the iPhone? A bigger battery or faster charging. Even though phone batteries are now more powerful than ever, 14% of readers who entered our contest want more juice in their iPhones.
